Abstract: Accurate geometric documentation of cultural heritage artifacts demands metrologically robust frameworks capable of quantifying measurement uncertainty across heterogeneous acquisition systems. This study proposes an integrated Digital Twin methodology for archaeological documentation, grounded in the Guide to the expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (GUM) and compliant with ISO 25178–600:2019 and EN 15757:2010 standards. The measurement framework integrates three complementary acquisition technologies: Structured Light 3D Scanners (SLS), Close-range Photogrammetry (SfM), and Smartphone-based LiDAR systems processed using SLAM algorithms (they process real-time depth measurements from smartphone LiDAR sensors), achieving sub-millimeter inter-system agreement (σ=0.57-0.80mm) validated through Cloud-to-Cloud comparison. The Combined expanded uncertainty 3 = ±2.62 (k = 2, 95% CI), is acceptable for heritage documentation. Metrological contributions include: (i) Uncertainty quantification for axial symmetry detection via Monte Carlo simulation (n=10,000), yielding positional uncertainties of ±3.2mm; (ii) Geometric quality assessment protocols achieving reconstruction precision (±2-4mm) below manufacturing tolerances of medieval ceramics (±6-8mm); and (iii) Environmental monitoring with calibrated sensors meeting EN 15757 requirements (T:±0.2°C,RH:±2%). Structural validation via finite element analysis confirmed mechanical stability with a high safety margin, while spectroscopic measurements exhibited reproducibility suitable for reliable material classification. Overall, the proposed Digital Twin framework enables the transformation of archaeological artifacts into traceable cyber-physical representations with quantified confidence intervals, advancing the role of measurement science in cultural heritage documentation and conservation. © 2026 The Author(s)

Abstract: Indoor floorplan reconstruction from 3D point clouds is a fundamental task for digital twin and architectural modeling. However, fully supervised approaches heavily rely on exhaustive polygon-level annotations, which are notoriously time-consuming and labor-intensive to acquire. To address this bottleneck, we propose SyneFloor, a weakly supervised framework that achieves accurate floorplan reconstruction under extreme label scarcity. First, to overcome the structural degradation caused by sparse supervision, we extract robust instance-aware structural priors by leveraging the zero-shot segmentation capabilities of vision foundation models (e.g., SAM3). We then propose an Adaptive Mask-Query Synergistic Fusion (AMQSF) module to dynamically fuse these explicit geometric priors into Transformer queries. Second, to maximize the data efficiency of the limited annotation budget, we design a stage-wise, multi-criteria active learning strategy. By comprehensively evaluating predictive uncertainty and architectural complexity, the model actively selects the most informative and challenging scenes for annotation. Third, to fully exploit the remaining unannotated data, we introduce a topology-aware pseudo-label generation mechanism within a dual-network collaborative framework. By explicitly detecting and resolving topological conflicts, this mechanism produces high-quality, structurally valid pseudo-labels, which fundamentally guarantees the robustness of the semi-supervised learning process. Extensive experiments on the synthetic Structured3D and real-world SceneCAD datasets demonstrate the superiority of SyneFloor. It not only exhibits robustness by consistently outperforming current state-of-the-art methods under extreme label scarcity (1% to 10% budgets), but also matches or surpasses several 100% fully supervised methods with much less labeled expenditure (e.g. utilizing only 40% of labels). This dual capability thereby establishes a highly scalable and annotation-efficient paradigm for automated indoor floorplan reconstruction in practical applications. © 2026 International Society for Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing, Inc. Title: A Digital Twin Framework for Proactive Enterprise Management: Research on Operational Decision-making Integrating IoT Data and Computational Modeling
Affiliations: School of Management, Zhengzhou Business University, China
Authors with affiliations: Liu H., School of Management, Zhengzhou Business University, China
Abstract: Digital twin technology provides a powerful computational approach for representing and controlling complex enterprise systems by continuously integrating real-time sensing with dynamic modeling and predictive analytics. The main aim of this study is to develop and demonstrate a reproducible protocol for constructing an IoT-enabled digital twin that enables proactive, data-driven enterprise management. The methodology integrates nonlinear dynamic modeling, observer-based state estimation, uncertainty propagation, risk quantification, and stochastic model predictive control into a unified cyber-physical decision framework. Simulated sensor measurements are assimilated by a state estimator to synchronize the digital twin with the modeled enterprise system, enabling simulation-based prediction of future operational states within a defined computational environment. Uncertainty and risk measures are propagated through the dynamic model to identify emerging instabilities before they escalate into critical failures. A predictive control layer then optimizes multi-objective performance by generating control actions intended to reduce operational risk, stabilize system behavior, and evaluate potential long-term operational efficiency improvements within the simulated scenario. Representative results obtained from a simplified production–inventory–energy simulation model demonstrate the potential advantages of the digital-twin-driven method compared with conventional reactive strategies. The computational example shows smoother operational trajectories, lower cumulative risk, reduced uncertainty, and improved control efficiency across several evaluated performance dimensions. However, these findings are based on a defined simulation workflow and should be interpreted as a proof-of-concept demonstration rather than direct evidence of universal real-world performance. Although the protocol is computational, platform-independent, and potentially adaptable to enterprise domains such as manufacturing, logistics, supply-chain operations, and energy-intensive systems, broader deployment in practical industrial environments would require additional validation using real operational datasets and large-scale implementation studies. By following this procedure, researchers and practitioners can reproduce and further evaluate a scalable, data-driven, and risk-aware digital twin framework for enterprise decision-support applications. © 2026, Journal of Visualized Experiments Journal of Visualized Experiments.

Abstract: The accelerated transition toward renewable energy, sustainable infrastructure, and circular economies is driving adoption of advanced materials, including bio-based composites, recycled polymers, nanostructured coatings, and hydrogen-resistant alloys. While critical for net-zero goals, these materials often exhibit heterogeneous architectures, interface-controlled transport, and evolving degradation pathways that complicate reliability, safety, and certifiable long-term performance. Conventional micro- and nano-scale characterization provides indispensable mechanistic insight but frequently relies on destructive sampling and limited coverage, restricting applicability to in-service assets. Nondestructive testing (NDT) therefore provides a complementary life-cycle evidence layer for characterization, monitoring, and qualification under realistic operating conditions. Advances in ultrasonics, eddy currents, infrared thermography, X-ray computed tomography, and optical-fiber sensing enable in situ and real-time assessment across composites, metals, and multifunctional coatings. Combined with artificial intelligence, multimodal sensor fusion, and digital-twin frameworks, NDT is moving beyond diagnostic defect detection toward predictive state estimation that informs design, manufacturing control, maintenance planning, and circular reuse decisions. This Review synthesizes progress across sustainable composites, battery and hydrogen storage systems, smart and self-healing polymers, and nanomaterial-enabled coatings, and distills evidence requirements for credibility at scale, including calibration transfer, robustness to variability and environmental drift, and uncertainty-aware reporting for reuse certification. We also address the sustainability paradox of inspection by highlighting evidence-efficient workflows that balance confidence against energy, resource, and computational costs. Finally, we outline a roadmap toward Inspection Science as a foundational pillar that aligns materials innovation with scalable, decision-grade characterization across full life cycles. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Reliability-aware vibration measurement framework for predictive maintenance of rotating machinery: Probability of detection, uncertainty-quantified remaining useful life, and simulator-based hardware-in-the-loop reliability evaluation
Source title: Measurement: Journal of the International Measurement Confederation
Affiliations: Department of Electrical Engineering, Yanbu Industrial College, Yanbu, Saudi Arabia
Authors with affiliations: Sayghe A., Department of Electrical Engineering, Yanbu Industrial College, Yanbu, Saudi Arabia
Abstract: Vibration-based predictive maintenance (PdM) of rotating machinery is increasingly informed by data-driven models, yet two measurement-system limitations restrict deployment in safety-relevant industrial settings: classification accuracy on benchmark data does not characterise the conditional probability of detecting a fault at a given severity along an instrumented measurement chain, and remaining-useful-life (RUL) point estimates do not quantify the uncertainty that risk-informed scheduling requires. This paper develops a reliability-oriented measurement framework that formalises uncertainty propagation from sensor noise and bearing-geometry tolerance through to the inference outputs, and reports three metrological indicators that conventional accuracy-only evaluation does not deliver. The framework combines (i) a Wasserstein conditional GAN with gradient penalty (WCGAN-GP), conditioned on fault label and operating regime, whose synthetic vibration signals are screened by a narrowband signal-to-noise physics-consistency score derived from bearing characteristic frequencies; (ii) a hybrid digital shadow at the edge that fuses a lumped-parameter bearing model with an LSTM-autoencoder anomaly score through a Kalman filter, with Monte Carlo Dropout (pd=0.10, M=100 stochastic forward passes) providing calibrated predictive intervals on RUL; and (iii) a severity-stratified probability-of-detection (PoD) protocol implemented on a simulator-based hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testbed with controlled fault injection (n=300 trials per fault × severity cell). The framework is evaluated on CWRU for imbalanced bearing-fault classification (with bearing-wise cross-validation to prevent window-overlap leakage), on the four C-MAPSS sub-datasets for RUL uncertainty calibration, and on the simulator-based HIL testbed for severity-resolved PoD. Augmentation raises minority-class macro-F1 from 0.71±0.05 to 0.95±0.02 (p<0.001, paired Wilcoxon, five random seeds, Holm–Bonferroni-corrected); the 90% RUL prediction interval achieves empirical coverage 88.4–91.2% on FD001–FD004; HIL PoD exceeds 95% for inner-race, outer-race and ball faults at severity Level 2 and above, falling to 68–79% at incipient severity. End-to-end edge latency on NVIDIA Jetson Orin remains below 85 ms at the 95th percentile, including uncertainty quantification. The results support simulated-HIL reliability evaluation for single bearing faults under controlled severity and stress conditions; field PoD stability for naturally degraded bearings and compound faults remains future work. The contribution is positioned as a reliability-oriented vibration measurement methodology rather than as an AI classifier: uncertainty is propagated from accelerometer noise and bearing-geometry tolerance through to the reported indicators; sensor calibration is traceable under ISO/IEC 17025; severity and PoD are calibrated against the broadband noise floor estimated from a 30-minute baseline acquisition; and every reported headline figure is paired with a confidence interval. The AI components are the means by which the measurement-system indicators are produced, not the contribution itself. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Introduces programmable essential oil delivery architectures for adaptive food systems

Abstract: Background: Essential oils (EOs) have emerged as promising natural alternatives to synthetic food preservatives owing to their broad-spectrum antimicrobial, antioxidant, antifungal, and antibiofilm activities. However, their practical application in food systems remains limited by high volatility, oxidative instability, hydrophobicity, uncontrolled release behavior, and inconsistent performance within complex food matrices. Scope and approach: This review introduced a reprogramming paradigm for EO valorization through the integration of programmable delivery architectures, process intensification (PI), artificial intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled sensing, and multi-omics technologies. Unlike previous reviews that primarily address extraction, antimicrobial activity, or encapsulation independently, this work adopts a systems-level perspective that links molecular mechanisms, advanced materials, intensified processing, computational intelligence, and translational implementation within a unified framework for adaptive food preservation. Key findings and conclusions: Recent advances in nanostructured and stimuli-responsive delivery systems, including nanoemulsions, nanostructured lipid carriers, electrospun nanofibers, mesoporous nanomaterials, and biohybrid carriers, have enhanced EO stability, encapsulation efficiency, and controlled-release performance. PI technologies offer opportunities to improve extraction efficiency, sustainability, and manufacturing scalability, whereas AI, machine learning, IoT-enabled sensing, image-based food quality assessment, digital twins, and multi-omics analytics provide powerful tools for predictive optimization, real-time monitoring, and mechanistic elucidation of EO–food–microbe interactions. Nevertheless, significant challenges persist, including limited scalability, food matrix complexity, sensory constraints, fragmented datasets, poor interoperability, regulatory uncertainty, and insufficient industrial validation. This review identifies interconnected scientific, engineering, and digital bottlenecks and proposes a comprehensive gap–solution framework and strategic research roadmap. A conceptual foundation for intelligent, closed-loop EO preservation systems capable of adaptive and predictive functionality is presented. Collectively, this review advances EO research beyond conventional preservation approaches toward scalable, sustainable, and digitally integrated food preservation systems aligned with next-generation industrial and circular bioeconomy objectives. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Accounting for approximation errors using surrogate-based parameter estimation of cardiac mechanics digital twins
Source title: Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine

Abstract: Background and Objective: Parameter estimation for complex physics-based cardiac models is computationally demanding. Surrogate models can be used to speed up model evaluations and improve the feasibility of estimation and uncertainty quantification. However, the use of surrogates introduces additional sources of error that, if neglected, can cause bias or overconfidence in inferences. Here, we present a general approach to account for such model errors when carrying out surrogate-based parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification. Methods: We use the Bayesian approximation error approach to develop a general framework that systematically accounts for modelling errors and uncertainties induced from the use of a surrogate model. We detail and implement this approach for the task of estimating cardiac stiffness from in-silico 3D left ventricle passive deformation data. We use a finite element model of cardiac mechanics with a neural network-based surrogate, and compare the results with those obtained from a simple regression approach. Results: We show that, despite the sophistication of the neural network, neglecting model errors in the estimation stage leads to biased and overconfident estimates. We demonstrate that our proposed framework allows for simple model-error corrections that provide substantially better inferences. We also demonstrate that our approach can decrease the required number of forward simulations and computational cost for training a neural network by augmenting a low-complexity neural network with a Bayesian approximation error model. Conclusions: We have developed a framework for augmenting surrogate models that improves inference and decreases training time. This has potential for use in the clinical estimation of cardiac stiffness as a biomarker of disease, where efficiency is required at the point of care. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier B.V.

Title: Automated and robust system discovery in power systems assets using physics-informed machine learning
Affiliations: Hitachi Energy Research, Montreal, Canada; Hitachi Energy Research, Baden-Dätwil, Switzerland; Hitachi Energy Research, Västerås, Sweden
Authors with affiliations: Chakravorty J., Hitachi Energy Research, Montreal, Canada; Ripamonti N., Hitachi Energy Research, Baden-Dätwil, Switzerland; Laneryd T., Hitachi Energy Research, Västerås, Sweden
Abstract: System discovery, such as parameter estimation or model reconstruction, in complex power system assets can play crucial roles in condition monitoring, troubleshooting and root cause analysis. However, robust system discovery in presence of noisy or sparse data is a challenging problem that requires solving an inverse problem and quantifying uncertainties. In this paper we address this problem and propose an approach to find the solution by using Physics-Informed Machine Learning approach for modeling cause and effect in power systems assets with polynomial dynamics. In a probabilistic setting we establish the merits of the proposed approach using empirical results. In particular, we benchmark our proposed end-to-end method with a baseline that uses Bayesian Neural Network with dropout and show that our approach outperforms baseline by 79% of reduction of validation error, 34% reduction of training time and 97.5% reduction of inference time. © 2026

Abstract: Abstract – Peripheral nerve injuries impose a substantial strain on the lives of millions of people worldwide. Engineered neural tissues provide a promising avenue to improve peripheral nerve repair strategies, potentially allowing the precise seeding of cells and materials that support regenerative processes. Current optimization of cell-seeding strategies relies on testing the impact of relevant parameters in vivo, requiring considerable time and resources. We propose an alternative approach to the design of cellular hydrogels based on a mathematical cell–solute model, informed via in vitro experiment, to identify promising cell-seeding strategies in silico at a limited cost. These designs are manufactured using 3D-printed moulds and validated in vivo. We evaluate the regenerative potential of these designs by focusing on the impact of different cell-seeding strategies on vascular endothelial growth factor secretion and gradient generation, both crucial elements of regenerative angiogenesis in early nerve repair. In this way, we provide a first proof-of-concept of a digital twin for nerve tissue engineering, which uses in silico, in vitro and in vivo repair models. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Agentic Control Towers: Multi Agent LLM RL Orchestration for Autonomous and Resilient Supply Chains
Source title: Accelerating Logistics Through Generative AI, Digital Twins, and Autonomous Operations
Affiliations: University of Bisha, Saudi Arabia
Authors with affiliations: Awad A., University of Bisha, Saudi Arabia; Alahmari D., University of Bisha, Saudi Arabia
Abstract: Supply chains exist today under chronic volatility, uncertainty, complexity, and ambiguity. Batch based planning and decision rights fragmentation render companies sluggish to detect disruption and costly to rebound. This paper develops an integrated concept—Agentic Control Towers (ACTs)which combines large language model (LLM) agents, multi agent reinforcement learning (MARL), and digital supply chain twins to provide closed loop, explainable autonomy for plan, source, make, move, and serve. We integrate findings across inventory and logistics reinforcement learning, LLM tooling and multiagent coordination, digital twin orchestration, and resilient operations. We position ACTs as a decision fabric that continuously senses, simulates, negotiates, and performs while placing guardrails for safety, sustainability, cost, and service. The paper provides an integrated architecture, end to end decision flows, stability and governance design decisions, and evidence informed pathways of impact. We also establish evaluation criteria. Title: Development of a digital twin for monitoring the autonomy of intelligent and connected electric vehicles
Source title: Proceedings - 2026 Brazilian Conference on Robotics, CROS 2026
Affiliations: Universidade Federal de Lavras (UFLA), Departamento de Automática (DAT), Brazil
Authors with affiliations: Do Carmo M.L., Universidade Federal de Lavras (UFLA), Departamento de Automática (DAT), Brazil; De Lima D.A., Universidade Federal de Lavras (UFLA), Departamento de Automática (DAT), Brazil; E Silva F.O., Universidade Federal de Lavras (UFLA), Departamento de Automática (DAT), Brazil
Abstract: The accurate estimation of the energy consumption of an Electric Vehicle (EV) under variable conditions, such as topography, traffic, and road characteristics, is essential for predicting range, planning trips, and ensuring operational safety. However, the uncertainty associated with the real battery behavior remains one of the major concerns for EV users, motivating the development of tools capable of representing and anticipating this consumption more reliably. In this context, this work proposes a Digital Twin (DT) architecture dedicated to energy monitoring and decision-support for Intelligent and Connected EVs (ICEVs). The system integrates the SUMO (Simulation of Urban MObility) traffic simulator with an external energy model, employing the A∗ algorithm for initial route planning, in which the selected route corresponds to the one with the lowest estimated energy consumption. Elevation data obtained through the Google Elevation Application Programming Interface (API) are also incorporated into the route topology to compute road gradients and their impact on energy consumption. The validation considers data from a simulated EV, where the DT continuously compares the estimated consumption with the observed one during the simulation, identifying deviations greater than 15% and applying autonomous decision rules based on critical (20%) and safety (10%) battery levels. When necessary, the system performs dynamic route re-planning or redirects the vehicle to a charging point. The results demonstrate that the DT identifies consumption anomalies, adapts to operational variations, and guarantee a safe autonomy margin for the vehicle. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: Transitioning to resilient, renewable, and EV-integrated power systems demands computational frameworks capable of handling high uncertainty, distributed decision-making, and large-scale dynamics. Classical AI and optimisation struggle with high-dimensional interactions among generators, storage, EV fleets, and real-time grid states. This paper proposes a quantum-AI smart grid architecture combining quantum machine learning, quantum-inspired combinatorial optimisation, and hybrid quantum-classical control. Grid states are encoded in variational quantum circuits and Quadratic unconstrained binary optimisation models, accelerating dispatch, scheduling, congestion management, and optimal power flow. A layered design integrates edge-level classical controllers with cloud-based quantum solvers for utility-compatible deployment. Evaluations on a high-fidelity quantum-assisted digital twin of a renewable- and EV-rich IEEE 14-bus network show 40-60% faster optimisation, improved stability, and enhanced solution robustness over classical baselines, demonstrating quantum-AI as a transformative enabler for next-generation power systems.  © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Scan-to-engineering: From reality capture to digital models in civil engineering

Abstract: Reality capture technologies, including terrestrial laser scanning, mobile laser scanning, and UAV-based sensing, offer non-contact means to document civil infrastructure. The ultimate goal of Scan-to-Engineering is to convert dense point clouds into engineering-usable models for measurement, information management, simulation, and decision support. Drawing on 123 core studies, this review examines recent advances in acquisition, point cloud processing, model generation, and downstream applications across civil infrastructure. The reviewed work is organized into three task-specific outputs: Scan-to-Geometry, Scan-to-BIM, and Scan-to-FEM. Engineering Model Readiness Levels and Validation Maturity are used to relate model content to evidence strength. Current studies show substantial progress in geometry-ready, information-ready, and selected analysis-ready workflows, but decision-ready applications remain limited. The review concludes by identifying challenges in observability, automation, uncertainty traceability, interoperability, and updatable digital twins. © 2026 Published by Elsevier B.V.

Abstract: The rapid growth of renewable generation and electric mobility introduces substantial uncertainty into modern power systems, requiring demand-response (DR) strategies that are both intelligent and physically reliable. This paper proposes DR-DL, a unified deep learning and digital-twin architecture for real-time, adaptive DR in smart grids. Using a high-resolution 100,000-sample operational dataset capturing consumer load, coordinated EV charging, solar/wind profiles, and time-varying prices, DR-DL combines multi-horizon probabilistic forecasting (Temporal Fusion Transformers) with a deep reinforcement learning controller to achieve peak-load mitigation, cost-effective load shifting, and constraint-aware EV charging. A physics-informed digital twin operates in parallel to synchronise grid states, validate control actions, and assess robustness under disturbances. Results show that DR-DL reduces the peak-to-average ratio by up to 27%, increases renewable utilization, and eliminates violations of voltage and operational constraints. DR-DL also exhibits faster, more stable convergence during learning than conventional deep reinforcement learning baselines, yielding sustained cost savings and improved resilience to abrupt load and generation fluctuations. These results demonstrate a scalable, grid-aware DR solution suitable for practical deployment.  © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: The realization of resilient autonomous systems is currently impeded by the difficulty of translating abstract design requirements into verifiable control policies that can withstand significant model uncertainty. Here we present the Agentic Control Framework, a full-stack neuro-symbolic architecture that unifies semantic reasoning with game-theoretic hardening to maximize robustness. The workflow initiates with a Large Language Model (LLM)-based agent that leverages a domainspecific Knowledge Graph to comprehend unstructured design specifications and retrieve optimal control constraints. These formal specifications characterize a high-fidelity Digital Twin, which incorporates a Reduced Order Model (ROM) integrated via Runge-Kutta (RK4) methods. Within this adaptive environment, we solve the robust control problem as a multi-agent zero-sum differential game using Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), where a stabilizing Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) policy competes against an adversary injecting worst-case stochastic disturbances. We benchmark this adversarial formulation against classical H∞ synthesis and standard Vanilla PPO, demonstrating that the system converges to an empirical Nash Equilibrium that rivals theoretical robust control baselines. Our results indicate that grounding agentic comprehension in rigorous game-theoretic training produces self-organizing controllers that maintain operational stability under severe uncertainty, bridging the gap between theoretical robust control and adaptive autonomy. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Intelligent Control and System Integration of Process Equipment Based on Deep Reinforcement Learning

Authors with affiliations: Liu X., Hefei University of Technology, AnHui, 242000, China
Abstract: Industrial process equipment is characterized by strong nonlinearity, multivariable coupling, and dynamic uncertainty, posing significant challenges to traditional control methods. To address these issues, this paper proposes an intelligent control and system integration framework based on deep reinforcement learning. A Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) algorithm is adopted and enhanced with safety-constrained reward design to ensure reliable operation under industrial constraints. Additionally, an LSTM-based state encoder is incorporated to capture temporal dependencies and improve control performance in dynamic environments. A digital twin-assisted hybrid learning strategy is further introduced to enable safe and efficient training. The proposed framework integrates control, optimization, and fault diagnosis into a unified closed-loop architecture. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms conventional PID, MPC, and baseline DRL methods in terms of tracking accuracy, energy efficiency, and safety. These findings highlight its potential for practical industrial applications. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: Background: Advances in the theory and methods of computational oncology have enabled accurate characterization and prediction of tumor growth and treatment response on a patient-specific basis. This capability can be integrated into a digital twin framework in which bi-directional data-flow between the physical tumor and the digital tumor facilitate dynamic model re-calibration, uncertainty quantification, and clinical decision-support via recommendation of optimal therapeutic interventions. However, many digital twin frameworks rely on bespoke implementations tailored to each disease site, modeling choice, and algorithmic implementation. Results: We present TumorTwin, a modular and differentiable software framework for initializing, updating, and leveraging patient-specific cancer tumor digital twins. TumorTwin is publicly available as a Python package, with associated documentation, datasets, and tutorials. Novel contributions include the development of a patient-data structure adaptable to different disease sites, a modular architecture to enable the composition of different data, model, solver, and optimization objects, and CPU or GPU parallelized implementations of forward model solves and gradient computations. We demonstrate the functionality of TumorTwin via an in silico dataset of high-grade glioma growth and response to radiation therapy. Conclusion: The TumorTwin framework enables rapid prototyping and testing of image-guided oncology digital twins. This allows researchers to systematically investigate different models, algorithms, disease sites, or treatment decisions while leveraging robust numerical and computational infrastructure. © The Author(s) 2026.

Abstract: This study outlines the development and testing of a Digital Twin Ocean (DTO) framework, aimed at improving coastal ocean forecasts through the use of autonomous underwater gliders. A fleet of gliders were deployed in the western English Channel during August-September 2024 to collect measurements of temperature, salinity, chlorophyll and oxygen, aiming to track the movement of the harmful algal bloom Karenia mikimotoi. Measurements were assimilated into a very high resolution (1.5 km) numerical forecast model, with an implementation of biogeochemistry data assimilation for this purpose. The model forecast was then used by a probabilistic uncertainty model to plan a series of waypoints to navigate the glider fleet towards features of interest. By utilising a continuous feedback loop of measurement, prediction, guidance, and refinement a system with real time coupling between the real ocean environment and its digital counterpart has been established. Building upon a prior pilot study of, this work improves every element of the system to address several limitations of the prior configuration. Whilst a bloom was present in the wider area, measurements and modeling suggest it didn't enter the glider operation zone. Despite this and other operational challenges the mission clearly demonstrates the benefits of such a system. The ability to simultaneously track multiple features of interest, namely chlorophyll maxima and oxygen minima, would not have been possible with a single glider resulting in significant benefits to the system. Furthermore, the improvement to biogeochemical forecasting has been demonstrated through a series of post mission experiments, highlighting the advantages of high temporal resolution observations and increased spatial resolution of the model. © 2026 Dale Partridge et al.

Title: One Health Cyber-Biotechnology for Nano-Plastic Intelligence Systems and Logic Integration: From Exposure to System-Level Interpretation
Source title: One Health Approaches to Nanoplastics Contamination: Biotechnological and AI Solutions
Affiliations: Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology Research Institute (GEBRI), City of Scientific Research and Technological Applications (SRTA-City), Alexandria, Egypt

Abstract: This chapter per the authors develops a One Health cyber-biotechnology framework for interpreting nanoplastic exposure as a multiscale environmentalsignaling system rather than an isolated contaminant phenomenon. It integrates digital nanoplastic science (DNPS), plasto-signaling interference (PSI), transductive signalload (TSL), Polybiome Interfacial Signaling Cascade (PISC), and systemic risk scoring (SRS) to structure exposure propagation, interface-level perturbation, and biological signaling disruption within a unified analytical architecture. Environmental matrices including water, soil, and air are conceptualized as dynamic signal-generating interfaces transmitting disturbances across interconnected ecological and physiological networks under uncertainty regimes. The chapter critiques conventional compartment-based risk assessment and advances multiomics integration, digital twin modeling, and cyber-biotechnological analytics for early-warning systems, exposure intelligence, and One Health–driven environmental decision support. Abstract: Accurate prediction of battery degradation, aging trajectories, and lifetime is critical for electrochemical energy storage systems, with direct implications for safety, reliability, and lifecycle cost. Although artificial intelligence (AI)–based approaches have shown strong short-term performance in state-of-health and remaining useful life estimation, many remain data-driven and show limited robustness under long-term cycling, operating-regime shifts, and extrapolation beyond training data. Physics-based degradation models provide mechanistic insight, but face challenges related to computational cost, parameter uncertainty, and scalability. This review positions physics-informed artificial intelligence (PIAI) as an integrative modeling paradigm that can improve data efficiency, physical consistency, uncertainty awareness, and decision reliability when appropriately constrained and validated. Unlike reviews that examine AI algorithms, degradation mechanisms, hybrid models, digital twins, or uncertainty-aware prognostics separately, this work provides a unified multiscale synthesis linking degradation physics, PIAI model construction, uncertainty quantification, structured validation, and BMS/digital-twin deployment. We examine how physical laws, degradation constraints, and uncertainty representations are embedded into learning architectures and analyze failure modes of black-box and poorly constrained hybrid models. The review proposes a five-layer framework for trustworthy battery lifetime prediction and identifies directions for physically credible, uncertainty-aware, and deployment-ready battery intelligence. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: AI for Science in Next-Gen Power Systems: A Perspective

Abstract: In this perspective, we present a concise, visionary abstract that highlights the challenge of ever-increasing complexity in future power grids and our proposed artificial intelligence for science (AI4S) framework. Next-generation grids, with high levels of renewables and distributed generation, create unprecedented uncertainty that strains traditional control and forecasting methods. Our AI4S framework integrates cutting-edge artificial intelligence (AI), including large language models (LLMs), physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), deep reinforcement learning (DRL), and autonomous multi-agent systems, within a domain-aware architecture that embeds grid physics, operational constraints, and human oversight into learning. By fusing data-driven models with power-system laws, AI4S yields trustworthy, explainable AI that enables fast, real-time decision making and richer situational awareness via digital twins and advanced forecasting. We distinguish which AI4S elements are already demonstrated versus conceptual, and we envision benefits like accelerated simulation, improved resilience, and greater operator trust. © 2026 THE AUTHORS. Title: Progress Towards Digital Twin Integration for Online Battery Health Estimation in the SWIFT-UAV Platform
Affiliations: Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of South Carolina, Columbia, 29208, SC, United States
Authors with affiliations: Garcia-Sandoval M.E., Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of South Carolina, Columbia, 29208, SC, United States; Adebajo K.O., Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of South Carolina, Columbia, 29208, SC, United States; Burnett M., Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of South Carolina, Columbia, 29208, SC, United States; Allibada V., Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of South Carolina, Columbia, 29208, SC, United States; Downey A.R.J., Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of South Carolina, Columbia, 29208, SC, United States
Abstract: Effective digital twin integration is increasingly critical for the optimal operation of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) as missions demand greater autonomy, endurance, and reliability. Traditional UAV battery health monitoring and control strategies rely primarily on onboard sensors, static voltage thresholds, conservative safety margins, and post-flight analysis. While these battery monitoring approaches provide baseline protection, they often result in overly conservative mission planning or reactive warnings that occur too late to prevent degradation or failure. Conventional monitoring methods frequently lack predictive capability, limiting their ability to provide actionable insight during dynamic flight conditions. To address these challenges, this work presents the development and ground-based validation of a propulsion subsystem digital twin integrated within the SWIFT-UAV (Scientific Workhorse for In-Flight Field Tests), a modular 3D printed UAV platform initially developed at the University of South Carolina. SWIFT-UAV’s open architecture, high payload capacity, and compatibility with advanced autonomy make it an ideal testbed for digital twin implementation. Rather than immediate in-flight deployment, the digital twin framework is evaluated using a propulsion iron-bird configuration that isolates the electrical power subsystem from aerodynamic and flight control uncertainties. Abstract: Accurate prediction of emergency material demand after earthquakes is essential for effective disaster response following earthquakes is vital to disaster preparedness and relief activities; however, such forecasting can be difficult owing to lack of data, dynamic environment, and high uncertainties involved. Conventional models which depend on past experiences, along with static machine learning techniques, cannot adapt to changing situations and lack causal relationships. In this work, a new method called Causal Digital Twin-Driven Emergency Material Demand Prediction (CDT-EMDP) has been developed that incorporates causal reasoning, digital twin simulations, agent-based analysis, and Bayesian modeling to address the challenge. CDT-EMDP builds a causal graph showing the relationship between seismogenic intensity, damage, and human displacement. The simulation of a disaster scenario is conducted via digital twin, and the agent-based simulation predicts emergency material demands in an adaptive manner. Real-time feedback is used to refine predictions according to newly acquired data. The experiments conducted on the proposed method using simulated earthquake scenarios reveal that the model performs with an accuracy of 92.8%, outperforming traditional methods. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: The fidelity of a digital twin is maintained by continuously updating the models embedded in its virtual entity with real-time sensor data. Conditional invertible neural networks (cINNs) offer a promising data-driven approach for likelihood-free model updating. However, they struggle to capture strong couplings among model parameters and often fail to effectively use suboptimal or limited sensor measurements. Additionally, epistemic uncertainty cannot be rigorously quantified in standard cINNs. To address these issues, an invertible attention-enhanced cINN (IA-cINN) is proposed. A novel invertible attention layer is integrated into the architecture. This layer explicitly models intrinsic correlations among model parameters and cross-dependencies between parameters and measurements through self- and cross-attention mechanisms while rigorously preserving invertibility. Monte Carlo dropout is incorporated into the IA-cINN to quantify epistemic uncertainty. The method was validated on two engineering cases. In a simulated case of a material handling device, three material parameters of structural components were updated using only strain and deformation measurements. In an experimental bearing case, contact stiffness, defect length, and radial clearance were updated using vibration features. In both cases, the IA-cINN outperformed the conventional cINN, as well as a Bayesian updating method based on Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. The IA-cINN achieved significantly higher updating accuracy, especially for parameters that exhibited complex coupling relationships with others. It produced more reliable uncertainty intervals in both cases, as indicated by lower interval scores. These intervals were shown to be sensitive to key sources of epistemic uncertainty, including data scarcity and insufficient model learning. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Closed-loop intelligent quality control for robotic welding: A survey on architecture, technologies, and system integration

Authors with affiliations: Qiu C., School of Automation, Nanjing University of Science and Technology, Nanjing, China; Zhou W., School of Automation, Nanjing University of Science and Technology, Nanjing, China; Yang L., School of Automation, Nanjing University of Science and Technology, Nanjing, China; Peng Y., School of Materials Science and Engineering, Nanjing University of Science and Technology, Nanjing, China; Wang K., School of Materials Science and Engineering, Nanjing University of Science and Technology, Nanjing, China
Abstract: Weld quality formation involves strong multi-physics coupling under multiple sources of uncertainty. The conventional open-loop paradigm—pre-set parameters followed by post-weld inspection—therefore cannot deliver timely in-process intervention. Recent advances in multi-modal sensing, deep learning, advanced control, and digital twins have made closed-loop quality control technically feasible, yet integrating these isolated technologies into an end-to-end system remains a major challenge. Existing reviews predominantly address single functional layers and lack systematic analysis of cross-layer integration, engineering maturity, and fair evaluation protocols. We propose a unified analytical framework for robotic arc welding: a five-layer closed-loop architecture (Perception–Modeling–Decision–Execution–Assessment) coupled with three nested feedback loops (fast/medium/slow). We then review key technologies across all layers in a concept-centric manner: multi-modal sensing organized by physical observables and fusion hierarchy; physics-driven, data-driven, and hybrid modeling with trade-off analysis; hierarchical control from PID through MPC, ADRC, and reinforcement learning; and assessment covering inspection, diagnostics, and knowledge feedback. A Technology Readiness Level (TRL) assessment of over 40 technologies yields a maturity matrix with a pronounced “ends-high, middle-low” pattern. Inter-layer interface analysis exposes a critical asymmetry: the forward path from perception to execution is largely established, whereas the backward knowledge path from assessment to modeling/decision remains severely fragmented. Finally, we identify common pitfalls in method comparison and propose a two-tier comparison framework with a minimum reporting standard. We lay out a systematic roadmap for moving robotic welding from isolated single-layer demonstrations toward deployable and evolvable industrial closed-loop systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Integrating kinetic ODEs in neural networks: A physics-informed hybrid approach to reactor modeling
Affiliations: IFP Energies Nouvelles, Rond-point de l’échangeur de Solaize, BP 3, Solaize, 69360, France; Université de Lorraine, CNRS, LRGP, Nancy, F-54000, France

Abstract: Mechanistic models of catalytic reactors are robust but often fail to generalize across feedstocks and operating conditions due to incomplete kinetic representations and parameter uncertainty, while purely data-driven models lack physical consistency and require large datasets that are costly to obtain in process engineering. To address these challenges, this work proposes a physics-informed hybrid framework that integrates a kinetic ordinary differential equation (ODE) into a neural network through automatic differentiation, differential residual loss minimization, and physical boundary constraints, taking both operating conditions and feedstock descriptors as inputs. The approach is applied to industrial hydrotreating (HDT), focusing on the prediction of nitrogen slip concentration in vacuum gas oil (VGO) hydrodenitrogenation (HDN). Two methodological developments are proposed: a Delaunay-triangulation-based strategy to select the input locations at which the physical residual and boundary terms are enforced during hybrid training, and a feedstock oriented evaluation across 30 randomized splits in which entire feedstocks are withheld from training to assess extrapolation. The hybrid model consistently outperforms both the mechanistic and purely data-driven baselines, achieving lower RMSE, MAE, and temperature deviations, while trend analyses confirm stronger preservation of the underlying physical dependencies, even under extrapolation to unseen feedstocks. A systematic comparison using a simplified kinetic formulation further shows that the hybrid architecture remains effective when constrained by incomplete mechanistic knowledge, outperforming data-driven models and approaching the accuracy of the complete kinetic expression. These results highlight the robustness, flexibility, and practical relevance of physics-informed hybrid modeling for reactor systems, offering a promising pathway toward reliable and quickly developed digital twins in catalytic process engineering. © 2026 The Authors

Title: From artificial intelligence for science to autonomous chemical innovation: closing the loop in energy and chemical engineering
Affiliations: School of Chemistry and Molecular Engineering, East China Normal University, 3663 North Zhongshan Road, Shanghai, 200062, China; AI for Science Institute, 150 Chengfu Road, Beijing, 100080, China

Abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly capable of predicting chemical properties, generating candidate structures, and assisting experimental planning. Yet the rate-limiting step in energy and chemical innovation is no longer prediction alone: it is the conversion of computational proposals into reproducible experiments and deployable process decisions. In this Perspective, we argue that Artificial Intelligence for Science in chemistry is undergoing a decisive transition from model-centric performance improvement to executable, closed-loop research infrastructure. This transition involves three coupled layers. First, physically grounded models must connect molecular and materials structures with energetics, kinetics, experimental observations, and uncertainty. Second, design algorithms must operate in validation-aware workflows that link inverse design, mechanistic computation, experimentation, and process constraints. Third, autonomous laboratories require reusable agent infrastructure that integrates scientific software, instruments, analytical feedback, safety control, and human accountability. We discuss developments in molecular and catalyst design, reaction optimization, digital twins, and self-driving laboratories, and identify data provenance, physical execution, reliability benchmarking, and safety governance as central translational challenges. For energy and chemical engineering, the value of artificial intelligence will ultimately be determined not by the number of candidates it proposes, but by its ability to close the loop from hypothesis to validated technology. © The Author(s) 2026. Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into Digital Twin systems to enhance monitoring, prediction, optimization, and decision-making across industrial and infrastructure domains. However, existing research often reports AI-enabled Digital Twins within isolated application contexts, resulting in limited conceptual clarity regarding how AI methods align with the overall Digital Twin engineering workflow. This paper provides a focused conceptual synthesis of recent representative publications and organizes AI integration using a workflow-oriented analytical lens. Four dominant integration patterns are identified: AI-enhanced state estimation, hybrid data-driven modelling, reinforcement learning-based optimization, and AI-supported decision orchestration. Across domains, recurring challenges include workflow fragmentation, validation of embedded AI components, uncertainty management, interoperability, economic justification, and cybersecurity concerns. The findings highlight the need for architecture-level integration, standardized validation approaches, and governance-Aware design principles to support robust and scalable AI-enabled Digital Twins.  © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: Digital twin technology has been widely applied to the operational optimization of industrial processes, especially in process monitoring, performance prediction and fault tracing, where model accuracy directly affects application performance. However, industrial process models established from physicochemical mechanisms usually involve idealized assumptions and contain many undetermined parameters that must be calibrated using field measurements. To address the high computational cost of traditional Bayesian calibration in high-dimensional parameter spaces and its limited suitability for online rolling updates, a multiscale sequential Bayesian model parameter calibration method based on Gaussian process convolution was proposed. Within a Bayesian framework, the proposed method jointly characterized parameter uncertainty, model structural discrepancy and observation error, and the rolling correction was performed according to the deviation between model outputs and process observations. By introducing a multiscale model representation, the method enabled a flexible trade-off between calibration accuracy and computational efficiency under limited computational resources. Numerical simulation and an alumina evaporation process case study showed that the proposed method could separately represent the model output term and the systematic discrepancy term, while achieving efficient calibration with high prediction accuracy. Compared with the standard KOH method, the proposed method improved calibration efficiency by about 165, providing effective support for the high-fidelity operation of complex industrial digital twins. © 2025, CIMS. Abstract: Reliable real-time analysis of sensor data is essential for structural health monitoring (SHM) of high-value assets, where accurate prediction of the target field and uncertainty quantification are required for trustworthy decision-making. Such capabilities can help prevent structural fracture while reducing unnecessary maintenance and resource consumption. To reconstruct the target full-field from sparse sensor measurements, the high-dimensional full-field response is compressed into leading modes using principal component analysis (PCA). A Bayesian neural network (BNN) is then employed to predict these leading PCA modes from the sensor data. The parameters of the BNN are learned through pre-training followed by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) sampling, allowing reconstruction of the target full-field with uncertainty quantification. Data-inherent aleatoric uncertainty is quantified through mode-wise variances during the pre-training stage, while epistemic uncertainty is quantified during HMC sampling. The framework was validated through cyclic four-point bending tests on carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) specimens with varying crack lengths. The experimental data comprised sparse strain gauge measurements and high-dimensional strain fields. Based on these data, the framework achieved accurate strain field reconstruction (R² > 0.9) while simultaneously producing real-time uncertainty fields, remaining robust under sparse and noisy measurements. In addition, the full-field aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty estimates enable local diagnosis of whether low-confidence regions are driven by data-inherent noise or model-related limitations. Collectively, the results demonstrate that the proposed framework advances SHM toward trustworthy digital twin deployment and risk-aware structural diagnostics. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Korean Society for Precision Engineering 2026.

Title: Autonomous Multi-Agent Coordination for Dynamic Construction Project Scheduling Under Resource Constraints and Environmental Uncertainties
Affiliations: Construction Project Management, University of Portsmouth, London, United Kingdom
Authors with affiliations: Sepehri M., Construction Project Management, University of Portsmouth, London, United Kingdom
Abstract: The research proposes a new autonomous multi-agent framework that combines distributed AI algorithms and real-time construction project data to support scheduling decisions in a complex constraint environment. The framework employs a blockchain-based coordination protocol that enables reinforcement learning agents to adapt schedules and allocate resources dynamically, requiring only supervisory human oversight for exception handling. The framework was validated in a digital twin simulation environment parameterized from 47 completed construction projects using historical project data, supplemented by a prospective six-project pilot deployment to assess real-world feasibility. From the implementation, project delays have reduced by 34% and resource utilization efficiency improved by 28%. The methodology integrates stochastic modeling of weather, the supply chain, and labor into the decision-making process. Each agent specializes in domains such as materials procurement, equipment scheduling, and quality control. The architecture makes use of federated learning principles that help maintain data privacy and allow collective intelligence across project sites. The results of validation indicate major improvements in cost-performance indices and schedule variance. The framework provides real-time adaptive scheduling solutions to unexpected site challenges, addressing a critical gap in current construction management practice. Copyright © 2026 Mehran Sepehri. Abstract: Lifecycle performance of ceramic matrix composites (CMCs) in extreme environments is dictated by coupled thermo-mechanical, chemical, and environmental degradation mechanisms, which cannot be accurately predicted by single-physics models. In this review, recent advances in multiphysics phase-field (PF) modeling of CMCs are evaluated, emphasizing thermo-mechanical fracture, oxidation-assisted degradation, chemo-mechanical coupling, electro-chemo-mechanical interactions, interfacial damage, and microstructural evolution. Fundamental PF theories, including variational, interface-aware PF-CZM, and thermodynamically-consistent coupled models, are presented alongside advancements in adaptive simulations, multi-scale modeling, machine-learning acceleration, uncertainty quantification, and digital twins. It is demonstrated that multiphysics PF models effectively predict crack evolution, chemical degradation, interface debonding, oxide formation, and environmental stiffness changes in complex CMC architectures. Furthermore, 3D microstructure-resolved modeling capabilities have been enhanced by adaptive discretization, high-performance computing, and surrogate learning. However, substantial challenges remain, including oversimplified multi-species chemistry, high computational costs of fully coupled 3D simulations, parameter non-uniqueness, and inadequate experimental validation under service conditions. Moving forward, further development would require the use of scalable Multiphysics PF modeling frameworks combined with physics-informed machine learning, uncertainty-aware calibration, adaptive data assimilation, and digital twin approaches, supporting the intelligent design of resilient infrastructures operating under extreme thermo-chemo-mechanical conditions. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Digital twin stackelberg bayesian coordination of mobile storage for uncertainty-resilient renewable integration in offshore and coastal green hydrogen energy hubs
Affiliations: Energy Management Research Center, University of Mohaghegh Ardabili, Ardabil, Iran
Authors with affiliations: Shayeghi H., Energy Management Research Center, University of Mohaghegh Ardabili, Ardabil, Iran; Mohamadi B., Energy Management Research Center, University of Mohaghegh Ardabili, Ardabil, Iran; Zare P., Energy Management Research Center, University of Mohaghegh Ardabili, Ardabil, Iran
Abstract: The rapid deployment of renewable energy in offshore and coastal regions increases the need for storage systems that can manage intermittency, spatial mismatch, and grid integration constraints. Coordinated operation across offshore, coastal, and land-based energy hubs remains insufficiently developed when mobile storage logistics, green hydrogen pathways, multi-carrier coupling, and market mechanisms are considered together. This study proposes a digital twin-enabled optimization framework for mobile and hybrid storage management in offshore and coastal multi-energy communities. The architecture integrates electrical, thermal, cooling, hydrogen, and water subsystems, while offshore energy transport vessels relocate mobile storage units and support dynamic energy exchange among distributed hubs. A mixed-integer optimization model determines storage scheduling, inter-hub exchange, desalination operation, grid interaction, and market participation. A Stackelberg-Bayesian structure captures hierarchical interactions and information asymmetry among hubs, while a Wasserstein distance-based robust optimization framework handles uncertainty in renewable generation, demand, and market prices. Carbon emission trading and green certificate trading are embedded as market-based decarbonization incentives. Numerical results show that coordinated mobile storage operation improves renewable utilization and flexibility, eliminates curtailed electrical loads, and reduces operating costs by up to 21% compared with non-coordinated operation. Under environmental constraints, groundwater extraction is fully eliminated, with the cost increase partly offset by carbon and green certificate revenues. Coordinated operation increases carbon trading revenues by approximately 27% and green certificate revenues by up to 54%. These findings show that digital twin Stackelberg-Bayesian coordination of mobile storage can strengthen uncertainty-resilient renewable integration in offshore and coastal green hydrogen energy hubs. © 2026

Title: Intelligent Enterprise Financial Management using Cognitive Digital Twin-Driven Financial Optimization Framework

Abstract: In recent years, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been integrated into enterprise financial management to improve decision-making under uncertain economic environments. This management has undergone significant transformation with increasing availability of large-scale financial data and complexity of global economic settings. Existing AI technique-based Research and Development (AIT-R&D) investment management models rely on static modeling and lack adaptive decision mechanisms, which limits their ability to capture dynamic financial dependencies and uncertainty. To address these limitations, this research proposes Cognitive Digital Twin-Driven Financial Optimization (CDT-FO) framework for intelligent enterprise financial management. Initially, this framework constructed financial digital twin to represent multi-dimensional financial states with internal financial variables and external market conditions. A graph-based cognitive model captures interdependencies between financial entities, while Transformer-Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) architecture to learn temporal dynamics. Bayesian modeling is incorporated for probabilistic risk estimation, and multi-objective optimization mechanism is employed to balance profit, risk, liquidity and cost under practical constraints. Finally, Reinforcement Learning (RL)-based decision module enables adaptive and feedback-driven financial strategy execution. The proposed CDT-FO framework demonstrates improved prediction accuracy of 0.98, with improved risk-aware decision-making as well as optimization performance compared to conventional methods. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: Digital twins integrated with artificial intelligence (AI) are emerging as key enablers for realizing net-zero energy systems. AI-enhanced digital twins improve the intelligence, efficiency, resilience, and sustainability of energy infrastructures through continuous monitoring, predictive analytics, and intelligent control of modern power systems. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in AI-based digital twin applications in the energy domain, focusing on system architectures, enabling AI methodologies, practical deployments, and cybersecurity challenges. Core AI techniques, including machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, federated learning, physics-informed models, and generative AI, are analyzed for grid optimization, predictive maintenance, renewable energy integration, and carbon-aware energy management. This paper examines security and trust issues through Zero-Trust architectures and governance frameworks for protecting critical energy infrastructures. Open research challenges such as scalability, data uncertainty, interoperability, model interpretability, and regulatory compliance are discussed to highlight existing research gaps. These insights guide future research and practical deployment of intelligent energy twins. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: RhythmScheduler: Resilient TSN Scheduling under Temporal Uncertainty and Topology Churn
Affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, China; Nio, Shanghai, China; Hangzhou Dianzi University, Hangzhou, China
Authors with affiliations: Wang K., University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, China; Fu Z., University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, China; Yan Y., University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, China; Jia Y., Nio, Shanghai, China; Li W., Nio, Shanghai, China; Shen X., Hangzhou Dianzi University, Hangzhou, China; Li X.-Y., University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, China
Abstract: Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) underpins time-critical industrial systems with ultra-low-latency, deterministic communication. However, long-term observations in real factories reveal that temporal uncertainty from legacy devices (jitter and clock drift) and topology churn from reconfigurable workflows break the assumptions of existing TSN schedulers, sharply degrading their performance. Therefore, we present RhythmScheduler, a fast, scalable TSN scheduler that explicitly models jitter and drift via three components: a temporal-stochastic graph encoder capturing timing variation and topology; a dual-head Transformer decoupling offset selection from guard-band allocation; and a Bayesian meta-adaptation loop on a hybrid digital twin, achieving sub-second reconfiguration with 3-4 ms inference. Extensive experiments on both simulation and hardware-in-the-loop testbeds show that RhythmScheduler improves schedulability by 12.2%/25.9%, reduces guard-band waste by 55.6%/62.6%, and generates Gate Control Lists (GCLs) 11.2×/14.8× faster on 200-link networks compared to state-of-the-art RL/heuristics-based methods; and achieves a further 52.9% schedulability gain, 52.5% waste reduction, and 10.9× speedup on 400-link networks, where prior RL baselines fail due to resource exhaustion. By combining efficiency with robustness, RhythmScheduler bridges deterministic TSN theory and noisy shop-floor reality, removing traffic scheduling as a bottleneck to agile industrial automation. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Causal and uncertainty-aware digital-twin framework for ultra–low-noise geoscientific inertial sensors
Source title: Geoscientific Instrumentation, Methods and Data Systems
Affiliations: Istituto Nazionale di Geofisica e Vulcanologia, Osservatorio Nazionale, Rome, Italy
Authors with affiliations: D'Alessandro A., Istituto Nazionale di Geofisica e Vulcanologia, Osservatorio Nazionale, Rome, Italy
Abstract: Ultra–low-noise inertial sensors are a cornerstone of modern geoscientific instrumentation, enabling high-resolution observations across seismology, geodesy, gravimetry, and vibration isolation. Achieving and reliably predicting their performance requires a rigorous treatment of physical causality, noise propagation, and uncertainty, particularly in force-feedback architectures operating near fundamental limits. In this study, we introduce a causal and uncertainty-aware digital-twin framework for the design and metrological assessment of ultra–low-noise geoscientific inertial sensors. The proposed framework integrates mechanical dynamics, force-feedback control, transduction, and digital acquisition within a physically realisable model that explicitly enforces causality and stability constraints. Starting from a minimal equation-of-motion description, the digital twin is formulated in the frequency domain to construct causal transfer functions and a comprehensive noise-budget model. The framework enables the systematic separation of fundamental thermal noise limits from implementation-dependent noise sources, including readout, actuation, and digital acquisition effects. We introduce quantitative performance metrics based on self-noise spectra, dominant noise regimes, crossover frequencies, and nearplateau bandwidths, allowing complex spectral behaviour to be condensed into actionable design indicators. Parameter uncertainties are propagated through the digital twin to provide uncertainty-aware performance estimates and robustness diagnostics. Through a series of illustrative analyses, we demonstrate how the proposed digital twin supports informed design trade-offs, identifies performance bottlenecks, and prevents non-physical or overly optimistic sensitivity estimates arising from non-causal modelling assumptions. While focused on inertial sensors, the methodology is general and transferable to other classes of geoscientific instruments. The framework provides a transparent and extensible foundation for next-generation sensor design, virtual experimentation, and metrologically consistent performance prediction. © 2026 Antonino D'Alessandro.

Title: Dynamic Hierarchical Posterior Evolution for Bayesian Neural Network-Based Industrial Digital Twins under Non-Stationary Conditions
Source title: 2026 6th International Symposium on Computer Technology and Information Science, ISCTIS 2026
Affiliations: Henan University Of Science And Technology, Luoyang, China; Luoyang Sunrui Wanji Titanium Industry Co., Ltd., Luoyang, China; Huanghe University Of Science And Technology, Zhengzhou, China
Authors with affiliations: Li C., Henan University Of Science And Technology, Luoyang, China; Wang L., Luoyang Sunrui Wanji Titanium Industry Co., Ltd., Luoyang, China; Xu L., Luoyang Sunrui Wanji Titanium Industry Co., Ltd., Luoyang, China; Liu Y., Henan University Of Science And Technology, Luoyang, China; Kong Y., Huanghe University Of Science And Technology, Zhengzhou, China; Song X., Henan University Of Science And Technology, Luoyang, China
Abstract: Industrial digital twins must continuously ingest online data during long-term operation and revise the virtual-to-physical mapping under non-stationary factors such as operating-condition switching, equipment degradation, and observation bias. Conventional deterministic models cannot explicitly characterize predictive uncertainty, while existing Bayesian continual-learning methods still suffer from weak historical knowledge retention, limited physical-consistency constraints, and degraded uncertainty quality under drift. To address these issues, this paper proposes Dynamic Hierarchical Posterior Evolution (DHPE) for non-stationary industrial digital twins. In the representation layer, a hierarchical Gaussian-Inv-Gamma formulation with dynamic scale adjustment is introduced to maintain uncertainty health during online updating. In the evolution layer, complex posteriors are projected into Gaussian-mixture interface posteriors, and geometric Wasserstein distance is used to jointly incorporate historical posterior inheritance and physically anchored priors, thereby enabling smooth recursion under non-Gaussian conditions while preserving long-term physical consistency. A closed-loop mechanism integrating drift monitoring, state switching, and geometric feedback is further constructed to adaptively regulate inheritance strength, anchoring stiffness, and uncertainty width. Online experiments on titanium reduction furnace temperature prediction under three representative non-stationary scenarios show that DHPE delivers more stable error trajectories, more reasonable interval coverage, and more consistent probabilistic predictions, while maintaining strong posterior recovery capability and long-term robustness. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Noise-robust knowledge distillation for industrial digital twins

Abstract: Recent advances in Knowledge Distillation (KD) have highlighted the importance of decoupling target and non-target class knowledge. However, in complex scenarios such as industrial digital twins, input data is frequently corrupted by random noise due to electromagnetic interference or sensor aging. While existing fixed-weight distillation strategies perform well on clean data, they exhibit severe vulnerabilities in noisy environments: when the input image is perturbed, the teacher network's predictions for non-target classes contain substantial random fluctuations. Maintaining a high weight for these predictions forces the student network to mimic meaningless noise patterns, leading to significant performance degradation.To overcome this limitation, we propose Adaptive Noise-Aware Knowledge Distillation (ANA-KD), a parameter-free, bidirectional dynamic weight adjustment framework tailored for noisy industrial environments. First, we introduce an information entropy-based noise perception mechanism that quantifies the pollution level of the current sample by measuring the uncertainty in the teacher network's predictive probability distribution. Furthermore, we propose a "scissors-like"bidirectional adaptive weighting strategy. Upon detecting high-noise inputs, the algorithm dynamically reduces the weight β to actively filter out corrupted detailed dark knowledge, while simultaneously increasing the weight α to guide the student network to focus on robust backbone structural features. Extensive experiments across varying noise intensities and network architectures on CIFAR-100 demonstrate the effectiveness of ANA-KD. Particularly under severe noise interference, the proposed algorithm exhibits exceptional defense capabilities without introducing any additional convolutional parameters, ensuring high efficiency for edge deployment. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: Background Climate change and agricultural intensification have made light limitation a key constraint on crop light use efficiency and yield potential. Research has progressed from description to quantification, mechanistic understanding, and multiscale modeling. However, indicator systems remain fragmented, and cross-scale integration is weak. These gaps limit translation to breeding and on-farm practice. Aim of review This review integrates the multidimensional networks and key strategies of crop adaptation to light limitation. It identifies core methodological bottlenecks that hinder prediction and application. It proposes a forward-looking paradigm to support mechanistic insight, breeding for shade efficiency, and precision management under complex light environments. Key scientific concepts of review Crop adaptation to light limitation arises from coordinated networks of light signaling, metabolic regulation, and architectural optimization. Two strategic modes dominate: shade avoidance and shade tolerance. C3 and C4 species show distinct response logic due to differences in energetics, anatomy, and regulatory control. Progress is constrained by the absence of a unified, cross-scale indicator framework and by bottlenecks in model prediction and scale coupling. This review proposes an integrated systems-biology approach enabled by high-throughput phenotyping and artificial intelligence for science. The framework standardizes indicators and fuses multimodal data across scales. It further links data assimilation with physics-informed learning to build multiscale digital twins. This approach reduces indicator fragmentation, strengthens cross-scale coupling, and supports uncertainty-aware decisions and breeding targets for shade-efficient cultivars. It opens a path to quantitative prediction and actionable management of crop performance under complex light regimes. © 2026 The Author(s).

Authors: Walczak K.; Bergés M.
Author full names: Walczak, Krzysztof (60739986100); Bergés, Mario (26326769400)
Title: Exploring LLM-Powered Agents for Modeling Thermal Dynamics of Buildings
Source title: Proceedings of the 13th ACM International Conference on Systems for Energy-Efficient Buildings, Cities, and Transportation, BuildSys 2026
Affiliations: Amazon, Seattle, WA, United States; Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA, United States
Authors with affiliations: Walczak K., Amazon, Seattle, WA, United States; Bergés M., Amazon, Seattle, WA, United States, Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA, United States
Abstract: Modeling building thermal dynamics is essential for energy optimization, yet building heterogeneity and non-stationary dynamics demand per-building customization that typically requires expert intervention. Automated scientific discovery workflows powered by Large Language Models (LLM) could significantly decrease the human expertise requirements for generating custom thermal models at scale, but their performance varies considerably depending on configuration and task, raising a key question: how should we configure scientific agents for thermal dynamics modeling? To answer this, we developed ThermalForge1, a platform for experimenting with agentic approaches to hybrid neural-physics modeling of thermal dynamics. Using a year-long dataset from hundreds of U.S. residential smart thermostats, we investigate the impact of physics knowledge in prompts, constraints on neural architecture search, LLM effectiveness in determining physics-neural transition points, model stochasticity, cost-accuracy tradeoffs, and performance against benchmark methods. Our results show that agentic modeling can match or exceed state-of-the-art automated methods while offering greater flexibility and reduced expertise requirements. We found important differences in configuring the physics-neural transition point, and demonstrate how the inherent variability of LLM outputs can be transformed from uncertainty into a mechanism for robust model discovery. This work presents the first large-scale application of LLM-powered modeling agents to real-world observational data, demonstrating their viability for thermal dynamics modeling and paving the way to scalable methods that embed domain expertise within automated workflows. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).
