Title: Uncertainty-Aware Digital Twins for Industry 4.0: A Metrology-Driven Conceptual Framework with a Healthcare Robotics Case Study
Source title: Conference Proceedings - 2026 IEEE International Workshop on Metrology for Industry 4.0 and IoT, MetroInd4.0 and IoT 2026
Affiliations: DIMES University of Calabria, Rende, Italy
Authors with affiliations: Thakur D., DIMES University of Calabria, Rende, Italy; Barbuto V., DIMES University of Calabria, Rende, Italy; Savaglio C., DIMES University of Calabria, Rende, Italy; Guzzo A., DIMES University of Calabria, Rende, Italy; Fortino G., DIMES University of Calabria, Rende, Italy
Abstract: Digital twins have emerged as a key enabling technology in Industry 4.0, enabling virtual representations of physical systems that evolve in real time through data synchronization. They are widely applied to industrial robotic systems such as manipulators, collaborative robots, and automated production cells for applications including process monitoring, predictive maintenance, and control optimization. Despite their growing adoption, many existing digital twin implementations implicitly assume that sensor measurements are accurate and reliable. In practice, measurements of key variables such as position, velocity, force, and system states are affected by uncertainty arising from noise, bias, drift, and environmental disturbances, which can significantly impact the reliability of digital twin predictions. This paper proposes a metrology-driven conceptual framework for uncertainty-aware digital twins (UA-DTs), where measurement uncertainty is explicitly modeled, quantified, and propagated through the digital twin. The proposed framework integrates metrological principles such as calibration, traceability, and uncertainty evaluation with digital twin architectures to enable probabilistic state estimation and reliability-aware decision-making. Although the framework is developed in the context of Industry 4.0, its applicability is demonstrated through a healthcare robotics use case, where robotic systems operate in safety-critical environments requiring strict reliability guarantees. Healthcare robotics is considered a specialized cyber-physical application domain of Industry 4.0 technologies, where uncertainty-aware monitoring is essential for safe human-robot interaction. Simulation-based experiments demonstrate how the proposed framework enables reliable state estimation, uncertainty propagation, anomaly detection, and safety monitoring. The results highlight that explicitly modeling measurement uncertainty improves the trustworthiness of digital twin predictions and supports risk-aware operation in both industrial and healthcare robotic systems. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Computational intelligence for 6G networks: A survey of machine learning and optimization for enabling technologies and architectures
Source title: Journal of Network and Computer Applications
Affiliations: University of Pretoria, Pretoria, South Africa
Authors with affiliations: Lall S., University of Pretoria, Pretoria, South Africa; Nyathi T., University of Pretoria, Pretoria, South Africa; Pillay N., University of Pretoria, Pretoria, South Africa
Abstract: 6G wireless networks are envisioned to deliver pervasive, intelligent, and resilient connectivity across terrestrial, aerial, and space domains, supporting ultra-high data rates, sub-millisecond latency, massive device density, and tightly integrated communication, computation, and sensing. Realising this vision requires adaptive network intelligence capable of operating under uncertainty in highly dynamic environments, motivating the adoption of computational intelligence (CI), which brings together machine learning and optimisation for continual adaptation, autonomous decision-making, and robust control. Although a growing body of survey literature examines AI in 6G, most existing works focus on isolated technologies, application domains, or specific model classes, providing limited guidance on which CI methods are structurally suited to particular 6G tasks. This distinction matters because deep reinforcement learning, evolutionary algorithms, federated learning, graph neural networks, and fuzzy systems exhibit different inductive biases whose effectiveness depends on the underlying problem structure. This survey addresses this gap through a method-centric synthesis of CI across nine representative 6G enabling technologies: THz communications, reconfigurable intelligent surfaces, integrated sensing and communication, AI-native communications, extreme edge computing, zero-energy communications, space-air-ground integrated networks, semantic communications, and digital twins. For each technology, canonical tasks are identified, representative CI families are mapped to those tasks, and methodological trade-offs are analysed. The survey introduces the method–structure alignment principle as a unifying lens for CI method selection, identifies recurring conditions under which methods succeed or fail, and presents a consolidated research agenda for robust, scalable, cross-domain, and responsible CI in 6G. © 2026 The Authors. Title: Bio360: A Multimodal Framework for Health Digital Twin Modeling and Early Physiological Drift Detection
Source title: Proceedings - 2026 IEEE 14th International Conference on Healthcare Informatics, ICHI 2026
Affiliations: Clarksburg High School, Clarksburg, MD, United States; Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, United States; Nitte Meenakshi Institute of Technology, Department of Ece, Bangalore, India

Abstract: Continuous physiological monitoring through wearable devices and digital health applications has become increasingly prevalent; however, clinically meaningful interpretation of these signals remains limited due to fragmented data ecosystems, heterogeneous sampling characteristics, and reliance on isolated threshold-based alerts. This paper presents Bio360, a multimodal Health Digital Twin (HDT) framework designed to integrate wearable biosignals, health and fitness applications, nutrition and lifestyle inputs, and longitudinal clinical data into a unified, continuously evolving digital health representation. The framework emphasizes longitudinal analysis, personalized baseline-relative interpretation, and contextual multisignal convergence rather than isolated physiological measurements. Bio360 incorporates a four-pillar multimodal architecture supported by a harmonization and normalization pipeline capable of integrating heterogeneous physiological streams across wearable platforms with differing temporal resolutions, signal fidelity, and device-specific schemas. The system further introduces a Contextual Event Evaluator (CEE) that aggregates baseline-relative deviations, signal weighting, and trend persistence into a composite Event Confidence Score (ECS) for identifying potentially meaningful physiological drift. To strengthen predictive interpretation under uncertainty, the framework incorporates Bayesian probabilistic modeling that continuously updates confidence estimates as new physiological and contextual data become available. A representative cardiovascular monitoring scenario demonstrates how persistent convergence among elevated resting heart rate, reduced heart rate variability, altered sleep architecture, behavioral stress patterns, laboratory biomarkers, and family history may collectively indicate emerging physiological risk despite individually nominal measurements. Bio360 further extends beyond physiological modeling through the introduction of a Behavioral Digital Twin (BDT), which incorporates adherence, behavioral routines, and wellness engagement into the broader digital twin ecosystem. The proposed framework aims to support early physiological drift detection, simulation-driven predictive health modeling, and scalable longitudinal health intelligence for future preventive healthcare systems. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: AI for EV battery health: Statistical meta-analysis and Autonomous Intelligence Pyramid
Affiliations: Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Anil Neerukonda Institute of Technology and Sciences, Sangivalasa, Andhra Pradesh, Visakhapatnam, 531162, India
Authors with affiliations: Tanala S., Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Anil Neerukonda Institute of Technology and Sciences, Sangivalasa, Andhra Pradesh, Visakhapatnam, 531162, India; Venkatesh A., Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Anil Neerukonda Institute of Technology and Sciences, Sangivalasa, Andhra Pradesh, Visakhapatnam, 531162, India
Abstract: The transportation sector accounts for approximately 21% of global CO2 emissions (≈[jls-end-space/]8.4Gt CO2 in 2024), and the electrification of road transport is a critical lever for decarbonisation. Annual global EV battery deployment reached 1.2TWh in 2025, making accurate battery health monitoring essential for both performance and sustainability. This review, conducted via a PRISMA-based protocol over 531 peer-reviewed studies (2018–2026), provides a statistical meta-analysis of all major AI families deployed in battery management: classical machine learning, ensemble methods, deep sequential networks, hybrid CNN architectures, Transformers, Physics-Informed ML (PIML), Explainable AI (XAI), Federated Learning, and Large Battery Foundation Models. A DerSimonian–Laird random-effects meta-analysis with 95% confidence intervals and I2 heterogeneity statistics confirms that CNN–LSTM achieves a pooled RMSE of 0.47% (95% CI: 0.41%–0.53%, (Formula presented) vs EKF baseline) and Transformer architectures reach 0.42% (0.36%–0.48%, (Formula presented) ). The Foundation Model group, based on only nine studies at TRL 2–3, yields a preliminary pooled RMSE of 0.42% that is sensitivity-dependent on a single influential study; this figure should not be directly compared with the more robustly supported Transformer estimate. Critical limitations of all emerging methods are explicitly characterised. Environmental and social impacts of battery energy systems, including CO2 lifecycle analysis, are discussed. An author-proposed five-layer Autonomous Battery Intelligence Pyramid is presented as a speculative research roadmap, with a dedicated implementation pathway discussion, clearly distinguished throughout from experimentally validated findings. © 2026 The Authors. Title: Saltation-consistent event-aware digital twins for uncertainty transport in non-smooth dynamical systems
Affiliations: Sir Geoffrey Leigh Academy, Kent, Dartford, United Kingdom; Institute of Physics, London, United Kingdom
Authors with affiliations: Mosekari S., Sir Geoffrey Leigh Academy, Kent, Dartford, United Kingdom, Institute of Physics, London, United Kingdom
Abstract: Non-smooth mechanical systems challenge prediction not only because their trajectories contain impacts, frictional transitions, and unilateral constraints, but because these events reorganize state propagation, sensitivity, uncertainty, and control authority. Existing digital-twin, hybrid-systems, Bayesian-estimation, and reduced-order frameworks each address part of that difficulty, yet they are usually developed on separate mathematical layers and therefore become least reliable precisely where engineering decisions are most event-sensitive. This paper introduces an event-aware mechanics and inference architecture for non-smooth dynamical systems in which event surfaces are treated as first-class transport interfaces rather than as numerical exceptions. Starting from a high-fidelity hybrid mechanical model with unilateral contact, friction, and measure-valued impulses, we derive saltation-consistent transport laws for sensitivities and covariance, formulate forced Bayesian correction at mechanically determined event times, and establish reduced-order error bounds that isolate jump mismatch as a distinct approximation channel. The resulting framework couples full-order mechanics, event-aware uncertainty propagation, online parameter updating, and reduced-order approximation within a single mathematically consistent architecture. Benchmarks involving impact, stick–slip, and shock-response dynamics show that event-aware transport preserves post-event state accuracy, concentrates parameter information in short event windows, and improves reduced-order fidelity during discontinuity-dominated transients. The central advance is the identification of event surfaces as the structural interfaces through which mechanics, inference, uncertainty transport, and control are coupled in non-smooth digital twins. © The Author(s) 2026.

Abstract: Modern digital twins integrated with artificial intelligence (AI) provide significant opportunities for real-time financial governance of critical infrastructure. This paper presents the design and theoretical validation of an intelligent financial decision support system (FDSS) embedded within digital twin ecosystems, spanning the full lifecycle of infrastructure assets. The proposed methodology integrates AI-driven predictive models for cost estimation and failure forecasting, digital twins as continuous real-time data sources, capital and operational expenditure (CAPEX/OPEX) optimization algorithms, and risk-aware investment management strategies that account for cyber threats and systemic uncertainties. The framework introduces a Risk-Aware Financial Digital Twin (RA-FDT) architecture that synchronizes technical state parameters with financial performance indicators through a three-layer integration model encompassing data fusion, analytical intelligence, and decision orchestration. An illustrative scenario-based assessment on energy and transportation infrastructure datasets indicates that the RA-FDT may reduce lifecycle costs by approximately 12-18% under the assumed maintenance, failure-probability, and cybersecurity-risk parameters, while improving risk-adjusted return on infrastructure investment. The principal contribution lies in formalizing the coupling between physical degradation dynamics and financial decision logic within a unified computational environment, thereby advancing transparency, accountability, and effectiveness in critical infrastructure management. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: As digital twins (DTs) become foundational technologies for critical infrastructure (CI), their integration with artificial intelligence (AI) creates new opportunities and risks for financial security, financial intelligence, and governance resilience. Beyond technical and cybersecurity threats, human factors - including decision-making biases, operator trust, and organisational behaviour - significantly influence cyber-financial exposure and the economic performance of DT ecosystems. This paper proposes a human-centric and AI-augmented financial risk management (FRM) framework for secure DTs in CI. The approach integrates real-time DT data, AI-based predictive analytics, explainable decision support, and human-in-the-loop (HITL) mechanisms. It comprises four interconnected components: (1) AI-based forecasting of operational failures and financial losses; (2) behavioural modelling of decision-makers under uncertainty; (3) trust-aware and explainable AI (XAI) mechanisms; and (4) dynamic allocation of financial resources according to risk exposure and infrastructure state. Its methodological contribution is a hybrid decision architecture that links technical system conditions with financial decision-making through a trust-weighted optimisation function, formalised alongside an aggregate financial risk index (FRI) and a Markowitz-style cybersecurity-budget allocation. The framework is assessed through scenario-based simulation for energy and smart-city infrastructure, with parameters informed by open-source cybersecurity and risk-management materials (ENISA threat-landscape reports, NIST IR 8286 Rev. 1, IBM/Ponemon Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025). For the illustrative configuration considered, total expected financial losses across five representative disruption scenarios decrease from 5.82 to 2.70 million USD - a reduction of 53.6% - relative to a baseline FRM without HITL/XAI integration. The results indicate that integrating human expertise, explainable AI, and secure DT technologies can improve financial resilience, reduce disruption costs, and increase trust in AI-supported infrastructure governance. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: Slow pyrolysis is a widely investigated thermochemical pathway for biochar production and long-term biogenic carbon sequestration. This review critically assesses the evolution and recent advances in slow pyrolysis reactor technologies from 1950 through December 2025, based on publication availability, focusing on reactor design, transport phenomena, product characteristics, scalability, and commercialization barriers. Four primary reactor configurations—fixed-bed, auger, rotary-kiln, and modified fluidized-bed systems—are systematically evaluated. The analysis indicates that reactor architecture strongly influences thermal management, residence-time distribution, and product selectivity. Under appropriate feedstock characteristics and operating conditions, rotary-kiln reactors can offer favorable prospects for large-scale continuous operation due to effective solids mixing, feedstock flexibility, and heat integration, whereas auger reactors may be particularly suitable for intermediate-scale and decentralized applications under appropriate operating conditions. Fixed-bed systems can remain advantageous for small-scale production, particularly where simple reactor configurations are preferred, although they are constrained by conductive heat-transfer limitations and low throughput. Conversely, fluidized-bed reactors, despite their high heat-transfer rates, require substantial hydrodynamic modifications for biochar-oriented slow pyrolysis and careful control of operating conditions to achieve the desired product characteristics. Biochar yield is strongly influenced by operating temperature, residence time, particle dimensions, and feedstock composition, with reported yields commonly falling within the range of approximately 25 to 45 wt% (dry basis) depending on these factors. Current industrial deployment is impeded by feedstock heterogeneity, thermal non-uniformity, process control limitations, and techno-economic uncertainties. Emerging digitalization strategies, including machine learning and digital twins, show potential for predictive monitoring and optimization, though their industrial implementation requires rigorous validation under transient operational conditions. Life-cycle and techno-economic assessments indicate that slow pyrolysis can contribute to carbon dioxide removal, while emphasizing the critical need for standardized evaluation frameworks. Ultimately, future commercialization will depend on the context-specific integration of advanced reactor engineering, intelligent process control, efficient energy recovery, and robust sustainability metrics. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Integrating Data-Driven Technologies for End-to-End Supply Chain Transformation
Source title: Data-Driven Innovation in Supply Chains and Manufacturing: From Predictive Analytics to Natural Language Processing
Affiliations: Shiv Nadar University, IOE, New Delhi, India
Authors with affiliations: Shukla S.D., Shiv Nadar University, IOE, New Delhi, India
Abstract: To assist operational choices, data-driven supply chain systems are increasingly using digital twin simulations, machine learning models, statistical forecasting, and Internet of Things–based monitoring. The Fragmented Uncertainty Modeling (FUM) problem, which occurs when uncertainty is estimated locally within individual functions—like demand forecasting, logistics monitoring, or disruption detection—but is not propagated coherently across procurement, production, and fulfillment decision layers, largely plagues current approaches despite these advancements. This fragmentation makes it impossible to reason cohesively about how environmental volatility and exogenous shocks impact the stability and resilience of the entire supply chain. We propose Uncertainty-Propagating Supply Chains (UP-SC), an end-to-end data-driven paradigm that explicitly propagates uncertainty across interdependent decision layers and models supply chains as linked economic–environmental networks. Through a single architectural design, UP-SC combines exogenous climatic volatility signals with global trade dependence structures to enable resilience-oriented decision intelligence and network-aware stability estimates. The NOAA Global Surface Summary of the Day repository and the United Nations Comtrade International Trade Statistics Database are two extensive public datasets that we use to assess UP-SC. Empirical findings demonstrate that, in comparison to function-isolated baselines, explicit uncertainty propagation shortens disruption recovery times by up to 41%, increases turnover efficiency by 22%–35%, and decreases trade corridor lead-time variability by 18%–27%. © 2027 selection and editorial matter, Parth Saxena, Srinivas R. Title: Digital twins and explainable AI across the vaccine life cycle: from mRNA manufacturing to thermostability, cold-chain logistics, and immunisation services
Affiliations: Department of Research Publication and Extension, Kampala International University, Uganda
Authors with affiliations: Ugwu O.P.-C., Department of Research Publication and Extension, Kampala International University, Uganda; Okon M.B., Department of Research Publication and Extension, Kampala International University, Uganda; Ogenyi F.C., Department of Research Publication and Extension, Kampala International University, Uganda; Ugwu J.N., Department of Research Publication and Extension, Kampala International University, Uganda; Ugwu C.N., Department of Research Publication and Extension, Kampala International University, Uganda
Abstract: The COVID-19 era accelerated the deployment of mRNA vaccines while exposing persistent weaknesses in manufacturing, thermostability and cold-chain systems, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). This narrative review, informed by an explicit search of PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, IEEE Xplore and the ACM Digital Library (2019–2025), synthesises over 50 studies of digital twins (DTs) and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) across the vaccine life cycle. The evidence indicates that DTs are progressing from static simulations to operational twins for plasmid-to-mRNA production, supporting virtual commissioning, rapid scale-up and real-time optimisation. In parallel, XAI-enabled approaches improve stability prediction, and artificial intelligence of things (AIoT) architectures strengthen cold-chain monitoring and route planning. At the service level, twins of mass vaccination centres and primary-care immunisation services can improve throughput and temperature management; however, current implementations are often siloed, weakly validated and rarely designed with equity considerations. Priorities for the field include integrated, multi-scale ‘vaccine system twins’, rigorous validation, effective human-AI collaboration and deployment strategies tailored to LMIC contexts. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Abstract: Power grid digital twins (DTs) face a fundamental challenge: uniformly modeling and maintaining consistency across time scales from microsecond-level electromagnetic transients to hour-level economic dispatch. Existing multi-rate simulation techniques have not been systematically integrated into DT frameworks, and current research lacks a theoretical definition for cross-scale consistency. This paper proposes a physics-informatics cross-domain consistency-driven method. A hierarchical multi-rate simulation architecture decomposes the grid DT into Electromagnetic Transient (EMT), electromechanical Transient (RMS), and quasi-steady-state layers. A cross-scale state synchronization algorithm with error propagation suppression is developed. A novel 'Layered Age-of-Information (LAoI)' and 'Twin Bias' framework quantifies uncertainty and consistency. Theoretical analysis establishes boundedness of error propagation, asymptotic stability of the multi-scale observer, contraction of uncertainty propagation, and LAoI thresholds derived from dominant time constants. This work provides a rigorous theoretical framework for multi-time scale consistent DT modeling, including stability proofs, error bounds, and convergence guarantees. © 2026 IEEE.

Affiliations: “ItalianMeteo” National Agency, Bologna, Italy; Dipartimento di Matematica ed Informatica “Ulisse Dini”, Università di Firenze, Viale Morgagni 67/a, Firenze, 50134, Italy
Authors with affiliations: Cacciamani C., “ItalianMeteo” National Agency, Bologna, Italy; Vespri V., Dipartimento di Matematica ed Informatica “Ulisse Dini”, Università di Firenze, Viale Morgagni 67/a, Firenze, 50134, Italy
Abstract: Modern weather forecasting relies on the integration of observational systems, numerical modeling, data assimilation, high-performance computing, and increasingly artificial intelligence techniques. This paper reviews the scientific and technological foundations of contemporary weather prediction, with particular emphasis on the mathematical and computational tools that support operational forecasting. Weather prediction is based on the numerical solution of the nonlinear partial differential equations governing atmospheric dynamics. The accuracy of these forecasts critically depends on the availability of observations collected from heterogeneous sources, including ground-based networks, weather radars, satellites, aircraft, and other remote sensing platforms. These data are combined with model forecasts through advanced data assimilation techniques, which provide dynamically consistent estimates of the atmospheric state and improve forecast quality. Special attention is devoted to nowcasting, one of the most challenging areas of modern meteorology. At lead times of a few minutes to several hours, rapidly evolving phenomena such as severe thunderstorms, hailstorms, and flash floods require the integration of high-frequency observations, radar extrapolation methods, ensemble prediction techniques, and machine learning approaches. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to enhance the detection, tracking, and short-term prediction of convective systems, complementing traditional physics-based methodologies. The paper also discusses the requirements of a modern national forecasting system and presents the high-resolution ICON-2I modeling framework operational at the ItaliaMeteo Agency. Particular emphasis is placed on the role of high-performance computing infrastructures, ensemble forecasting systems, and kilometer-scale data assimilation methods. Finally, current challenges and future developments are examined, including convective-scale prediction, uncertainty quantification, exascale computing, digital twins of the atmosphere, and the growing integration of artificial intelligence with numerical weather prediction. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Next-generation electrified powertrain technologies for sustainable mobility: A systematic review of architectures, intelligent control, energy storage, and grid integration
Affiliations: Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Anil Neerukonda Institute of Technology and Sciences, Sangivalasa, Andhra Pradesh, Visakhapatnam, 531162, India
Authors with affiliations: Venkatesh A., Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Anil Neerukonda Institute of Technology and Sciences, Sangivalasa, Andhra Pradesh, Visakhapatnam, 531162, India; Tanala S., Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Anil Neerukonda Institute of Technology and Sciences, Sangivalasa, Andhra Pradesh, Visakhapatnam, 531162, India
Abstract: The global imperative to decarbonise road transport has required the automotive and energy sectors to reconceptualise vehicular powertrain engineering across all scales, from atomic-level electrochemistry to fleet-level grid interaction. This PRISMA-compliant systematic review synthesises 120 peer-reviewed publications, standards, and archival documents identified from a four-database search covering January 2018 to June 2026 (1204 records identified; 847 screened; 120 included). Four interconnected technology frontiers are examined in depth: (i) advanced vehicle architectures spanning Battery Electric Vehicles (BEVs), Hybrid Electric Vehicles (HEVs), Plug-in Hybrid Electric Vehicles (PHEVs), and Fuel Cell Electric Vehicles (FCEVs), including distributed propulsion with active torque vectoring, in-wheel motors, and grid-connected renewable-source integration; (ii) next-generation electrochemical energy storage covering solid-state, sodium-ion, and lithium–sulfur batteries alongside hybrid supercapacitor architectures, with critical appraisal of conflicting experimental findings on dendrite formation, sodium storage mechanisms, and commercialisation timelines; (iii) intelligent Energy Management Systems (EMS) spanning rule-based control, Equivalent Consumption Minimisation Strategy (ECMS), Model Predictive Control (MPC), the full spectrum of Sliding Mode Control (SMC) variants including super-twisting second-order SMC with adaptive gain laws, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), and physics-informed neural networks (PINNs); and (iv) grid-interactive infrastructure encompassing Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) systems, wireless power transfer under SAE J2954, and cloud–edge digital twin frameworks with federated learning and cybersecurity provisions. Wide-bandgap SiC and GaN power electronics and six thermal management strategies are analysed as cross-cutting enablers. All quantitative comparison figures in this review (Figs. 13–27) are illustrative reconstructions digitised from data reported in the cited primary literature; they are not independently simulated results, and no new experimental or simulation data are reported in this work. A bibliometric analysis of the 120 included studies reveals growth from 8 papers (2018) to 35 papers (2025). A four-criterion quality assessment framework grades each reviewed technology. A structured technology readiness roadmap with 2030 quantitative projections derived from learning-rate battery cost models and IEA fleet scenarios projects battery costs of $55–70/kWh, SiC penetration of 80–95% in premium BEV inverters, and V2G participation of 8–20% of the EU passenger fleet. These are scenario projections carrying explicitly stated model assumptions and uncertainty ranges, not forecasts; the accompanying sensitivity analysis (Section 12.1) identifies the learning rate and the cumulative-deployment trajectory as the dominant drivers, and a demonstrated-versus-projected classification is applied throughout to separate laboratory or pilot evidence from extrapolation. © 2026 The Authors

Abstract: We propose an integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) architecture capable of simultaneously performing distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) and distributed temperature sensing (DTS) in a single-mode fiber (SMF) and experimentally evaluate its coexistence feasibility using a discrete-component proof-of-concept setup. This system supports parallel multi-parameter sensing based on phase-sensitive optical time-domain reflectometry (ϕ-OTDR) and Raman optical time-domain reflectometry (ROTDR). The present experiment is conducted using discrete commercial components, while integrated polarization–wavelength de/multiplexing is retained only as a possible future compact implementation route. Hybrid amplification techniques, including Raman distributed amplification and optical-bias-assisted superimposed enhancement, are introduced to improve the communication link budget and ROTDR detectability under a reduced sensing-probe power. In addition, polarization-diversity reception is analyzed as a potential extension to mitigate polarization fading and improve the stability of Rayleigh-based vibration sensing. Experimental results demonstrate system-level coexistence of ϕ-OTDR-based DAS, ROTDR-based DTS, and single-polarization 2.5 Gbit/s non-return-to-zero/intensity-modulation direct-detection (NRZ/IMDD) communication over a 10 km SMF link. The simplified proof-of-concept experiment achieves a spatial resolution of 5 m, a temperature uncertainty of 2.8°C, and a vibration-sensing signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 12.1 dB under a sensing-probe peak power of 100 mW, while no bit errors are observed in the communication branch during the experimental test. Fiber-optic communication and sensing integration technology can support traditional applications such as oil and gas pipelines, power lines, and environmental monitoring, and may provide useful sensing capability for emerging scenarios such as digital twins and intelligent optical networks. © 2009-2012 Optica Publishing Group.

Abstract: The fast pace of urbanization, tightening discharge requirements, and efficient wastewater treatment require that municipal wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) move to adaptive and intelligent modes of operation. The present review provides an analysis of the application of artificial intelligence (AI) to different pre- and posttreatment steps in the context of municipal WWTPs. Specifically, this review considers how machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), evolutionary optimization, reinforcement learning, and hybrid AI–mechanistic models can be utilized in municipal wastewater processes. AI-based approaches are reviewed in the area of activated sludge processes such as dissolved oxygen control, nutrient removal, effluent quality estimation, and energy management; membrane bioreactor (MBR) processes such as membrane fouling and transmembrane pressure prediction; anaerobic digestion (AD) processes for biogas generation, stability, energy recovery, and nutrients recovery; and sludge processes such as dewatering, polymer dosage optimization, digestion, and resource recovery. Moreover, AI methods are critically evaluated in the areas of nitrogen and phosphorus removal, N2O emissions prediction, fault detection, predictive maintenance, and plant-wide optimization. Evidence is provided on the implementation of AI in full-scale municipal and WWTPs with a shift from prediction and soft sensing to optimization and supervision, including aeration control, carbon dosing, coagulant optimization, and sludge dewatering. Nevertheless, the findings heavily depend on plant layout, data quality, sensor accuracy, AI architecture, and validation scheme, and none of the AI architectures currently exist that can be deemed superior to other architectures across all applications. Digital twins, explainable AI, edge computing, and federated learning represent exciting directions for future integrated and robust WWTP management. In addition, autonomous plant-level control and AI-assisted AD-nutrient recovery have not been sufficiently developed yet. The main issues to solve are cross-plant validation, uncertainty analysis, cybersecurity, interpretability, seamless integration into existing supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA)/programmable logic controller (PLC) networks, and long-term benefits demonstration. © 2026 Wiley-VCH GmbH.

Title: Edge-Based Digital Twins for QoS-Aware Orchestration in Heterogeneous UAV Fleets

Abstract: Heterogeneous multi-UAV fleets act as highly dynamic mobile Internet of Things (IoT) nodes, but they often integrate platforms with incompatible telemetry and control semantics, hindering safe and scalable coordination. This paper presents an Asset Administration Shell (AAS)-driven digital twin architecture for the cloud continuum that decouples protocol translation from mission orchestration, pushing compute power closer to the edge. The first contribution of this work is a four-layer communication model mapped across the IoT and edge continuum, spanning physical-digital synchronization at the network edge, inter-digital-twin interaction, digitaltwin/ GCS supervision in the fog/cloud layer, and a safety-critical physical/GCS bypass. The second contribution is a UAV AAS submodel that standardizes runtime state, energy, payload, and wireless QoS descriptors. The third contribution is an analytical validation framework based on bounded digital-twin staleness (δSmax = 30 ms) to evaluate semantic task reallocation and QoS-aware telemetry adaptation. At a representative cruise speed of 15 m/s, the worst-case position uncertainty induced by semantic latency is 0.45 m, which is acceptable for highlevel mission handoff. For degraded links, stability conditions are derived for queue-bounded latest-state forwarding and hysteresis-based telemetry control. The analysis indicates that AAS enables protocol-agnostic interoperability while preserving orchestration timeliness.. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: A comprehensive review of reinforcement learning approaches in peg-in-hole insertion for robotic assembly tasks
Source title: International Journal of Intelligent Robotics and Applications

Authors with affiliations: Shoura A.A., Department of Mechatronics Engineering, Ain Shams University (ASU), Cairo, Egypt; Awad M.I., Department of Mechatronics Engineering, Ain Shams University (ASU), Cairo, Egypt; Maged S.A., Department of Mechatronics Engineering, Ain Shams University (ASU), Cairo, Egypt; Fattah D.E.A., Department of Mechatronics Engineering, Ain Shams University (ASU), Cairo, Egypt
Abstract: Robotic peg-in-hole insertion is a fundamental operation in industrial assembly; however, its automation remains challenging because of tight tolerances, variations in component geometries, contact uncertainties, and the complexity of real-world operating environments. Conventional preprogrammed robotic systems often struggle to cope with such uncertainties, motivating the adoption of reinforcement learning (RL) as a more adaptive paradigm for robotic insertion tasks. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of RL-based approaches for peg-in-hole insertion and examines their evolution from traditional reinforcement learning algorithms to modern deep reinforcement learning (DRL) frameworks. This review systematically categorizes the literature according to the learning paradigm, sensing modality, control strategy, and training environment. Key methodologies are discussed, including Q-learning, SARSA, deep reinforcement learning, model-based RL, meta-RL, transformer-based reinforcement learning, transfer learning, and domain randomization techniques. Particular attention is given to multimodal perception strategies that integrate visual, force, and tactile information, as well as hybrid learning frameworks that combine RL with imitation learning and classical control methods to improve the robustness, training efficiency, and deployment reliability. In addition, this review analyzes recent advances in sim-to-real transfer, digital twin technologies, and real-time deployment strategies that facilitate the transition of learned policies from simulations to industrial robotic systems. A comparative analysis of representative studies is presented to highlight current trends, methodological differences, and practical limitations in the literature. Despite substantial progress, several challenges continue to limit large-scale industrial adoption, including simulation-to-real transfer, sample efficiency, safety, generalization, interpretability, and deployment scalability. Finally, emerging research directions are discussed, including multimodal learning, digital twin-assisted training, hybrid control architectures, multi-agent reinforcement learning, and real-time edge deployment. By consolidating recent advances, limitations, and future opportunities, this review provides a structured reference for researchers and practitioners seeking to develop next-generation intelligent robotic assembly systems. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026.

Abstract: As satellite structures become increasingly lightweight, adaptive, and highly integrated, conventional design–simulation workflows struggle to predict dynamic responses and assess structural health under coupled and uncertain conditions. Digital twins, which integrate multi-physics modeling, reduced-order techniques, and modern data-driven approaches, provide a promising paradigm for enabling structural intelligence. This review systematically synthesizes recent advances in structural digital twins, focusing on functional architectures, modeling strategies, and validation frameworks. Representative applications—including thermal control structures, deployable mechanisms, antennas, and propulsion components—are discussed to illustrate the integration of sensing, modeling, and closed-loop control. Key challenges are identified, including heterogeneous data fusion, real-time multi-field coupling, uncertainty quantification, model calibration, and cross-subsystem coordination. Future directions are outlined, such as AI-native digital twins that incorporate physics priors with foundation-model knowledge (i.e., large pretrained AI models), on-orbit edge learning for adaptive real-time inference, federated digital twin systems for distributed knowledge sharing, and trustworthy frameworks with certifiable reliability. These developments are expected to pave the way for adaptive, reliable, and continuously evolving structural digital twins, supporting high-fidelity satellite operations across the full lifecycle. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to The Brazilian Society of Mechanical Sciences and Engineering 2026.

Title: Smart nanoparticle sensors and IoT integration for real-time monitoring of environmental quality in mining systems
Affiliations: Saveetha College of Pharmacy, Saveetha Institute of Medical and Technical Sciences, Chennai, 602105, India
Authors with affiliations: Eluri K., Saveetha College of Pharmacy, Saveetha Institute of Medical and Technical Sciences, Chennai, 602105, India; Vaganan H.M., Saveetha College of Pharmacy, Saveetha Institute of Medical and Technical Sciences, Chennai, 602105, India; Elumalai K., Saveetha College of Pharmacy, Saveetha Institute of Medical and Technical Sciences, Chennai, 602105, India
Abstract: The transition toward low-carbon energy systems, electric mobility, and digital infrastructure has intensified the global dependence on mineral extraction while simultaneously increasing the need for real-time, transparent, and predictive environmental governance in mining operations. Conventional monitoring strategies remain largely periodic, spatially limited, and reactive, making them insufficient for detecting rapidly evolving risks such as acid mine drainage, heavy metal mobilization, methane accumulation, airborne pollutants, tailings instability, and operational carbon emissions. This review aims to critically evaluate how nanoparticle-based sensors, when integrated with Internet of Things (IoT) architectures, edge computing, artificial intelligence, and digital twin systems, can transform environmental monitoring in mining from delayed compliance assessment to continuous predictive intelligence. This review synthesizes advances in metal oxide nanoparticles, carbon nanomaterials, plasmonic nanostructures, and hybrid nanocomposites, emphasizing their sensing mechanisms, target analytes, sensitivity, selectivity, matrix interference, durability, and field-deployment constraints. It further examines IoT-enabled wireless sensor networks, localized edge analytics, cloud-based predictive modelling, uncertainty-aware digital twins, and human-in-the-loop governance frameworks for translating nanoscale detection into actionable environmental decision support. Particular attention is given to technology readiness, calibration drift, ruggedization, cybersecurity, interoperability with supervisory control systems, lifecycle sustainability, nanoparticle ecotoxicity, green synthesis, and end-of-life management. The analysis indicates that nanoparticle sensors should not be viewed as replacements for certified laboratory and industrial monitoring tools but as complementary high-resolution screening platforms that can provide early warning, spatial mapping, and dynamic risk prediction. Future progress will depend on standardized validation protocols, long-term field trials, safe-by-design nanomaterials, self-powered sensing nodes, federated environmental data systems, and regulatory pathways that support credible deployment. Abstract: Modern satellite payload modules require high structural stiffness, low mass, and thermal stability under coupled thermo-mechanical environments. Conventional separation of load-bearing and thermal-control subsystems often leads to inefficient heat transfer and degraded system performance. This study proposes an integrated structural–thermal design and data-driven digital twin framework combining CFRP honeycomb sandwich panels, a TC4 titanium-alloy ring frame, and integrated heat-transfer paths. Multiphysics simulations predict an in-plane temperature gradient of 3.2K and a maximum elastic thermal deformation of 0.075mm after removal of rigid-body motion. A literature-based comparison with conventional separated configurations indicates a 60%−80% shorter heat-transfer path and a 10%−20% lower structural mass. Model credibility was assessed through mesh-sensitivity analysis and independent analytical benchmarks, with differences of 1.48% in thermal resistance and 7.16% in structural displacement. The digital twin framework supports state prediction, parameter updating, uncertainty quantification, and health assessment. For maximum-displacement prediction, Gaussian process regression achieved R2=0.9996and an RMSE of 0.0136mm, while sequential data assimilation further reduced parameter uncertainty. Using precomputed FEM databases, the platform updated three-dimensional structural–thermal fields within 1.5s, enabling near-real-time response without online full-order FEM re-solution. Overall, the proposed approach provides an efficient and scalable solution for structural–thermal co-design, near-real-time monitoring, and health management of next-generation spacecraft payload modules. © 2026 Elsevier Masson SAS.

Title: Assessing the impact of AI-enabled BIM digital twins on construction risks: a Bayesian Network of Jordanian expert beliefs
Affiliations: Faculty of Engineering, Civil Department, Jadara University, Irbid, Jordan; Faculty of Engineering Technology, Zarqa University, Zarqa, Jordan; Faculty of Engineering, Isra University, Amman, Jordan
Authors with affiliations: Albtoush F., Faculty of Engineering, Civil Department, Jadara University, Irbid, Jordan; Al-Btoosh J.A.A., Faculty of Engineering Technology, Zarqa University, Zarqa, Jordan; Rawashdeh T.M., Faculty of Engineering, Isra University, Amman, Jordan; Al-Btoush M.A.K.A., Faculty of Engineering, Isra University, Amman, Jordan
Abstract: Building projects in Jordan routinely experience substantial schedule delays and cost overruns, yet robust empirical evidence on the impacts of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Building Information Modelling (BIM)-based Digital Twins remains scarce. This study develops a belief-based, probabilistic causal model of how AI-enabled BIM Digital Twin technologies may affect time–cost risks in Jordanian reinforced-concrete building projects. Using structured expert elicitation with 600 experienced practitioners (contractors, consultants, project managers, and academics), we capture expert judgements on causal links between four technology clusters—AI-based progress detection, contract-aware BIM assistants, predictive cost–schedule twins, and AI-assisted design/constructability—and key project mechanisms and outcomes. All quantitative results in this study come from these expert judgements; no project-level before–after performance data are used. Accordingly, results are reported as pooled expert beliefs under stated scenarios, not empirically validated predictions. Hierarchical Bayesian models pool elicited probabilities into a Bayesian Network (BN) representing collective expert beliefs, rather than observed project performance. Monte Carlo simulations, Global Sensitivity Analysis (GSA), and Expected Value of Perfect Information (EVPI) are then used to explore technology-adoption and policy scenarios and to rank influential levers. Experts believe that, under idealized, high-readiness conditions, AI-enabled BIM Digital Twins could sharply reduce the probabilities of schedule delays >20% and cost overruns >10%. These figures are belief-based, optimistic upper-bound expectations derived from expert judgement, not empirically measured or validated impacts. The Bayesian Network therefore serves as an uncertainty-aware decision-support tool for early policy and investment decisions in data-poor contexts. It highlights the roles of training, organizational readiness, and client demand alongside technology adoption. Copyright © 2026 Albtoush, Al-Btoosh, Rawashdeh and Al-Btoush.

Title: Generative Digital Twin-Enabled Prognostics and Health Management: A Systematic Review of Concepts, Architectures, and Key Technologies

Abstract: Prognostics and health management (PHM) for industrial equipment is still constrained by scarce fault samples, incomplete observation of degradation processes, limited cross-condition generalization, and fragmented maintenance knowledge. Digital twins (DTs) provide a physical–virtual integration basis for PHM through state synchronization, model updating, and service feedback. However, conventional DT-enabled PHM remains limited in data supplementation, degradation inference, knowledge organization, and maintenance decision-making. The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers a new pathway for enhancing DT-enabled PHM. This review focuses on generative digital twin (GDT)-enabled PHM. It clarifies the conceptual boundaries and functional enhancement logic of GDT-enabled PHM, summarizes the roles of key GenAI models, and reviews technical progress across health data synchronization, twin data processing, virtual modeling, prognostic reasoning, and maintenance decision feedback. A cross-process perspective is introduced to trace how data, model, and reasoning errors propagate into PHM reliability risks. Representative applications in aero-engines, rotating and transmission equipment, and energy equipment are then examined with attention to their validation boundaries. Finally, the review discusses generated-data validity, physical consistency, lifecycle updating, uncertainty, and engineering deployment under Industrial Internet of Things constraints. © 2014 IEEE.

Title: A Digital Twin Model for Real-Time Electric Vehicle Energy Consumption Estimation and Validation Using Unity–Simulink Co-Simulation
Affiliations: Department of Energy, Politecnico di Milano, Milan, 20156, Italy; School of Electrical Engineering, China University of Mining and Technology, Xuzhou, 221116, China
Authors with affiliations: Canali G., Department of Energy, Politecnico di Milano, Milan, 20156, Italy; Martino A.D.I., Department of Energy, Politecnico di Milano, Milan, 20156, Italy; Longo M., Department of Energy, Politecnico di Milano, Milan, 20156, Italy; Rong C., School of Electrical Engineering, China University of Mining and Technology, Xuzhou, 221116, China
Abstract: Accurate real-time estimation of electric vehicle (EV) energy consumption is essential for range prediction, energy management, and the development of digital twins for advanced mobility applications. However, existing driving simulators often rely on simplified vehicle models that fail to capture the interaction between driver behavior, vehicle dynamics, and battery-state evolution under realistic operating conditions. This paper presents a high-fidelity digital twin framework for real-time EV energy consumption estimation based on the co-simulation of a Unity driving environment and a physics-based battery model developed in MATLAB/Simulink. The proposed architecture combines immersive vehicle dynamics, detailed road and terrain reconstruction, and a second-order equivalent circuit battery model through a low-latency User Datagram Protocol (UDP) communication layer, enabling synchronized real-time execution. The framework was calibrated using a Tesla Model 3 Standard Range and validated against experimental measurements collected on three real-world routes characterized by different traffic and operating conditions. Model accuracy was assessed through the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE), and coefficient of determination (R2). Experimental results demonstrate high predictive accuracy, with route-dependent MAPE values ranging from 2.63% to 5.40% and a maximum R2 of 0.859. Furthermore, the proposed digital twin accurately reproduces energy-consumption trends over a wide range of initial battery State of Charge (SoC) conditions, from 96% to 28%. The analysis of residual errors highlights the influence of terrain elevation uncertainty, thermal effects of battery, and auxiliary loads on prediction accuracy. The results obtained demonstrate that the proposed framework provides a reliable and computationally efficient tool for EV energy assessment, digital-twin applications, eco-driving studies, and future intelligent charging and energy-management strategies. © 2013 IEEE.

Title: Digital Twin Readiness of Mechanical Coffee Dryers: A Systematic Review
Affiliations: Faculty of Electronic Engineering and Telecommunications, Universidad del Cauca, Popayán, 190001, Colombia; Cluster Creatic, Popayán, 190001, Colombia
Authors with affiliations: Valencia-Payan C., Faculty of Electronic Engineering and Telecommunications, Universidad del Cauca, Popayán, 190001, Colombia; Casanova Olaya J.F., Cluster Creatic, Popayán, 190001, Colombia; Corrales J.C., Faculty of Electronic Engineering and Telecommunications, Universidad del Cauca, Popayán, 190001, Colombia
Abstract: Thermal drying is a critical phase in coffee processing, significantly influencing energy consumption, moisture uniformity, storage stability, and sensory quality. Despite the superior throughput of mechanical dryers over open-sun drying, these systems often operate with limited observability and manual control. This systematic review evaluates the readiness of mechanical coffee drying for Digital Twin (DT) integration. A comprehensive search across Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and ScienceDirect identified 22,859 records. Following multi-stage screening, 58 studies were retained for qualitative synthesis, categorized into a primary coffee-drying corpus and a secondary transferable corpus of methods from related food-processing applications. Findings indicate that while DT-enabling components, such as CFD models, drying-kinetics models, IoT monitoring, and non-destructive sensing, are established, they remain fragmented. No fully implemented and operationally validated DT for mechanical coffee drying was identified. Based on the evidence, a hybrid reduced-order physics-based model integrated with constrained supervisory control represents the most defensible near-term architecture. Future research should prioritize standardized datasets, uncertainty-aware soft sensors, and field validation across diverse dryer topologies and operating conditions. © 2026 by the authors.

Abstract: Background – Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection remains a global health challenge, necessitating personalized treatment strategies to optimize patient outcomes. Digital twin technology—synchronized with real-world entities—offers a pathway to precision medicine in HIV care. Methods – We analyzed 5, 436 HIV patients (2016–2024) with demographic, immunologic, and antiretroviral therapy (ART) information. Core algorithms comprised gradient boosting and random forest ensembles; deep architectures (LSTM and Transformer networks) were evaluated as comparative benchmarks on longitudinal feature tensors under identical supervision. Models used five-fold cross-validation, regularization, dropout, and early stopping. A probabilistic treatment ranking layer generated diversified regimen suggestions conditioned on model outputs. Results – Ensemble models achieved strong explained variance on the registry-defined CD4 label (test R2 up to 0.97; cross-validation stability reported in the Results). Deep models achieved comparable held-out accuracy on the same endpoint; the ranking module produced balanced regimen distributions in an illustrative optimization cohort. Simulated digital twin scenarios demonstrated counterfactual CD4 projections under alternative ART strategies for low, moderate, and higher baseline immunology profiles. Discussion – The specific contribution is an explicit patient-state → prediction → regimen exploration pipeline suited to integration with telehealth analytics (risk dashboards, adherence supports), while transparently acknowledging endpoint and leakage limitations and the need for prospective outcome validation. A pragmatic HIV treatment optimization strategy is to route model-supported prioritization into clinician-facing dashboards and remote monitoring workflows rather than autonomous prescribing. Title: Robust Adaptive Predictive Control for Hook-Based Aerial Transportation Between Moving Platforms

Abstract: This letter presents a novel model predictive control (MPC) approach for autonomous pick-and-place between moving platforms with a hook-equipped aerial manipulator. First, for accurate and rapid modeling of the complex dynamics, a digital twin model of the quadcopter equipped with a hook-based gripper, implemented in MuJoCo, is constructed and used as the predictive model for the MPC. To handle uncertainties of the predictive model (e.g. due to aerodynamics and uncertain payloads), a robust adaptive MPC approach is proposed. By systematic integration of zero-order robust optimization (zoRO) based uncertainty propagation and an extended Kalman filter (EKF) for parameter estimation, the MPC algorithm ensures robust constraint satisfaction, high performance, and computational efficiency. The effectiveness of the proposed method is evaluated in complex simulated scenarios and in real-world flight experiments. © 2016 IEEE.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming lithium-ion battery (LIB) research by linking heterogeneous data, predictive modeling, mechanistic interpretation, and experimental validation within a closed-loop paradigm. AI does not uniquely enable nonlinear representation; rather, it complements electrochemical, statistical, and control models by learning high-dimensional relationships among composition, structure, processing, interfacial chemistry, operating history, and performance. This review critically examines three connected domains: AI-assisted materials discovery, battery state prediction, and trustworthy intelligent management. To distinguish this contribution from recent topic-specific surveys, we organize methods along four complementary axes—model architecture, learning strategy, physics integration, and deployment strategy—and compare landmark studies using quantitative evidence such as independent cell count, validation design, reported error, experimental budget, and closed-loop acceleration. Materials applications include cathodes, anodes, liquid and solid electrolytes, and electrode-electrolyte interphases; operational applications include state of charge, state of health, remaining useful life, degradation diagnosis, safety warning, and digital twin-enabled management. The critical synthesis identifies data leakage, inconsistent metadata, domain shift, uncalibrated uncertainty, black-box reasoning, computational constraints, and limited external validation as recurring barriers. Future progress will depend less on model complexity alone than on FAIR data, cell-independent evaluation, physics-informed learning, uncertainty-aware decisions, autonomous experimentation, human oversight, and deployment-aware design. These elements define an evidence chain for moving LIB AI from proof-of-concept prediction toward reproducible, closed-loop, and trustworthy battery innovation. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Synthetic aperture radar and digital twin framework of the bridge monitoring systems: A review

Abstract: The integration of Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) with Digital Twin (DT) frameworks offers a transformative pathway for modern bridge management, enabling satellite-data selection of structures to engage decision-making across the asset life cycle. This approach supports proactive Structural Health Monitoring (SHM), prioritization of predictive maintenance (PM) over repair and rehabilitation interventions, and enhanced informed planning. Therefore, promising case studies demonstrating the practicability of fusing satellite-derived displacement data with Building Information Modelling (BIM), based digital representations, taking into consideration several barriers, such as semantic interoperability, uncertainty quantification, real-time data assimilation, and institutional integration into Bridge Management Systems (BMS). This work outlines a systematic framework for implementing InSAR-enhanced digital twins according to a literature review, emphasizing their role in integration with BIM, lifecycle administration, and predictive assurance. By synthesizing recent advances and identifying key research gaps, this contribution aligns with ongoing international efforts to standardize and operationalize digital twin adoption for sustainable, resilient, and optimized bridge infrastructure management. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Orthopedic Mechanophenotype: A Structured Narrative Review of Multiscale Biomechanics, Mechanotransduction, and Clinical Decision-Making
Affiliations: The First School of Clinical Medicine, Yunnan University of Chinese Medicine, Kunming, China; The First People's Hospital of Yunnan Province, Kunming, China
Authors with affiliations: Lan Z., The First School of Clinical Medicine, Yunnan University of Chinese Medicine, Kunming, China; Mu Z., The First School of Clinical Medicine, Yunnan University of Chinese Medicine, Kunming, China; Li H., The First School of Clinical Medicine, Yunnan University of Chinese Medicine, Kunming, China, The First People's Hospital of Yunnan Province, Kunming, China
Abstract: Orthopedic disorders are still classified mainly by anatomy or end-stage morphology, yet osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, fracture nonunion, spinal degeneration, and bone-implant interface failure share a common mechanobiological logic: external load is filtered by hierarchical tissue architecture, converted into cell-scale signals, and integrated with inflammation, metabolism, and repair capacity to determine whether adaptation or failure occurs. This structured narrative review synthesizes recent evidence on multiscale biomechanics, finite element analysis (FEA), mechanotransduction biology, tissue engineering, and emerging digital-twin approaches. Rather than introducing a separate disease entity, we define the orthopedic mechanophenotype as a clinically oriented integrative framework that describes the disease-relevant state generated by three interacting axes: load exposure, tissue susceptibility, and biological adaptability. We summarize how this three-axis state differs across bone, articular cartilage and the osteochondral unit, the intervertebral disc, fracture repair, and bone-implant interfaces. Particular emphasis is placed on evidence hierarchy, model assumptions, and persistent uncertainties, including timescale mismatch, idealized boundary conditions, incomplete cross-scale validation, and overinterpretation of cell-level causality from organ-level surrogates. We further illustrate how mechanophenotyping can be integrated with existing clinical pathways for osteoarthritis load redistribution, fracture fixation and rehabilitation, and spinal or implant-related planning. The central argument is that future progress will depend less on accumulating isolated mechanical variables and more on validated cross-scale markers that connect real-world loading, patient-specific structure, and stage-dependent biology to actionable orthopedic decisions. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Active Learning for Data-Driven Reduced Models of Parametric Differential Systems with Bayesian Operator Inference
Affiliations: Department of Mathematics, Brigham Young University, 275 TMCB, Provo, 84602, UT, United States; Centre for Mathematical Sciences, Lund University, Box 118, Lund, 22100, Sweden; Oden Institute for Computational Engineering and Sciences, The University of Texas at Austin, 201 E 24th St., Austin, 78712, TX, United States

Abstract: This work develops an active learning framework to intelligently enrich data-driven reduced-order models (ROMs) of parametric dynamical systems, which can serve as the foundation of virtual assets in a digital twin. Data-driven ROMs are explainable, computationally efficient scientific machine learning models that aim to preserve the underlying physics of complex dynamical simulations. Since the quality of data-driven ROMs is sensitive to the quality of the limited training data, we seek to identify training parameters for which using the associated training data results in the best possible parametric ROM. Our approach uses the operator inference methodology, a regression-based strategy which can be tailored to particular parametric structure for a large class of problems. We establish a probabilistic version of parametric operator inference, casting the learning problem as a Bayesian linear regression. Prediction uncertainties stemming from the resulting probabilistic ROM solutions are used to design a sequential adaptive sampling scheme to select new training parameter vectors that promote ROM stability and accuracy globally in the parameter domain. We conduct numerical experiments for several nonlinear parametric systems of partial differential equations and compare the results to ROMs trained on random parameter samples. The results demonstrate that the proposed adaptive sampling strategy consistently yields more stable and accurate ROMs than random sampling does under the same computational budget. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: From Nano-Enabled Multimodal Biosensing to Health Digital Twins: A Scoping Review and Evidence-Gated Roadmap

Abstract: Rapid advances in nanomaterials, wearable biosensors, multimodal acquisition, and artificial intelligence have enabled increasingly integrated health-monitoring systems, yet their progression toward health digital twins remains unclear. We conducted a protocol-driven scoping review of original studies combining nano-enabled multianalyte or multimodal sensing, AI-supported analysis, and health applications. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and IEEE Xplore were searched using a publication cutoff of 10 July 2026; platform execution was completed on 13 July 2026. Two reviewers independently screened 528 unique records and assessed 20 full-text reports. A 79-item charting form was jointly verified for 12 included studies. Nine studies reported reference-method or matrix-relevant analytical validation, nine included human-sample or on-body evidence, and six acquired longitudinal or continuous data. Under the author-proposed, corpus-specific functional classification, six systems were L0, five L1, and one L2; none of the 12 met the L3 or L4 functional criteria. No included study combined dynamic individual-state assimilation with prospective prediction or simulation, and none reported external-site validation or formal predictive uncertainty quantification. Because eligibility required nano-enablement, multiple analytes or channels, AI integration, and selected clinical domains, these findings do not estimate the prevalence or maturity of health digital twins in the wider literature. Progress requires longitudinal multimodal data, validated state updating, external generalization, confidence-aware AI, and prospective evaluation of governed feedback. © 2026 by the authors.

Source title: Trends in Food Science and Technology
Affiliations: Bioprocessing Laboratory, Centre for Technology Alternatives for Rural Areas, Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, Powai, Mumbai, 400076, India
Authors with affiliations: Sahu C.K., Bioprocessing Laboratory, Centre for Technology Alternatives for Rural Areas, Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, Powai, Mumbai, 400076, India; Arora A., Bioprocessing Laboratory, Centre for Technology Alternatives for Rural Areas, Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, Powai, Mumbai, 400076, India
Abstract: Background: Agro-industrial residues are promising sources of phenolics, pigments, polysaccharides, proteins, and other functional ingredients, but food-grade valorization remains constrained by feedstock heterogeneity, sensor uncertainty, empirical scale-up, solvent and energy burdens, and contaminant co-extraction. Scope and approach: This review critically evaluates digital twins and physics-informed machine learning (PIML) as a safety-bounded framework for residue valorization. It examines process analytical technology, laboratory assays, soft sensors, unit-operation models, model predictive control, techno-economic assessment, life-cycle assessment, and regulatory audit trails. Particular emphasis is placed on coupling target-bioactive recovery with the transport and concentration of pesticides, mycotoxins, metals, residual solvents, and process impurities. Key findings and conclusions: PIML can embed transport, reaction, rheological, and degradation constraints into learning architectures, thereby improving extrapolation from sparse and drifting food-process datasets. Digital twins can extend these models into synchronized cyber-physical systems that optimize recovery while enforcing calibrated uncertainty, contaminant boundaries, explainability, traceability, and dossier-ready comparability for EFSA Novel Food, FDA GRAS, Codex, and related pathways. Persistent barriers include sensor fouling, calibration drift, missing benchmark datasets, computational latency, interoperability gaps, and limited toxicological validation. A staged maturity roadmap is proposed, from data shadows to qualified autonomous twins. An updated search through 6 June 2026 identified adjacent reviews, but no publicly indexed source jointly formalized PIML-constrained unit-operation twins, coupled bioactive-hazard states, uncertainty-bounded release invariants, and regulatory comparability. However, DT/PIML should be implemented as staged, risk-based decision-support systems, not universal replacements for conventional optimization, because scale-transfer uncertainty, rare-event coverage, and computational burden determine whether industrial use is justified. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Strategic Management of Airport Readiness for Digital-Twin-Enabled Smart-Energy Systems: A Reliability-Aware Bayesian Decision Framework
Affiliations: Atlas University, Department of Management Information Systems, Istanbul, 34403, Turkey; Department of Property Protection and Security, Istanbul Bilgi University, Istanbul, 34060, Turkey
Authors with affiliations: Mizrak F., Atlas University, Department of Management Information Systems, Istanbul, 34403, Turkey; Elbir U., Department of Property Protection and Security, Istanbul Bilgi University, Istanbul, 34060, Turkey
Abstract: Airports face growing pressure to decarbonize energy-intensive infrastructure while integrating digital twins, artificial intelligence, real-time monitoring, electrification, renewable-energy systems, and resilient operational controls. This study develops a reliability-aware Bayesian framework for assessing readiness for digital-twin-enabled smart-energy systems across 20 major international airports. The preferred latent model uses 15 airport-level capability indicators organized into four theory-defined domains: smart-energy infrastructure, digital twins and intelligent systems, managerial and organizational readiness, and governance and resilience. A sixteenth indicator, evidence transparency, is retained separately as an auxiliary reporting-quality measure. Eight additional variables describe the airport scale and country- or economy-level enabling environment. Evidence was compiled from official airport reports, sustainability disclosures, regulatory records, project documents, and international datasets, with explicit distinctions between operational systems, pilots, planned investments, and group-level claims. Observation-level reliability incorporates source quality, verification, temporal relevance, consistency, and completeness, while missing observations contribute no direct likelihood to the Bayesian measurement model. The preferred PyMC/NUTS specification produced stable posterior estimates with no divergent transitions, a maximum overall readiness R-hat of 1.003, and acceptable posterior predictive performance (RMSE = 0.094; MAE = 0.057). Singapore Changi, Hong Kong, Amsterdam Schiphol, and Copenhagen formed the highest-readiness group. Sensitivity analyses showed that the broad ordering was robust to alternative reliability assumptions, variance-floor choices, prior specifications, and high-information restrictions, although stronger informative-missingness assumptions affected several evidence-sparse airports. A complementary rule-based threshold screen identified capability shortfalls and evidence gaps without interpreting them as causal necessary conditions. The framework provides an uncertainty-aware basis for benchmarking, investment sequencing, procurement, and integrated digital and energy transition planning. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Research Gaps in AI-Supported Disassembly Sequence Planning in Remanufacturing
Affiliations: Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, Poznan University of Technology, 1 J. Rychlewski Street, Poznań, 60-965, Poland
Authors with affiliations: Dudkowiak A., Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, Poznan University of Technology, 1 J. Abstract: Artificial intelligence has become increasingly important in research on Disassembly Sequence Planning (DSP). AI-based methods can now solve more complex problems and consider several economic, environmental and operational objectives. However, most studies still focus on optimizing the disassembly process after the recovery strategy and target components have already been selected. This study reviews AI-supported disassembly planning in remanufacturing and identifies the main research gaps and future research directions. The review combines bibliometric mapping of 241 publications with a qualitative analysis of 35 selected studies. Of these studies, 23 directly address DSP, seven concern related disassembly problems, and five focus on remanufacturing planning or scheduling outside DSP. The results show progress in metaheuristic optimization, reinforcement learning, digital twins, knowledge graphs, computer vision, large language models and robotic planning. At the same time, the analysis identified several recurring limitations that can be grouped into three broader dimensions: product-state knowledge and adaptability, validation and transferability, and decision scope and strategic-operational integration. The reviewed studies show that uncertainty, adaptive planning, digital twins and multi-objective optimization have already received considerable attention, but their application remains limited by predefined product representations, case-specific validation and weak integration between product-level recovery assessment and operational disassembly planning. The findings suggest that future research should complement further algorithmic development with more integrated, adaptive and knowledge-supported decision-support approaches that connect recovery assessment with the planning of the required disassembly process. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Sparse sensing reconstruction in MILD combustion using Flamelet-Generated Manifold

Abstract: This work presents a data-driven framework for reconstructing thermochemical states in MILD combustion by coupling Sparse Sensing (SpS) with a Flamelet-Generated Manifold (FGM) formulation to reconstruct species fields from a limited number of temperature measurements. A non-adiabatic FGM database is first generated from counterflow flamelets and used to describe the thermochemical state through a reduced set of control variables. These variables are then reconstructed by a SpS model based on Proper Orthogonal Decomposition and Bayesian inference, using a predetermined sensor layout consistent with the reference experimental burner. The coupled framework is assessed on a lab-scale cyclonic MILD combustor. Results show accurate reconstruction of the main control variables and good prediction of major species, with R2 values above 0.94 for CH4, CO2, H2O, and O2, while intermediate and minor species exhibit larger deviations but remain correctly captured in terms of spatial trends and order of magnitude. Finally, the analysis of uncertainty propagation shows that species uncertainty is mainly governed by mixture fraction, while the contribution of the variance of the progress variable is negligible. Novelty and significance statement: Reduced-order models (ROMs) for turbulent combustion describe complex reactive flows by exploiting latent structure (Parente and Sutherland, 2013). Previous work (Procacci et al., 2023; Rosati et al., 2026) reduces the state by selecting key species to recover information for analysis, but the choice of target variables and the size of the state can degrade reconstruction accuracy and runtime. This work introduces, to the authors’ knowledge, the first application in a MILD cyclonic burner of an integrated framework coupling Sparse Sensing (Manohar et al., 2018) with Flamelet Generated Manifolds (FGM) (Van Oijen and De Goey, 2000) to reconstruct thermochemical states from a limited set of control variables. By combining physics-based tabulated chemistry with data-driven sparse reconstruction, the proposed SpS-FGM approach reduces sensing demand and decouples reconstruction performance from full-state dimensionality. The framework is compatible with established diagnostic workflows and can be extended to other reduction or data assimilation strategies, supporting the development of reliable, low-cost digital twins or soft-sensing tools for applications focused on low-emission combustion systems. © 2026 The Authors.
