Title: Fuel surrogate temperature prediction for microreactor using heat pipe under transient conditions
Affiliations: Department of Nuclear Engineering, Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST), 50 UNIST-gil, Ulju-gun, Ulsan, 44919, South Korea
Authors with affiliations: Jin I.J., Department of Nuclear Engineering, Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST), 50 UNIST-gil, Ulju-gun, Ulsan, 44919, South Korea; Bang I.C., Department of Nuclear Engineering, Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST), 50 UNIST-gil, Ulju-gun, Ulsan, 44919, South Korea
Abstract: Remote operation and digital twin implementation for heat pipe cooled reactor systems require simplified and reliable thermal state estimation methods. In applications, fuel temperature should be inferred using a limited set of accessible measurements, while maintaining sufficient performance under transient operating conditions. In this study, a fuel surrogate temperature prediction method was developed using temperature measurements obtained from the adiabatic and condenser sections of a heat pipe with heat exchanger temperature. Deep learning architectures were applied to represent transient thermal behavior. An integrated LSTM–Transformer architecture was adopted to reflect short term temporal continuity and long term temporal dependency in the measured temperature signals. Model performance was evaluated using both separate and sequential transient datasets. The integrated LSTM–Transformer model achieved a mean absolute error of 1.68 K and a mean absolute percentage error of 0.19% for separate transient conditions. For sequential transient conditions, which included compounded and previously unseen transients, the mean absolute error and mean absolute percentage error increased to 4.74 K and 0.55%, respectively, while maintaining a coefficient of determination above 0.99. Model behavior was examined using attention weight analysis and SHAP-based feature attribution, confirming that interpretable temperature contributions were captured. Prediction uncertainty was quantified using Monte Carlo Dropout, with 95% confidence intervals remaining within 5–7 K for most operating conditions. The proposed approach provides a basis for fuel surrogate temperature monitoring and thermal assessment in heat pipe cooled microreactor systems, particularly for remote operation and digital twin applications where model complexity and instrumentation availability are constrained. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enabled digital twins are increasingly used to improve monitoring, prediction, control, and sustainability assessment in circular biorefineries. However, the literature remains fragmented, with many studies focusing on isolated prediction tasks rather than validated, decision-oriented digital-twin systems. This review critically examines AI-enabled digital twins for circular biorefineries that convert heterogeneous bioresources into biogas, hydrogen, volatile fatty acids (VFAs), microbial products, algal products, bio-oil, syngas, and biochar. The review differs from earlier studies by linking digital-twin architecture with soft sensing, hybrid modeling, constrained control, embedded techno-economic analysis (TEA), life-cycle assessment (LCA), and deployment-readiness requirements. Particular attention is given to VFA-platform biorefineries, where product speciation, pH control, separation energy, product routing, and uncertainty strongly influence process value. Across the reviewed literature, the most useful digital-twin functions are early detection of instability, estimation of hard-to-measure variables, feedstock-adaptive optimization, energy-intensity reduction, and transparent cost-emission trade-off analysis. The main barriers are limited online observability, weak external validation, poor transferability across sites, incomplete reporting of uncertainty, and insufficient integration between AI models and TEA-LCA decision layers. Future work should move from stand-alone predictive models toward validated hybrid twins with transfer learning, auditable data pipelines, constrained model predictive control (MPC), and carefully governed large-language-model interfaces to support operators and interpret scenarios. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: A modular Digital Twin architecture for the data-driven reactive planning of disassembly systems

Abstract: Disassembly is key to circular production, enabling end-of-life products to be recovered through reuse, remanufacturing, or recycling. However, disassembly is characterized by high uncertainty about product condition and process feasibility, which requires dynamic, product-specific planning. While predictive disassembly planning anticipates uncertainties, disassembly systems must additionally be able to adapt their plans in real time when deviations occur. This is addressed by Reactive Disassembly Planning (RDP), which enables the dynamic adaptation of disassembly processes and schedules during disassembly. However, unlocking RDP's full potential requires complex decision-making based on comprehensive real-time data. To support such data-driven RDP, a modular Digital Twin architecture is presented that integrates all decision-making steps into an automated, real-time planning pipeline. The architecture is instantiated and deployed as a Digital Twin in a learning-factory disassembly system to demonstrate the feasibility and end-to-end operation of the proposed modules and connectors. Its potential is illustrated in a representative scenario, in which the instantiated Digital Twin achieves a 78% reduction in lead time and a 2% increase in profit compared to operating without RDP, and a 529% profit increase compared to a rule-based process-termination strategy. These results serve as illustrative proof of applicability, indicating that data-driven RDP via Digital Twins can support efficient, resilient disassembly operations and thereby strengthen the business case for circular factories and the transition to more sustainable production. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Toward autonomous infrastructure management: Agentic AI for structural health monitoring, robotics, and digital twins
Affiliations: Department of Civil Engineering, University of Texas at Arlington, Arlington, 76010, TX, United States
Authors with affiliations: Khan M.A., Department of Civil Engineering, University of Texas at Arlington, Arlington, 76010, TX, United States; Hong P., Department of Civil Engineering, University of Texas at Arlington, Arlington, 76010, TX, United States; Lin Z., Department of Civil Engineering, University of Texas at Arlington, Arlington, 76010, TX, United States
Abstract: Modern sensing, robotics, artificial intelligence (AI), and digital twins (DTs) are reshaping the design, construction, operation, and maintenance of civil infrastructure. This review examines the evolution of structural health monitoring (SHM) from predictive models toward agentic AI for autonomous infrastructure management. Current research has achieved substantial progress in vibration-based monitoring, vision-based inspection, robotic sensing, and transformer-enabled analytics; however, most workflows remain diagnostic and lack autonomous reasoning and decision-making capabilities. This review defines the emerging concept of Agentic SHM, synthesizes recent advances in reinforcement learning, large language models, robotics, and DTs, and proposes layered architecture integrating perception, reasoning, planning, execution, and governance. Key challenges, including trustworthy autonomy, uncertainty-aware decision-making, reproducibility, standards compliance, and multi-agent coordination, are identified. The review concludes that progressively validated, human-supervised agentic AI provides a practical pathway toward safer, more resilient, and lifecycle-oriented infrastructure automation, while providing a roadmap for future research and practical implementation across infrastructure. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Title: AgriTwin-SA: A Multimodal, Physics-Informed GeoAI Architecture Toward an Agricultural Digital Twin for Southern Africa
Affiliations: South African National Space Agency (SANSA), Earth Observation Research, Applications and Development (EO-RAD), Pretoria, South Africa
Authors with affiliations: Masemola C., South African National Space Agency (SANSA), Earth Observation Research, Applications and Development (EO-RAD), Pretoria, South Africa; Ngcoliso N., South African National Space Agency (SANSA), Earth Observation Research, Applications and Development (EO-RAD), Pretoria, South Africa
Abstract: Southern African agriculture is dominated by rain-fed maize and is acutely exposed to recurrent drought, flooding, and heat extremes, yet no operational multi-country system couples continuous Earth observation (EO) with predictive simulation at district scale. We propose AgriTwin-SA, an agricultural digital-twin architecture that fuses Sentinel-1 synthetic aperture radar (SAR), harmonized optical reflectance, satellite rainfall, climate reanalysis, terrain, soil, and open cropland reference products into a continuously updated virtual representation of the regional cropping system. The architecture couples a two-branch temporal encoder (a temporal convolutional network and a Transformer self-attention encoder) with a physics-informed latent crop-state layer, a spatial graph-neural-network module, and a weekly data-assimilation loop, exposing three coupled outputs: in-season crop-stress monitoring, pre-harvest district yield forecasting with calibrated uncertainty, and a counterfactual scenario-simulation engine. In a simulation-based proof-of-concept calibrated to regional agronomic statistics, AgriTwin-SA attains the highest monitoring accuracy and the lowest yield error among compared baselines while producing better-calibrated probabilities; ablation attributes forecast lead-time skill to the climate branch, cloud-window robustness to SAR, and probability reliability to the calibration layer. We outline operational pathways, limitations, and data-sovereignty considerations, and identify multi-season operational validation as the essential next step. This paper presents the methodological framework and a simulation-based proof-of-concept; the full multi-season, multi-country empirical validation is reported in a forthcoming full paper. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Critical aspects of hybrid microgrids: Architectures, energy management, optimization techniques, and future research directions-A review

Abstract: The increasing penetration of renewable energy resources has accelerated the development of hybrid microgrids as a key solution for enhancing the sustainability, reliability, and operational flexibility of modern power systems. However, the intermittent nature of renewable generation, the growing integration of distributed energy resources (DERs), and the increasing complexity of energy management require advanced control, optimization, and storage technologies. This paper presents a comprehensive critical review of hybrid microgrids, covering their architectural configurations, hierarchical control strategies, energy management systems (EMSs), optimization techniques, and hybrid energy storage systems (HESSs). A systematic methodology supported by PRISMA-based literature screening, bibliometric analysis, and a taxonomy framework is employed to ensure a transparent and structured evaluation of the literature. Comparative analyses are conducted to assess conventional and artificial intelligence (AI)-based control strategies, mathematical and metaheuristic optimization methods, and emerging HESS configurations in terms of efficiency, scalability, computational complexity, and practical implementation challenges. Furthermore, critical issues including communication latency, interoperability, cybersecurity, battery degradation, explainable AI, and uncertainty-aware energy management are comprehensively discussed. Based on the identified research gaps, future directions are proposed, emphasizing digital twins, federated learning, distributed intelligence, resilient cyber-physical architectures, and next-generation AI-driven energy management. This paper provides a comprehensive reference study for researchers and practitioners involved in the design, control, optimization, and deployment of intelligent hybrid microgrid systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Digital Twin-driven Visual Analytics and Spatio-Temporal Collaborative Intelligent Monitoring for Guangxi Karst Terrain
Source title: Proceedings of the 2nd International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Virtual Reality and Interaction Design, AIVRID 2026
Affiliations: Xiangsi Lake College, Guangxi University for Nationalities, Guangxi, Nanning, China
Authors with affiliations: Chen Z., Xiangsi Lake College, Guangxi University for Nationalities, Guangxi, Nanning, China; Lei L., Xiangsi Lake College, Guangxi University for Nationalities, Guangxi, Nanning, China; Wang Y., Xiangsi Lake College, Guangxi University for Nationalities, Guangxi, Nanning, China
Abstract: Karst landforms are widely distributed in Guangxi. Their unique geological structures, characterized by developed karst caves, interlaced underground rivers, and thin overburden layers, lead to frequent geological disasters such as landslides and karst collapses, posing a severe threat to the safety of people's lives and property. Traditional monitoring methods primarily rely on single-sensor data or manual inspections, which struggle to meet the requirements for real-time, accurate, and reliable disaster warning in complex terrains. This paper proposes a Static Perception-Dynamic Inspection Spatio-Temporal Collaborative Intelligent Monitoring System (KSTFN) tailored for the karst terrain in Guangxi. The system achieves early identification and precise warning of geological disasters by deeply integrating static geological models (InSAR, LiDAR) with dynamic inspection data (UAV multi-sensors). The core innovations include: (1) The Karst Spatio-Temporal Fusion Network (K-STFN), which utilizes a multi-scale dilated attention mechanism to capture multi-scale geological features ranging from micron-level fractures to hundred-meter-level karst caves. (2) A static-dynamic collaborative reasoning framework that achieves deep coupling of static knowledge and dynamic observations through geological prior-guided feature extraction and a bidirectional cross-modal attention mechanism. (3) An edge-cloud collaborative architecture, where a lightweight edge model supports real-time processing on UAVs (25 FPS), while a cloud-based deep model performs complex analysis and long-term trend forecasting. Experimental results demonstrate that the KSTFN system achieved a Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) of 0.75 in landslide detection within typical karst areas of Guangxi, which is 19.5% higher than the current state-of-the-art method (FTransUNet). Additionally, disaster warning accuracy increased by 22.3%, and emergency response time was shortened by 35.6%. This study not only provides technical support for geological disaster monitoring in Guangxi's karst regions but also offers a scalable solution for disaster prevention and control in similar complex terrains. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: Physics-driven and data-driven hybrid digital twin framework for methanol fuel supply system based on dynamic Bayesian network

Abstract: Methanol has attracted increasing attention as a potential low-carbon marine fuel. However, the safe operation of methanol fuel supply systems is challenged by coupled hydraulic, thermal, and control dynamics, together with time-varying degradation and operational uncertainty. To address these challenges, this study proposes a physics-driven and data-driven hybrid digital twin framework based on a dynamic Bayesian network (PDH-DBN) for methanol fuel supply systems. The framework combines a conservation law-based physics-driven model, a temporal convolutional network (TCN)-based data-driven model, online Bayesian updating through particle filter, and adaptive model fusion. The physics-driven branch updates pump-related parameters online, while the data-driven branch updates correction parameters for the TCN outputs. The two branches are then fused adaptively using their current posterior residuals. The updated parameters are further used to construct pump health indices. The proposed approach was validated on a laboratory test bench under varying flow conditions and a preset pump fault. Under normal operation, the fused framework achieved RMSEs of 0.104–0.110 Hz for pump frequency, 0.022–0.031 bar for pressure, and 0.015–0.017 °C for temperature. Under the preset pump fault scenario, PDH-DBN effectively isolated primary-pump degradation. These results indicate that PDH-DBN can support accurate state estimation, adaptive fusion, uncertainty-aware health assessment, and pump-level fault isolation for methanol fuel supply systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Navarro-Meneses F.J.
Author full names: Navarro-Meneses, Francisco J. (57222596929)
Title: How AI–Driven Transformation Reshapes Competitiveness in Incumbent Firms
Source title: AI for Sustainable Digital Transformation: Governance and Innovation
Affiliations: Nebrija University, Spain
Authors with affiliations: Navarro-Meneses F.J., Nebrija University, Spain
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping how firms compete, innovate, and coordinate value creation in increasingly complex economic systems. While contemporary discourse remains largely focused on automation and productivity gains, this chapter examines how AI-driven transformation alters the strategic foundations of incumbent organizations. It develops a framework that distinguishes three stages in the evolution of AI capabilities: algorithmic consolidation, anticipatory integration, and architectural transformation. A longitudinal comparative analysis of five multinational incumbents shows how machine learning, digital twins, and simulation platforms reshape decision-making, business models, and stakeholder coordination. The findings suggest that competitive advantage increasingly depends on embedding anticipatory capabilities into organizational governance and value architectures. In doing so, AI-driven transformation enables firms to align innovation, sustainability objectives, and long-term resilience in environments characterized by systemic uncertainty. © 2027 by IGI Global Scientific Publishing. Title: Physics-guided digital-twin-ready surrogate framework for predictive design of double-bridge compliant mechanisms in advanced manufacturing systems
Affiliations: G H Raisoni College of Engineering and Management, Pune, India; Savitribai Phule Pune University, Pune, India; Sinhgad Institute of Technology and Science, Pune, Narhe, India; Government College of Engineering Karad, Satara, India

Abstract: The integration of physics-based modeling and data-driven prediction is creating new opportunities for predictive design, optimization, and the deployment of digital twins in advanced manufacturing systems. In compliant mechanisms, particularly double-bridge configurations used in precision positioning and surface engineering applications, accurate prediction and optimization of amplification ratio remain challenging due to coupled geometric interactions and nonlinear design trade-offs. This study presents a Physics-Guided Digital-Twin-Ready Framework for the predictive design and multi-objective optimization of double-bridge compliant mechanisms. A physics-consistent dataset comprising 8, 000 design samples was generated using Latin Hypercube Sampling, analytical compliance modeling, constraint-based filtering, and response-space stratified sampling. The resulting dataset provides balanced coverage of amplification ratios within the range of 5–50, enabling robust learning across diverse design regimes. Machine-learning models, including Random Forest and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), were developed to predict amplification ratio from geometric and material parameters. The models achieved excellent predictive performance, with coefficients of determination (R2) exceeding 0.99, mean absolute errors below 0.93, and root mean square errors below 0.65. Uncertainty quantification was incorporated through ensemble variance estimation, yielding prediction intervals with less than 5% relative uncertainty in well-sampled regions. SHAP-based explainability and sensitivity analyses revealed that amplification behavior is primarily governed by geometric parameters, particularly beam lengths and flexure thickness, whereas material stiffness has comparatively lower influence. NSGA-II-based multi-objective optimization identified Pareto-optimal solutions that balance amplification ratio and equivalent stiffness, highlighting the inherent trade-off between displacement amplification and structural rigidity. The developed surrogate models enable rapid design exploration, uncertainty assessment, and optimization, while achieving computational speed-ups of approximately 103–107times compared with finite-element-based evaluation workflows, depending on the evaluation method. The primary contribution of this work is the integration of analytical compliance modeling, physics-consistent dataset generation, uncertainty-aware machine learning, explainable artificial intelligence, and multi-objective optimization within a unified predictive framework. The proposed methodology should be interpreted as a digital-twin-ready surrogate architecture rather than a fully implemented digital twin, as real-time sensing, and online model updating are beyond the scope of the present study. Nevertheless, the framework provides a scalable foundation for future integration with experimental measurements, multi-fidelity datasets, and digital-twin-enabled manufacturing environments. Title: Remote sensing of building height estimation: A review of data, products, methods, and prospects
Source title: Physics and Chemistry of the Earth

Abstract: Building height is a key variable for characterizing three-dimensional urban morphology, vertical development intensity, and spatial exposure, supporting applications in urban climate, air pollution, energy and carbon assessment, disaster risk, population mapping, planning, and digital twins. Remote sensing enables large-scale and updatable height mapping, but most sensors do not directly observe building height. Except for active measurements such as LiDAR, height is generally inferred from indirect cues, including shadows, stereo parallax, SAR scattering, street-view facades, spatial texture, and urban functional priors. Accordingly, remote sensing-based building height estimation should be viewed as a scale-dependent three-dimensional information retrieval problem constrained by observability, observation geometry, reference data, modeling approaches, and application requirements. This review examines data sources, height products, estimation methods, scale effects, uncertainty propagation, applications, and future challenges. We compare passive optical imagery, SAR, LiDAR, and street-view imagery in terms of height cues, applicable scales, and error mechanisms, and review representative products and methods, including geometry- and physics-driven approaches, statistical learning, deep learning, and multisource fusion. Particular attention is given to height definition, product comparability, accuracy assessment, scale transformation, and uncertainty propagation into environmental and socioeconomic applications. We argue that building height products should be evaluated not only by RMSE or MAE, but also by height definition, evaluation unit, reference data, aggregation strategy, uncertainty structure, and intended use. Future research should emphasize application-oriented reliability, standardized validation, cross-city generalization, interpretable modeling, dynamic mapping, and application-adaptive product generation. Title: Data challenges and metrological approaches in the agrifood supply chain: Data accuracy, data availability, and data privacy issues

Abstract: The agrifood supply chain is undergoing a profound digital transformation driven by the adoption of advanced sensing technologies, data analytics, and interconnected information systems. While these innovations create unprecedented opportunities to improve food safety, traceability, authenticity, and sustainability, they also introduce major challenges related to data accuracy, data availability, and data privacy and ethical governance . In this evolving landscape, metrology provides the scientific framework needed to ensure that digital data are reliable, comparable, and fit for decision-making. This review examines the principal data challenges affecting digital agrifood systems and discusses how metrological principles—including traceability, calibration, validation, uncertainty evaluation, and standardised measurement protocols—can be extended beyond traditional laboratory measurements to emerging digital technologies such as IoT, remote sensing, blockchain, Digital Twins, and artificial intelligence. By integrating these principles with FAIR data practices, digital agrifood ecosystems can improve data interoperability, transparency, and long-term reusability while supporting trustworthy data sharing and responsible governance. The review also highlights how research infrastructures such as METROFOOD-RI and governance initiatives such as DRG4FOOD provide complementary examples of implementing these principles in practice by combining metrological rigor with ethical and privacy-aware data governance. Overall, this review proposes a metrological perspective for addressing emerging data challenges and demonstrates how the integration of measurement science, digital technologies, and responsible governance can support trustworthy digital agrifood ecosystems, evidence-based decision-making, and more sustainable and resilient food systems. © 2026 The Authors.

Abstract: Low Impact Development (LID), such as permeable pavements, mitigates some of the urban runoff effects. Their hydrologic response can be enhanced with real-time forecasting and management. Digital Twins (DT), which integrate physical models with sensor data, offer a solution, yet require methods to handle uncertainties in model inputs and observations. This study presents a DT framework for permeable pavement systems that couples a one-dimensional, explicit-state hydrologic model with a Particle Filter (PF) data assimilation scheme. The framework assimilates real-time underdrain outflow observations to refine model states and provide probabilistic forecasts. Uncertainty characterization revealed that sensor measurement error depends on the underdrain outflow, while rainfall forecast error from the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh model is a function of the magnitude of the rainfall event. The DT framework was evaluated against a baseline model using field data from four permeable pavement types. The data assimilation approach reduced the ensemble forecast error by an average of 20%, as measured by the Continuous Ranked Probability Skill Score (CRPSS), with positive skill scores in 96.2% of forecast events. The deterministic performance of the PF ensemble median, evaluated by Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), also exceeded that of the baseline model. The data assimilation framework yielded more accurate forecasts than a deterministic modeling approach and is computationally efficient for operational deployment. However, outflow forecast accuracy is constrained by the structural limitations of the baseline model, evidenced by poor prediction interval coverage during some high-intensity events, highlighting areas for future model development. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Abstract: Photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting is a foundational capability for operating power systems with high shares of variable renewable generation. However, the methodological landscape is fragmented across physical-based models, statistical time-series approaches, machine learning (ML), and increasingly diverse hybrid and multi-modal pipelines combining SCADA measurements with numerical weather prediction (NWP) and remote-sensing data. This paper provides a unified, practice-oriented synthesis of PV power forecasting methods, linking forecasting tasks and horizons to data requirements, modeling assumptions, and deployment constraints. We first summarize PV plant architecture, the energy conversion chain and key definitional choices (AC vs. DC, power vs. energy, spatial aggregation, sampling interval). We then formulate the forecasting problem across point and probabilistic settings, distinguishing single- and multi-step strategies and showing how horizon choice shifts the balance between persistence, cloud-driven dynamics, and NWP-driven uncertainty. We propose a taxonomy covering (i) physics-based approaches (clear-sky and PV performance models), (ii) statistical and time-series baselines, (iii) ML/DL families — recurrent, convolutional, attention-based, and transformer architectures — and (iv) hybrid and ensemble methods, with attention to calibration and uncertainty quantification. Finally, we identify open challenges limiting robust deployment — non-stationarity, cross-site/climate generalization, probabilistic calibration, and explainability — and highlight emerging trends such as self-supervised learning, foundation models, and digital-twin-inspired forecasting loops. © 2026 Taylor & Francis Group, LLC.

Title: The Decision Twin: Metaverse Patient Digital Twins as Executable Clinical Reality
Source title: Proceedings of the ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining
Affiliations: Macquarie University, Sydney, NSW, Australia
Authors with affiliations: Cenacchi F., Macquarie University, Sydney, NSW, Australia; Cao L., Macquarie University, Sydney, NSW, Australia; Richards D., Macquarie University, Sydney, NSW, Australia
Abstract: Clinical AI is no longer bottlenecked only by model performance; it is bottlenecked by the accountable interaction loop through which clinicians and patients inspect evidence, test alternatives, and remain responsible for decisions under uncertainty. We argue that today's digital-twin systems, XR interfaces, and foundation-model copilots each address part of this loop, but they fail when deployed as separate products: predictions are not replayable across time, XR becomes descriptive visualization without executable state, and copilots are fluent without auditable grounding. We introduce the Metaverse Patient Digital Twin (MPDT) as a decision-grade clinical artifact defined by one requirement: every displayed claim or simulated scenario must be traceable to a versioned patient state, explicit assumptions, and replayable interaction logs. We specify minimal acceptance criteria, a reference loop in which stakeholders observe new evidence, update the twin state, run bounded simulations, generate explanations, commit decisions, and then log and monitor outcomes, along with a compact architecture that binds interoperability, simulation, governed interaction, and lifecycle controls. Finally, we outline workflows (risk stratification, diagnosis support, treatment rehearsal, training, cross-site coordination) and the evidence required to make MPDTs defensible: calibration over time, subgroup reliability, category-error prevention (observation vs simulation), and measurable workflow outcomes. © 2026 Owner/Author.

Title: PCA-OS: A Planetary Climate Adaptation Operating System
Source title: Proceedings of the ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining
Affiliations: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, Singapore; Alibaba Group, Hangzhou, China
Authors with affiliations: He C., Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, Singapore; Zhou X., Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, Singapore; Wang D., Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, Singapore; Xu H., Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, Singapore; Liu W., Alibaba Group, Hangzhou, China; Miao C., Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, Singapore
Abstract: Predictive climate machine learning is increasingly good at forecasting hazards, but hazard maps alone do not decide what to do, where, when, for whom, and under which futures. We argue that climate ML remains insufficient for adaptation unless interventions become first-class, versioned, and auditable objects. Many climate digital twins still prioritize state estimation and simulation, whereas adaptation requires intervention observability, counterfactual effect estimation, and constrained portfolio choice. We propose PCA-OS (Planetary Climate Adaptation Operating System), a decision-support operating abstraction built on an intervention-aware global causal knowledge graph. PCA-OS standardizes schemas, versioned updates, query primitives, and audit interfaces across three core objects: (1) an Adaptation Intervention Ledger recording measurable interventions with provenance and uncertainty; (2) a Causal Effect Atlas storing scenario-indexed, spillover-aware estimands, identification assumptions, diagnostics, and sensitivity bounds; and (3) a Robust Portfolio Decision Layer optimizing intervention portfolios under budget, equity, and no-harm constraints. Foundation models and intervention-aware world models should support, not replace, identification-aware causal analysis by surfacing candidate confounders, mechanisms, and spillover pathways for human review. We also outline AdaptBench, an evaluation suite where systems can fail for inequitable or maladaptive recommendations despite high predictive accuracy. The result is a field-level provocation: move climate ML from read-only hazard intelligence to auditable decision support for adaptation. © 2026 Owner/Author.

Title: Disagreement-and-Support Reliability Mapping for Point Cloud Completion in Architecture and Engineering
Source title: Proceedings of the International Conference on Education and Research in Computer Aided Architectural Design in Europe
Affiliations: The University of Osaka, Japan
Authors with affiliations: Hu A., The University of Osaka, Japan; Fukuda T., The University of Osaka, Japan
Abstract: Point cloud completion networks can rapidly densify partial building scans, but their primary risk in architecture and engineering is confident hallucination: geometrically plausible output weakly constrained by measurements, which can silently propagate errors into scan to building information modeling (BIM) workflows, dimensional verification, and digital-twin maintenance. Existing methods provide no spatial reliability estimates, leaving practitioners with an all-or-nothing choice between trusting or discarding AI-generated geometry. This paper introduces disagreement and support reliability mapping (DSRM), a training-free method that computes per-point reliability scores by combining two complementary cues: cross-model disagreement across an ensemble of completion networks with diverse architectures, as a proxy for epistemic uncertainty, and observation support distance from the original scan, as a proxy for extrapolation extent. The fused scores are visualised as a three-class reliability map distinguishing scan-supported regions, reliable completions, and high-risk regions requiring re-scan. Evaluated on 16 self-collected indoor scenes spanning four building types, DSRM achieves a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.827 in detecting large reconstruction errors, with low-reliability regions exhibiting a mean 5.77× higher reconstruction error than high-reliability regions. The method requires no model retraining and adds negligible computational overhead, making it immediately deployable in existing scan-to-BIM and digital-twin workflows. © 2026, Education and research in Computer Aided Architectural Design in Europe. Abstract: The large-scale integration of demand-side resources (DSR) into regional energy internet (REI) presents new challenges for traditional dispatch schemes, including diminishing scheduling patterns, evolving dispatching rules, and uncertain system outcomes. This paper, from a multi-agent intelligence perspective, examines the essence of such complexity and then proposes a digital-twin-based collective intelligence scheduling framework. The framework introduces a holistic cognitive view angle driven by emergent phenomena and leverages the digital twin’s multi-path dynamic simulation capabilities to support proactive dispatch. A hierarchical architecture is developed within the framework, consisting of a system simulator, a situational perceiver, and a decision-maker, which sequentially construct the sample subspace, the feature subspace, and the decision subspace. This structure enables an iterative evolution process that spans the entire cycle, from twin modeling and situational awareness to strategy generation, simulation-based evaluation, and system adaptation. The proposed framework effectively balances the proactive autonomy of DSRs with the system operator's macro-level dispatch capabilities. It overcomes the limitations of purely rule-based collaborative intelligence and fully decentralized swarm intelligence. By integrating collective intelligence mechanisms, emergent cognition, and twin-driven simulation, the framework breaks through traditional reductionist paradigms and establishes a systematic theoretical and methodological foundation for coordinated DSR dispatch in complex systems across multiple spatiotemporal scales and evolutionary paths under uncertainty. © (2026), (Power System Technology Press). Abstract: Salt marshes are climate-relevant blue-carbon ecosystems whose extent, vegetation, hydrology, elevation, biomass and sediment carbon respond to interacting ecological and geomorphic processes. This scoping review synthesizes a frozen inventory of 114 retained records and explicitly separates 23 core empirical salt-/tidal-marsh studies, 26 transferable coastal-wetland studies, and 65 review, contextual and methodological sources. The synthesis shows that optical, hyperspectral, synthetic aperture radar (SAR), LiDAR and uncrewed aerial system (UAS) data are most defensible when treated as complementary sources of spectral, structural and hydrological evidence rather than as direct measurements of total carbon stock. Recent site-specific studies illustrate high performance under particular calibration conditions, but their metrics are not pooled because targets, validation designs, spatial resolutions and study settings differ substantially. Field biomass plots, sediment cores, bulk density, organic carbon, vertical-datum control and independent validation therefore remain essential for accounting-grade blue-carbon estimates. The review further identifies feature-level fusion as a practical default for interpretable multi-sensor modeling, while highlighting the spatial-resolution limits of open Sentinel baselines for narrow and fragmented marshes. Finally, we distinguish demonstrated wetland/coastal digital-twin components from an original salt-marsh digital-twin research agenda proposed here. The agenda links observation-driven state updating, eco-geomorphic models, scenario testing, uncertainty and adaptive management without implying that operational salt-marsh digital twins are already established. Priority needs are stronger tropical and subtropical evidence, reproducible evidence inventories, transferability tests, uncertainty-aware validation and practitioner-ready monitoring workflows. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Digital Value Chain as a Circular Control Architecture

Authors with affiliations: Karakai M., Department of Manufacturing Management, Faculty of Manufacturing Technologies, Technical University of Košice, Bayerova 1, Prešov, Slovakia; Bobko D., Department of Manufacturing Management, Faculty of Manufacturing Technologies, Technical University of Košice, Bayerova 1, Prešov, Slovakia; Knapčíková L., Department of Manufacturing Management, Faculty of Manufacturing Technologies, Technical University of Košice, Bayerova 1, Prešov, Slovakia
Abstract: The transition from linear production models to circular manufacturing systems requires more than technological recovery capability; it demands lifecycle-wide governance of information and decision-making. Despite extensive research on Digital Twins and Industry 4.0 technologies, the practical implementation of short-loop circularity – maintenance, repair, and remanufacturing – remains constrained by fragmented lifecycle data and recovery uncertainty. Existing literature largely treats digital technologies as isolated enablers rather than as components of an integrated circular control system. This paper conceptualises the Digital Value Chain (DVC) as a lifecycle-spanning circular control architecture that regulates the transformation of product data into structured circular interventions. Using a conceptual research design based on structured synthesis and abstraction, the study develops a multi-layered framework comprising data acquisition, state estimation, circular intervention, and feedback-to-design layers. Building upon this architecture, hierarchical levels of digital circular enablement – informational, analytical, and decision – are formalised to explain how lifecycle transparency evolves into circular governance. The framework further introduces an operational decision logic structured around feasibility gates that govern maintenance, repair, and remanufacturing pathways. By reframing short-loop circularity as an information-dependent control problem, this research advances digital manufacturing and circular economy theory beyond technology adoption narratives toward systemic lifecycle regulation. The proposed model provides a conceptual foundation for assessing digital-circular maturity in manufacturing systems and offers a structured basis for future empirical validation and simulation-based modelling. © The Author(s) 2026.

Abstract: Hydrogen storage systems operate in a narrow pressure-temperature corridor, hence real installations rarely stay fixed long enough for reliable models. The operating conditions of real-world hydrogen storage systems are changing all the time as tanks age, as weather fluctuates and from other disturbances in the process. Sensor conditions beyond the norm are detected by optimization frameworks using static priors, uncoupled safety limitations, or physics-driven predictions. These limits continually divide the theoretically optimal operating region and the practically safe high-performance region. Present study proposes a novel Bayesian optimization framework that is aware of its environment and can be used with dynamic changes in hydrogen storage environments. A Contextual Sensor-Fusion Prior Builder compresses heterogeneous data streams into a thermodynamically grounded context and generates dynamic priorities to match the plant's instantaneous condition. Using these priors, a Physics-Respecting Contextual Surrogate Auditor validates a surrogate with calibrated uncertainty from physics-model outputs, digital-twin-generated responses, and learned expectations. A Contextual Safety Margin Quantifier estimates the probability of constraint violation more accurately and simplifies multi-constraint safety. The fourth layer, the Adaptive Contextual Safe-Region Explorer, optimizes only safe regions for performance and probabilistic assurances. Cycle-breaking, scenario-driven contextual deployment Emulator stresses-tests generative plant behavior model policy more than 1000 future operating scenarios generated from diverse contextual trajectories. A closely integrated data-driven and physics-respecting ecosystem improves accuracy, uncertainty estimates, and safety under simulated real-world process variability. Our operating policies improve storage efficiency, reduce exploration risk, and create reliable, context-adaptive hydrogen systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: A physics-chemistry-materials-informed neural digital twin for autonomous design, characterization, and optimization of green-synthesized antibacterial silver nanoparticles
Source title: Applied Physics A: Materials Science and Processing
Affiliations: ¹Department of Science, St. Louis Community College, St. Charles, United States; ²Department of Physical Sciences, Jaramogi Oginga Odinga University of Science and Technology, Bondo, Kenya
Authors with affiliations: Agumba J.O., ¹Department of Science, St. Louis Community College, St. Charles, United States, ²Department of Physical Sciences, Jaramogi Oginga Odinga University of Science and Technology, Bondo, Kenya; Okumu F., ²Department of Physical Sciences, Jaramogi Oginga Odinga University of Science and Technology, Bondo, Kenya
Abstract: Green synthesis of silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) offers an environmentally sustainable approach for producing functional nanomaterials, yet optimization of synthesis conditions remains challenging because transport phenomena, reduction chemistry, and nanoparticle growth are strongly coupled. This study presents a Physics-Chemistry-Materials-Informed Neural Digital Twin (PCMINN-DT) that integrates a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) for diffusion-reaction transport, a Chemistry-Informed Neural Network (ChINN) for phytochemical-mediated silver-ion reduction kinetics, and a Materials-Informed Neural Network (MINN) for nanoparticle growth and aggregation within a unified scientific machine-learning framework. The informed neural modules are coupled to a digital twin incorporating Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation, virtual UV-Vis, DLS, XRD, and FTIR characterization, and multi-objective optimization for synthesis design. The framework was developed and evaluated using synthetic physics-consistent datasets to systematically assess its scientific consistency, predictive capability, and digital-twin performance prior to experimental calibration and validation. The results demonstrate that the integrated framework accurately enforces governing physical, chemical, and materials-science constraints while predicting nanoparticle size, aggregation tendency, silver-ion release, reactive oxygen species generation, and antibacterial performance. Monte Carlo analysis indicates robust predictive behavior under simulated process variability, and autonomous optimization identifies synthesis conditions that maximize predicted antibacterial activity and colloidal stability while minimizing aggregation and toxicity. The proposed framework establishes a scalable foundation for AI-guided nanoparticle engineering and provides a pathway toward experimentally calibrated digital twins for sustainable nanomaterials design. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Abstract: Civil infrastructure assets are managed today through inspection cycles and calendar-based interventions that observe an asset only at discrete instants, so deterioration between visits is inferred rather than measured. Digital Twin (DT) research has addressed parts of this problem, but published frameworks remain confined either to a single lifecycle phase or to a single enabling technology, and few report reproducible validation against public benchmarks. This paper presents a unified DT framework that couples a cyber-physical sensing and communication layer, an entropy-weighted multi-sensor fusion scheme, a hybrid physics-plus-machine-learning surrogate, extended Kalman assimilation for continuous model updating, and a constrained multi-objective optimisation layer that closes the loop from measurement to intervention across all five lifecycle phases of an asset. The contribution is threefold: a phase-invariant state formulation in which design, construction, operation, maintenance and end-of-life are expressed as a single evolving state trajectory; an adaptive physics-to-data blending coefficient calibrated on held-out data rather than fixed a priori; and a reliability-constrained decision layer in which maintenance actions are selected subject to an explicit failure-probability bound. The framework is exercised on a provisional synthetic dataset generated deterministically from a calibrated finite element model of a three-span reinforced concrete girder bridge, and is benchmarked against traditional, IoT-only and AI-only baselines under an identical protocol. All reported results are simulation outcomes; no field validation, laboratory validation or real-time deployment has been performed. The DT configuration attains 96.0% detection accuracy, with a 95% Wilson interval of 95.0 to 96.8, and an area under the curve of 0.98, against 90.0% and 0.92 for the strongest AI-only baseline, every pairwise difference being significant at p below 0.001 after Holm-Bonferroni adjustment. Remaining useful life error falls from 4.80 to 1.30 years, median end-to-end latency from 250 ms to 120 ms, and the annual failure rate from 0.080 to 0.020, raising twenty-year reliability from 0.202 to 0.670 with a discounted break-even at year 5.8. Detection accuracy remains at or above 92% across high-temperature, heavy-load and seismic operating states. A component ablation attributes the margin principally to environmental normalisation at 7.4 percentage points, the physics constraint at 6.0 and continuous assimilation at 4.8, rather than to model capacity, which is held constant against the AI-only baseline. Deployment barriers - interoperability, cybersecurity, cost, power and validation under uncertainty - are quantified and mapped to mitigation measures and residual risk, and a reproducibility statement specifies the dataset generator, splits, hyperparameters, seeds and computing environment, from which every reported figure is exactly reproducible. © 2026 Seventh Sense Research Group®.

Abstract: The study examines the developmental stages of autonomous cyber-physical energy systems (CPES), concentrating on intelligent autonomous grids that incorporate self-stabilizing solar-wind hybrid generation, battery storage, electric vehicles, and AI-driven control mechanisms. A systematic critical review with some features of systematic reviews was carried out at this time. This research offers a thorough examination of the current literature concerning CPES architecture, integrated hybrid renewable and storage systems with electric vehicles, artificial neural networks employed for forecasting and control, digital twin technology, cybersecurity, and procurement trading in prominent indices. This organization employs a relative analysis coding framework that subdivides the study into system layers, optimization scenarios, uncertainty management strategies, implementation techniques, and validation contexts. The study demonstrates that genuine system autonomy is unattainable if isolated component optimization is regarded as the ultimate objective. It has a lot of parts, such as physical infrastructure, sensing and communication networks, predictive analytics and controls, resilience frameworks, and governance structures. HRES-EVS systems are very flexible and can pay off in the long run, but they are hard to use because of unclear policies, inconsistent compatibility with other systems, vulnerability to cyber and physical threats, and a lack of real-world experience that may come from not enough testing. Digital twins, edge computing, the Internet of Things (IoT), and artificial intelligence (AI) are all important parts of a flexible closed-loop intelligence system. The paper presents a cohesive conceptual framework that redefines CPES autonomy as an emergent, multi-faceted characteristic of smart energy ecosystems and suggests a future research agenda for the advancement of a resilient, carbon-conscious, decentralized, and governance-integrated Smart Grid. Abstract: Conventional cotton (Gossypium spp.) variety development requires 8–12 years - a timeline structurally incompatible with the accelerating urgency of climate-change adaptation, soil salinisation, and textile-industry demands for novel varieties within 3–5 years. Speed breeding (SB) compresses the generation interval by 30–80% through synergistic optimisation of LED spectra, temperature, nutrition, and immature embryo rescue (IER). However, SB alone is a temporal accelerator, not a breeding system: its transformative potential is realised only when it functions as the central engine of a genomics-assisted speed breeding (GASB) platform that integrates molecular marker-assisted selection (MAS), genomic selection (GS), CRISPR and New Genomic Technique (NGT) editing, high-throughput phenotyping (HTP), and AI-assisted decision-support tools. Building on previous reviews of cotton speed breeding and genomics-assisted breeding, the present review provides a mechanistic and implementation-oriented synthesis of these complementary technologies within a unified GASB framework. We evaluate: (i) the molecular architecture of photoperiodic flowering in predominantly Gossypium hirsutum, together with currently available evidence from other Gossypium species where appropriate and its manipulation through LED protocol design and CRISPR targeting of flowering suppressors; (ii) the mechanistic basis of multi-channel LED recipe design from SB 1.0 to SB 3.0; (iii) stage-specific thermal management including the operationally critical 33°C pollen safety ceiling; (iv) nutritional physiology, phytohormones, and biochemical monitoring; (v) in vitro biotechnologies—including callus culture, microspore-derived doubled haploids, and immature embryo rescue (IER)—together with the operational coordination of immature embryo rescue and pollen-stage temperature management within speed-breeding facilities; (vi) high-throughput phenotyping technologies experimentally validated in cotton, encompassing five cotton-specific applications reviewed in a dedicated section; and (vii) AI-assisted phenotyping and digital twin architectures for real-time decision support within the GASB pipeline. Critical analysis identifies allotetraploid genome redundancy, genotype × light environment (G×L) interaction with landrace germplasm, IER scalability, bioinformatics infrastructure gaps, SB-to-field correlation uncertainties, and SVT regulatory requirements as the primary barriers to widespread GASB deployment. A structured 2025–2035 roadmap with three time-horizon priorities and measurable KPIs is presented. Title: Human–AI Collaborative Neuromorphic Digital Twins with Adaptive Game-Theoretic Intelligence for Fuzzy Multi-Objective Optimization of Multi-Stakeholder Supply Chains
Affiliations: Institute of Economics and Politics, University of National and World Economy, Sofia, 1700, Bulgaria; Industrial Business Department, Business Faculty, University of National and World Economy, Sofia, 1700, Bulgaria
Authors with affiliations: Nozari H., Institute of Economics and Politics, University of National and World Economy, Sofia, 1700, Bulgaria; Yordanova Z., Industrial Business Department, Business Faculty, University of National and World Economy, Sofia, 1700, Bulgaria
Abstract: Multi-stakeholder supply chains require decision mechanisms capable of simultaneously interpreting dynamic system states, coordinating conflicting stakeholder interests, and managing uncertainty across interconnected operational decisions. This study proposes an integrated Human–AI Collaborative Neuromorphic Digital Twin framework in which synchronized supply-chain data are transformed into cognitive representations, enriched through human–AI collaborative intelligence, strategically coordinated through adaptive game-theoretic interactions, and subsequently mapped into a unified decision-knowledge representation for fuzzy multi-objective optimization. The principal innovation lies in this closed and interconnected decision architecture, where the outputs of cognitive, collaborative, and strategic intelligence layers are explicitly fused and transferred to the optimization space rather than being applied as independent analytical modules. The framework jointly optimizes economic, environmental, service, resilience, energy, and operational-risk objectives under fuzzy uncertainty. Evaluation was conducted using combined real and statistically consistent simulated data across six operational scenarios ranging from baseline conditions to a critical scenario involving simultaneous demand growth, capacity restrictions, cost escalation, uncertainty, and stakeholder conflicts. Results demonstrate progressive improvements in decision quality under increasingly complex conditions; in the critical scenario, Human–AI collaboration achieved a 19.6% cost improvement, while the service level reached 99.4%. The findings demonstrate that integrating cognitive representation, collaborative intelligence, strategic adaptation, and fuzzy optimization provides a unified mechanism for adaptive multi-stakeholder supply-chain decision-making. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Integrating passive design, renewable energy, thermal flexibility, and intelligent control in net-zero energy buildings: A system-level review
Affiliations: Department of Mechanical Engineering, College of Engineering in Yanbu, Taibah University, Yanbu Al-Bahr, 46421, Saudi Arabia; Department of Mechanical Engineering, Faculty of Engineering at Shoubra, Benha University, Cairo, 11629, Egypt
Authors with affiliations: Refaey H.A., Department of Mechanical Engineering, College of Engineering in Yanbu, Taibah University, Yanbu Al-Bahr, 46421, Saudi Arabia, Department of Mechanical Engineering, Faculty of Engineering at Shoubra, Benha University, Cairo, 11629, Egypt; Alsharif A.M.A., Department of Mechanical Engineering, College of Engineering in Yanbu, Taibah University, Yanbu Al-Bahr, 46421, Saudi Arabia
Abstract: Net-zero energy buildings require coordinated decisions across passive design, active systems, renewable generation, storage, occupants, and control. This article presents a structured evidence map and a focused critical review of these interactions. Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, and ScienceDirect were searched for English-language journal articles and reviews published from January 2015 to 11 August 2026. Database searches returned 4385 query-level records; the imported files contained 4423 occurrences due to a duplicate 38-record Scopus audit subset. Cleaning and cross-database deduplication produced 3180 unique records. Title-and-abstract screening retained 2622 records in a broad evidence map, while 66 sources were selected using predefined relevance criteria to support the focused synthesis. This source set represented the principal evidence types, performance dimensions, and system interactions rather than a statistically representative sample. Evidence was examined across energy performance, indoor environmental quality and well-being, flexibility, resilience, and whole-life carbon and cost. Reported performance depended strongly on climate, building type, occupancy, baseline, system boundary, and control strategy. Passive and hybrid envelope measures reshape building loads, whereas heat pumps, thermal and electrical storage, and predictive control provide operational flexibility. Their effectiveness depends more on coordinated sizing and operation than on individual component efficiency. Field evidence remains less common than simulation and short-term demonstrations, particularly for cyber-physical building systems. The review proposes a performance-oriented co-design and operation framework that integrates contextual conditions, design and control variables, and practical constraints within a coupled building-system model. Research priorities include long-term field validation, semantic interoperability, uncertainty-aware control, occupant-centered operation, resilience assessment, and whole-life evaluation. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Digital Twins for Sustainable Groundwater Resources Management: From Monitoring and Prediction to Governance and Resilience—A Review
Affiliations: Department of Mathematics, Computer Sciences, Physics and Earth Sciences, The University of Messina, Messina, 98166, Italy
Authors with affiliations: Borzì I., Department of Mathematics, Computer Sciences, Physics and Earth Sciences, The University of Messina, Messina, 98166, Italy
Abstract: This article presents a scoping review of the literature on digital twins (DTs) for sustainable groundwater resources management, which constitutes a very recent and rapidly expanding research field, with literature moving quickly from conceptual frameworks to application-oriented systems. The literature, selected through the PRISMA 2020 methodology, is organized into seven sub-topics: AI and ML foundations, digital twin architectures and frameworks, aquifer-scale DT applications, agricultural and water–energy–food (WEF) nexus DTs, basin and urban water DTs, sensing, monitoring and IoT infrastructures, and governance, resilience and socio-hydrology. This structure shows how the field is shifting from monitoring and prediction toward integrated decision support, where process-based models, machine learning surrogates, real-time sensing and optimization are combined to support drought mitigation, saltwater intrusion control, irrigation management, climate adaptation and basin-scale planning. Across the reviewed studies, the most recurrent contributions are the construction of hybrid model architectures, the use of DTs to close the loop between observation and control, and the growing recognition that groundwater management must incorporate governance, stakeholder decision-making and socio-hydrological feedbacks. At the same time, the literature still faces key limitations, especially uncertainty quantification, interoperability between models and data streams, transferability to data-scarce settings and limited validation under real operational conditions. Future research should therefore focus on physics-informed and explainable AI, federated and scalable DT architectures, stronger coupling with socio-hydrological and governance frameworks, and more field-tested implementations that can demonstrate robust performance across diverse hydrogeological and institutional contexts. © 2026 by the author.

Title: Intelligent Transportation Systems: A Review of Integration of Digital Twin and Machine Learning Control
Affiliations: School of Engineering, Computer and Mathematical Sciences, Auckland University of Technology, 6-24 St. Paul Street, Auckland, 1010, New Zealand
Authors with affiliations: Tun T., School of Engineering, Computer and Mathematical Sciences, Auckland University of Technology, 6-24 St. Paul Street, Auckland, 1010, New Zealand; Sabit H., School of Engineering, Computer and Mathematical Sciences, Auckland University of Technology, 6-24 St. Paul Street, Auckland, 1010, New Zealand
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive review of the integration of Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) and Digital Twin (DT) technologies for intelligent traffic management. It examines the role of key enabling technologies, including the Internet of Things (IoT), machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), reinforcement learning (RL), Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication, and edge computing. These technologies support real-time traffic monitoring, traffic prediction, and adaptive control in ITS. The review synthesizes recent research on conventional traffic control methods, optimization-based approaches, learning-based techniques, and DT-enabled traffic management solutions. Particular attention is given to the integration of DTs with intelligent traffic signal control, real-time synchronization, multi-intersection coordination, communication latency, sensing uncertainty, and scalability. The reviewed literature demonstrates the potential of DT-enabled ITS to improve traffic efficiency, reduce congestion, enhance transportation safety, and support sustainable mobility through data-driven decision-making. However, significant challenges remain regarding communication delays, sensor and data uncertainty, computational complexity, scalability, and validation under realistic urban conditions. Based on the reviewed literature, this paper identifies key research gaps and outlines future research directions toward scalable, reliable, adaptive, and real-time DT-enabled ITS architectures for next-generation smart cities. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Calorimeters for Concentrating Solar Thermal Applications: Experimental and Numerical Advances
Affiliations: Department of Chemical Engineering and Metallurgy, Universidad de Sonora, Blvd. Rosales y Luis Encinas, Sonora, Hermosillo, 83000, Mexico

Abstract: Solar thermal calorimeters serve as foundational reference instruments for quantifying absorbed thermal power, evaluating optical-to-thermal conversion efficiency, and validating computational models in concentrated solar thermal (CST) research. This review synthesizes recent numerical, thermo-hydraulic, and experimental advancements, evaluating the evolution from basic single-tube configurations to high-confinement cavity calorimeters (achieving apparent absorptances (Formula presented.)) and flat-plate architecture enhanced with impinging jets and internal fin arrays. The selection of working fluids is examined; water accounts for approximately (Formula presented.) of reported implementations due to low property uncertainty, whereas synthetic oils and gaseous coolants expand operating temperature ranges at the expense of thermochemical degradation and parasitic pumping penalties. Furthermore, critical thermo-hydraulic challenges induced by extreme non-uniform heat fluxes are identified, including structural thermal bowing, parallel-channel flow maldistribution, recirculation traps, and buoyancy-driven instabilities occurring at Richardson numbers (Formula presented.). Metrological constraints related to solar reflection interference in non-contact thermometry and calibration drift in photometric target arrays are also critically addressed. Finally, key strategic research directions are outlined, emphasizing high-temperature advanced materials, active flow equalization, real-time multi-physics digital twins, and standardized dynamic testing metrology. © 2026 by the authors.

Authors with affiliations: Adhikari S., James Watt School of Engineering, The University of Glasgow, Scotland, Glasgow, United Kingdom; Jacquelin E., Univ Lyon, Univ Gustave Eiffel, Univ Claude Bernard Lyon 1, LBMC UMR-T 9406, Lyon, F-69622, France
Abstract: Probabilistic updating of damped structural systems lacks closed-form expressions for operator statistics, leaving iterative numerical methods or implicit auxiliary variable formulations that obscure analytical uncertainty propagation. This work develops a closed-form second-moment framework for simultaneous updating of mass, damping, and stiffness matrices under combined eigenvalue, eigenvector, and modal damping uncertainty, a combination for which explicit operator statistics were previously unavailable. The formulation exploits a sequential property of weighted Frobenius norm minimisation subject to modal orthogonality constraints, whereby the three updates are obtained in three successive convex steps. Stiffness updating depends only on measured frequencies, damping updating depends only on measured modal damping, and mass updating is deduced from the measured modal mass matrix through Berman’s incomplete-mode correction. Gaussian moment closures give exact mean operators, and Fréchet derivative-based perturbation expansions give Kronecker-structured sensitivity matrices that map modal uncertainty to physical-space operator covariance without auxiliary variables or nonlinear solvers. The cross-covariances between the identified modal quantities are retained throughout. Numerical verification on a non-proportionally damped benchmark confirms close analytical-Monte Carlo agreement for mean and covariance predictions, with cross-correlation inclusion yielding order-of-magnitude improvement over independence assumptions. The methodology exchanges finite-element sparsity for analytical tractability, positioning it as a component of digital twin applications, in which the updated operators are interpreted as reduced models condensed onto the instrumented degrees of freedom and the measured modes are taken to span that reduced space. In that setting operator-level uncertainty quantification supports probabilistic forward prediction, data assimilation, and lifecycle prognostics that sampling-based alternatives render prohibitive. The scope of the paper is the operator statistics themselves, and their embedding in a particular assimilation architecture is left open. The framework requires as many sensors as identified modes, with the analytical operators condensed onto those sensors, and it recovers the true mass exactly on the span of the identified modes. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Stockpile Reclamation and Grade Blending for Processing Plant Feed: A Systematic Review of Methods, Models, and Research Gaps
Affiliations: School of Mining and Petroleum Engineering, University of Alberta, Edmonton, T6G 1H9, AB, Canada; NTWIST Inc., Edmonton, T6N 1G1, AB, Canada
Authors with affiliations: Khazaei S., School of Mining and Petroleum Engineering, University of Alberta, Edmonton, T6G 1H9, AB, Canada; Noriega R., NTWIST Inc., Edmonton, T6N 1G1, AB, Canada; Askari-Nasab H., School of Mining and Petroleum Engineering, University of Alberta, Edmonton, T6G 1H9, AB, Canada; Pourrahimian Y., School of Mining and Petroleum Engineering, University of Alberta, Edmonton, T6G 1H9, AB, Canada
Abstract: Stockpiles and run-of-mine (ROM) pads are critical control points between mine production and processing plant feed. The grade, quality mix, and variability of material delivered to the crusher and mill are largely determined by how these structures are designed, built, and reclaimed. Despite the operational significance of stockpile management, the field remains fragmented across five distinct research streams—physical blending theory, stockpile state modelling, reclaim sequencing and equipment scheduling, plant-feed and stockpile blending optimization, and sensor-driven reconciliation and closed-loop control—with limited integration between them. This paper presents a systematic review of 27 sources published between 1976 and 2025, including peer-reviewed journal articles, conference papers, a preprint, a book, and one industry publication. The literature search was conducted in May 2025 using Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, with records screened by title/abstract and full text for direct relevance to stockpile reclamation or grade blending in mining operations. A structured coverage matrix identifies that studies combining high spatial fidelity with strong optimization rigor are consistently absent from the literature, and that uncertainty handling and sensor-driven or real-time capability remain substantially underdeveloped. Six research gaps are identified and prioritized by practical significance, implementation readiness, and literature maturity. The four most operationally critical gaps concern: spatially explicit reclaim scheduling under live ROM-pad constraints; tractable multi-attribute blending formulations for polymetallic operations; uncertainty propagation to plant-feed predictions; and field-scale closed-loop validation. The review provides a structured development roadmap for ROM-pad optimization frameworks and identifies the specific integration challenges that must be addressed to move the field from static stockpile monitoring toward adaptive, sensor-updated decision support. © 2026 by the authors.

Abstract: Hydrogen storage remains a central bottleneck for scalable hydrogen energy systems due to the multiscale and coupled nature of the thermodynamics, kinetics, and microstructural evolution of hydrogen storage materials (HSMs). Although artificial intelligence (AI) has accelerated materials discovery, current approaches remain constrained by fragmented data, limited physical consistency, and weak integration with experimental validation. Here, we propose a unified framework that integrates coherent data infrastructure, physics-grounded modeling, and AI-driven inverse design within a closed-loop discovery paradigm. By constraining optimization with thermodynamics, kinetics, uncertainty, provenance, and experimental feedback, this approach enables adaptive, physically consistent optimization, thereby establishing a pathway toward autonomous, digital-twin-enabled discovery of HSMs. © 2026 The Authors. Title: A probabilistic physics-based framework for the development and continuous adaptation of lifecycle digital twins
Affiliations: Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and Institute for Computational and Mathematical Engineering, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; CMSoft, Inc., CA, United States; U.S. Air Force, United States
Authors with affiliations: Farhat C., Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and Institute for Computational and Mathematical Engineering, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; Daeninck G., CMSoft, Inc., CA, United States; Harp D.I., U.S. Air Force, United States
Abstract: Digital twins are increasingly employed to support predictive analysis, decision-making, and monitoring of complex physical systems. However, existing implementations often rely either on high-fidelity models that are computationally prohibitive for real-time operation or on purely data-driven surrogates that lack physical interpretability and robustness outside their training domain. We present a unified, physics-based computational framework for digital twinning that addresses these limitations through hierarchical projection-based model order reduction, nonparametric probabilistic representation of model-form uncertainty, and data-driven calibration and updating. The framework spans a hierarchy of reduced-order models, from high-dimensional models (HDMs) to hyperreduced stochastic surrogates, enabling computationally efficient predictions while preserving the essential physics of the underlying system. It establishes a systematic progression from an HDM to a digital twin prototype (DTP) through projection and hyperreduction, and subsequently to an operational digital twin instance (DTI) through asset-specific stochastic calibration. To achieve real-time predictive capability while capturing unsteady nonlinear behavior, the framework incorporates a novel trajectory-based perturbation formulation supported by a database of physical matrices acting as localized tangent operators of the underlying nonlinear equations. Interpretable and non-interpretable sources of model-form uncertainty are represented through low-dimensional stochastic parameterizations, enabling efficient uncertainty propagation, statistical inference, and continuous data-driven updating in reduced-order spaces. The framework is validated using two aerospace applications. The first demonstrates an operational DTP for an F-16D aircraft executing aggressive, unsteady maneuvers under the United States Air Force HAVE MIRAGE project, delivering physics-consistent online predictions from real flight data at 20 Hz (0.05 s intervals) in a faster-than-real-time setting – achieving speedup factors up to 57 × ahead of real-time on a single CPU. The second application demonstrates a DTI for structural health monitoring, inferring Level-1 damage presence through changes in the predictive consistency and confidence intervals of the digital twin, utilizing a synthetic dataset representing progressive degradation states. Within this structural tracking context, the hyperreduced stochastic forward solver yields a two-order-of-magnitude speedup factor of approximately 272 × over the HDM, enabling near-real-time tracking on a single standard core. Together, these applications demonstrate that the proposed framework provides a computationally efficient, physics-consistent foundation for digital twinning across the lifecycle of complex engineering systems. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Digital Twins in Oncology: From Multimodal Data Integration to Precision Clinical Practice
Source title: Indian Journal of Radiology and Imaging
Affiliations: Madha Medical College and Research Institute, Tamil Nadu, Thandalam, India; Department of Medical Sciences and Technology, Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Madras, Tamil Nadu, Chennai, India
Authors with affiliations: Vairavan A., Madha Medical College and Research Institute, Tamil Nadu, Thandalam, India; Bhattacharjee R., Department of Medical Sciences and Technology, Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Madras, Tamil Nadu, Chennai, India; Raghavan B., Department of Medical Sciences and Technology, Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Madras, Tamil Nadu, Chennai, India
Abstract: Oncology digital twins are patient-specific computational models that are built by combining electronic health records, multiomics genomic data, and diagnostic imaging to simulate individual tumor biology and predict multiple treatment-related outcomes. Conceptually originated from aerospace engineering, it has matured clinically through convergent advances in radiomics, mechanistic tumor modeling, pharmacokinetic- pharmacodynamic systems, federated machine learning, and, most recently, large language model (LLM)-based clinical interfaces and agentic artificial intelligence (AI). For a practicing radiologist, digital twins offer a transformative role: imaging-derived quantitative features serve as the primary data, positioning diagnostic imaging at the center of these personalized oncology workflows. Key clinical applications especially in oncology span from chemotherapy response prediction, immunotherapy patient selection, personalized radiation planning, tumor progression modeling, and treatment toxicity forecasting. Several of these applications are achievable with current technology without any significant infrastructure investment. Substantial challenges include imaging data standards, absence of prospective validation, algorithmic bias in underrepresented populations, and regulatory uncertainty for continuously self-updating AI. This narrative review provides radiologists with a balanced, comprehensive overview of digital twin architecture, advanced enabling technologies, current clinical evidence, a practical roadmap for implementation, and a candid appraisal of barriers to adoption. © 2026 Indian Radiological Association.
