Title: Mechanism–AI fusion in refining simulation software: A module-level review
Affiliations: Petro-CyberWorks Information Technology Co., Ltd., Beijing, 100007, China; China Petrochemical Corporation (SINOPEC), Beijing, 100728, China
Authors with affiliations: Han J., Petro-CyberWorks Information Technology Co., Ltd., Beijing, 100007, China; Zhao X., China Petrochemical Corporation (SINOPEC), Beijing, 100728, China; Han L., Petro-CyberWorks Information Technology Co., Ltd., Beijing, 100007, China
Abstract: Refining simulation software has remained functionally static for decades: property calculation, reaction kinetics, unit-operation modeling, and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solving modules are hard-coded, unidirectional, and cannot be calibrated online against drifting plant conditions. Purely mechanistic approaches provide irreplaceable rigor but are constrained by computational cost; purely data-driven approaches offer speed and adaptivity but lack the interpretability, generalization, and physical guarantees required for safety-critical deployment. This review examines how mechanism–AI fusion—encompassing physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), reduced-order models (ROMs), operator learning, and closure-model augmentation—is reshaping these functional modules at the architectural level. We propose a module-level taxonomy that maps each fusion strategy to the specific simulation module it transforms, and we distinguish this paradigm from related concepts (hybrid modeling, physics-informed machine learning, grey-box modeling, and digital twins) by specifying the bidirectional information flows between mechanistic and AI components. A systematic literature survey following PRISMA-style methodology identified 133 references from Web of Science, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore (2000–2025). We provide enhanced comparative tables that include training cost, data requirements, extrapolation ability, uncertainty quantification (UQ), scalability, and industrial maturity for each method class. Industrial software benchmarking is presented as a qualitative comparison rather than a subjective ranking. Three industrial case studies (gasifier, FCC unit, distillation column) are analyzed with explicit baselines, deployment durations, and performance indicators, clearly identifying vendor-reported versus independently verified data. We discuss emerging topics—AI-native scientific software, foundation models for scientific computing, autonomous engineering agents, trustworthy and explainable AI, verification & validation (V&V), and MLOps for scientific applications—that will shape the next decade. The review concludes with graded findings (verified, supported, emerging, conceptual, and policy-level) to clearly distinguish established results from industrial observations and conceptual proposals. The central finding is that mechanism–AI fusion transforms refining simulation software from a fixed-algorithm tool into an adaptive multi-fidelity platform, but the transition from advisory and optimization applications to safety-critical closed-loop control requires standardized V&V protocols, UQ frameworks, and process-industry-specific safety governance that do not yet exist. Abstract: This study synthesizes the rapidly expanding evidence base on machine learning that links renewable variability to green-hydrogen production optimisation and proposes an integrated PM–CFL–OPT architecture that embeds uncertainty handling, safety constraints, and interpretability across the decision chain. The architecture represents a synthesis-derived and testable functional hypothesis rather than a quantitatively validated superior pipeline. Because the included studies use heterogeneous datasets, horizons, system boundaries and performance measures—and only three studies are primarily classified as CFL—the present corpus cannot support a pooled estimate of the framework’s incremental performance over standalone alternatives. A PRISMA-aligned, feedback-loop workflow was executed across Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, Taylor & Francis, and SpringerLink, yielding 244 records; 48 duplicates were removed, and 129 critical studies were retained for synthesis. Bibliometric profiling revealed a transition from early exploratory contributions during 2016–2019 to a marked acceleration after 2022, with publication output peaking in 2025 and expanding geographically across established research economies and emerging regions. A systems-map synthesis organises the literature using an Energy/System Vector–Machine-Learning Method–Application/Decision Domain (E–M–A) framework and overlays it with three functional roles: predictive modelling (PM), clustering and feature learning (CFL), and optimisation and control (OPT). E–M–A locates each study by physical context, computational method and decision task, whereas PM–CFL–OPT identifies how ML contributes to the forecast–representation–action chain. Persistent gaps include limited transferability across climates and grids, weak decision-focused learning pipelines, and under-specified safety cases for real-time and market participation. The review concludes with a deployment-oriented roadmap for climate-robust, privacy-preserving, and auditable ML that can scale hydrogen-integrated renewable operations. Findings clarify maturity, trust, and transferability bottlenecks for deployment. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: FROM DIAGNOSTIC AUTOMATION TO TRUSTWORTHY CLINICAL INTELLIGENCE: A SYSTEMATIC SCOPING REVIEW AND EVIDENCE-TO-DEPLOYMENT ROADMAP FOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN DIGITAL DENTISTRY
Source title: Journal of Theoretical and Applied Information Technology
Affiliations: Computer Science and Engineering, Koneru Lakshmaiah Education Foundation, Telangana, Hyderabad, 500075, India; Computer Science and Engineering, Koneru Lakshmaiah Education Foundation,, Telangana, Hyderabad, 500075, India
Authors with affiliations: Devi G.P., Computer Science and Engineering, Koneru Lakshmaiah Education Foundation, Telangana, Hyderabad, 500075, India; Kumar P.R., Computer Science and Engineering, Koneru Lakshmaiah Education Foundation,, Telangana, Hyderabad, 500075, India
Abstract: Digital dentistry increasingly reports high-performing computational models, yet a central knowledge gap remains: existing reviews often catalogue technologies or deployment concerns without a common framework that distinguishes analytical performance from transportability, clinical validity, clinical utility, and lifecycle safety. Consequently, it remains unclear what level of real-world use is actually justified by a reported benchmark result. This systematic scoping review critically appraised literature available through July 2026; 147 records were screened and 56 studies were included for evidence synthesis. Rather than pooling incomparable accuracy values, the review evaluated data provenance, partitioning and leakage, reference standards, external validation, calibration and uncertainty, fairness, human factors, cybersecurity, prospective impact, and lifecycle monitoring across imaging, natural-language processing, multimodal and foundation models, robotics, AR/VR, tele-operation, synthetic data, and digital twins. The synthesis identifies an accuracy-to-deployment gap: evidence is comparatively mature for selected two-dimensional imaging and segmentation tasks, whereas multimodal assistants, generative systems, robotics, teleoperation, and digital twins remain limited by external, prospective, human-factor, or lifecycle evidence. The novelty of this review is an integrated evidence-to-deployment taxonomy, an M0-M5 clinical utility ladder, minimum reporting requirements, and staged evidence gates. The new knowledge created is that evidence maturity, not nominal accuracy alone, determines the defensible level of clinical use, and that the validation burden increases as autonomy, multimodality, generative behaviour, and post-deployment change increase. These outputs provide a practical basis for designing, reviewing, and governing clinically credible digital-dentistry research. © Little Lion Scientific

Abstract: Personalized rehabilitation requires repeated assessment of movement, physiological tolerance, fatigue, and adherence, yet conventional clinic-based measurements provide only intermittent snapshots. The convergence of wearable biosensors with artificial intelligence, edge-cloud computing, and connected data infrastructures creates an opportunity to convert continuous multimodal signals into timely rehabilitation decisions. This critical narrative review synthesizes physiological, biochemical, electrophysiological, biomechanical, and behavioral sensing within a monitoring–interpretation–feedback–adaptation–outcome framework. We first evaluate analytical validity, real-world robustness, biocompatibility, wearability, calibration drift, and power continuity. We then examine signal-quality control, multimodal fusion, digital biomarkers, federated learning, digital twins, and predictive models according to latency, uncertainty, generalizability, privacy, and decision utility. The review follows biosensor-derived information across a graded spectrum of action, from clinician-reviewed monitoring and real-time biofeedback to assist-as-needed adaptation, functional electrical stimulation, and state-responsive neuromodulation. Applications include motor and physiological assessment, fatigue-aware dose adjustment, musculoskeletal and neurological rehabilitation, posture correction, sensor-rich prosthetics, and Internet of Things–enabled home rehabilitation. Across these settings, greater autonomy increases the evidence and safety requirements: models should expose confidence, systems should degrade safely when signal quality falls, and digital infrastructures should preserve interoperability, version traceability, privacy, and accountable clinician oversight. The central translational gap is not sensor sensitivity alone but whether an integrated biosensor system produces a reliable metric, supports an explicit and proportionate decision, and improves an outcome important to the patient. Decision-centered evaluation can help move wearable biosensing from fragmented technology demonstrations toward secure, personalized, continuous, and clinically accountable rehabilitation. Authors: Mueller M.R.
Author full names: Mueller, Michael Robert (60739699700)
Title: SOMA: a preventive health governance framework for adaptive, consumer-facing digital health guidance
Affiliations: Bratislava University of Economics and Management (BUEM), Bratislava, Slovakia
Authors with affiliations: Mueller M.R., Bratislava University of Economics and Management (BUEM), Bratislava, Slovakia
Abstract: This paper introduces SOMA, a conceptual preventive health governance framework for adaptive, consumer-facing digital health guidance, designed to support everyday preventive health self-governance. Non-communicable and lifestyle-sensitive chronic diseases account for the majority of global mortality, yet existing consumer-facing digital health tools rarely provide coherent, governed preventive guidance that integrates multimodal personal health data, scientific evidence, user-defined goals, real-world feasibility, relational support, and explicit safety constraints within a unified architecture. SOMA conceptualizes preventive health self-governance as the iterative, user-governed process through which individuals interpret their evolving health state, define goals and feasibility constraints, receive evidence-informed guidance, and act within boundaries that reduce the risk of unsafe or inappropriate digital health guidance. The framework theorizes an architecture of five interdependent components: a Digital Twin Core synthesizing a multimodal Health State Vector across biological, wearable, subjective, behavioral, and contextual layers; a Scientific Intelligence Core evaluating evidence quality, uncertainty, and applicability; a Relational Avatar Core supporting disclosure, trust calibration, and user-facing communication; a Personal Health Governance Profile embedding user-defined goals, feasibility constraints, and autonomy preferences; and a Continuous Learning Engine updating the model based on outcomes, evidence, and user feedback, all bounded by non-negotiable Safety and Medical Escalation Boundaries. The theoretical contribution lies in integrating previously siloed approaches (digital health twin logic, evidence-weighted scientific intelligence, relational guidance, behavioral self-governance theory, and personal health governance) into a unified preventive architecture whose governance properties emerge from the structured interdependence of its components. Five testable hypotheses are derived from the architecture to guide a staged empirical validation programme. SOMA is a conceptual framework that has not been empirically validated and makes no claims regarding clinical effectiveness, disease prevention, or deployment readiness. © 2026 Mueller.

Title: From Aging-Aware Operation to Circular Value Retention: A Circular Battery Digital Twin for Electric Bus Fleets
Source title: IFIP Advances in Information and Communication Technology
Affiliations: DigiCircle Research Group, Mälardalen University, Eskilstuna, Sweden
Authors with affiliations: Fattouh A., DigiCircle Research Group, Mälardalen University, Eskilstuna, Sweden; Dahlquist E., DigiCircle Research Group, Mälardalen University, Eskilstuna, Sweden; Chirumalla K., DigiCircle Research Group, Mälardalen University, Eskilstuna, Sweden
Abstract: The electrification of public transport has introduced new challenges in managing lithium-ion battery degradation, operational efficiency, and lifecycle sustainability. While battery digital twins (BDTs) have emerged as a promising solution for monitoring and prediction, most existing approaches remain limited to short-term state estimation and do not exploit lifecycle data for circular decision-making. This paper proposes a Circular Battery Digital Twin (CBDT) framework that integrates aging-aware operation, predictive lifecycle modeling, and circular value retention within a unified architecture. The framework combines real-world operational, environmental, and maintenance data to continuously calibrate a semi-empirical degradation model supporting multiple use cases, including route reassignment and second-life assessment. The framework is demonstrated using a multi-year dataset from a real electric bus operating in Sweden. The bus operates with a 60 kWh LFP battery pack and relies exclusively on pantograph charging at terminus stops. The results show that CBDT enables consistent degradation estimation, supports cost-aware operational decisions, and provides a pathway toward circular battery management. The framework successfully identified an optimal reassignment threshold at 70% load that extends operational life by 45%. The study demonstrates how integrating multi-source data and lifecycle intelligence enables the transition from reactive battery management to proactive and circular decision-making. © IFIP International Federation for Information Processing 2027.

Title: A critical review: Machine learning and advanced simulation in steel heat treatment

Abstract: Steel heat treatment is governed by coupled heat transfer, diffusion, phase transformation, and stress development, yet industrial practice still relies on empirical diagrams and trial-and-error. This review critically examines machine learning and advanced simulation as design tools for that practice, spanning physics-based simulation, supervised learning, computer vision, physics-informed learning, surrogate modeling, inverse design, and digital twins. Quenching and tempering, thermochemical carburizing, localized induction and laser processing, press hardening, and additive-manufacturing post-processing are analyzed as separate mechanism-specific families rather than pooled as one process class. The evidence base is uneven: most studies rely on simulation or retrospective internal validation, only isolated reports include prospective component-scale tests, and none documents sustained closed-loop production control. Tree ensembles and kernel methods are strong baselines for the small, structured datasets typical of heat-treatment research, but no model family is universally superior. Validation design matters more than architecture: in one vision study, yield-strength R2 rose from 0.43 under specimen-grouped validation to 0.97 under a leaky image split, and equation-generated targets merely emulate encoded correlations rather than validate physics. Hybrid models improve data efficiency and physical consistency, but evidence for extrapolation and plant transfer remains limited. A six-level validation hierarchy is proposed to separate random-holdout accuracy from grouped, external, temporal, prospective, and closed-loop evidence. Critical gaps persist in multimodal data integration, uncertainty quantification, causal process understanding, benchmarks, and safety-constrained control. © IMechE 2026

Abstract: Underground hydrogen storage is increasingly positioned as a long-duration flexibility option for renewable-dominated energy systems. Dependable deployment, however, is constrained by coupled uncertainties spanning multiphase flow, pore-scale interfacial physics, reactive transport, and potential microbiological effects. To improve the applicability and generalisability of physics-informed artificial intelligence for underground hydrogen storage, we conducted a PRISMA 2020 systematic literature review of studies published from 2020 to 2026. The Scopus and Google Scholar searches retrieved 1071 records. After deduplication, 872 unique records remained, and 676 full texts were assessed for eligibility. From these, 51 primary studies relevant to PI-AI for UHS were retained for synthesis after an evidence-quality appraisal gate, comprising 49 UHS-explicit studies and 2 methodologically adjacent studies, retained for transferable PI-AI insights. We examined the complexity of applying physics-informed learning across pore-to-field scales and how this complexity contributes to barriers to transferability, reproducibility, and decision readiness. Specifically, we synthesised evidence across five themes: pore-scale interfacial physics; reactive transport, sorption, and biogeochemistry; reservoir-scale surrogate architectures; uncertainty and data assimilation readiness; and multi-objective design and operational optimisation. Each study was also coded by task, model family, uncertainty practice, and validation strength. Only 9 of the 51 included studies (17.6%) reported predictive intervals or distributions consistent with quantified predictive uncertainty (UQ-A), and just one of these reported fully calibrated empirical-coverage checks, identifying uncertainty quantification as the most consequential evidence gap in the reviewed corpus. Title: Phase-Guided Bayesian Model-Based Imputation for Missing Sensor Data in Mass-Spring-Damper Systems
Source title: Conference Record - IEEE Instrumentation and Measurement Technology Conference
Affiliations: Missouri University of Science and Technology, Department of Computer Engineering, Rolla, United States
Authors with affiliations: Bouraima M.O., Missouri University of Science and Technology, Department of Computer Engineering, Rolla, United States; Zawodniok M., Missouri University of Science and Technology, Department of Computer Engineering, Rolla, United States
Abstract: Missing sensor data severely degrades parameter estimation in dynamic systems. In digital-twin applications for mechanical equipment, gaps in vibration or displacement measurements corrupt phase estimates, causing the virtual twin to diverge from the physical system and undermining both real-time monitoring and predictive-maintenance decisions. To address this challenge, we propose a novel Phase-Guided Bayesian Model-Based Imputation (PGMI-Bayesian) that uses a physics-guided two-stage scheme for reconstructing missing samples and refining phase estimation in a mass-spring-damper system. The approach first generates model-consistent estimations and then applies a weak Bayesian shrinkage update. Monte Carlo results show that PGMI-Bayesian consistently achieves lower variance, Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and Mean Squared Error (MSE) than both observed-only estimation and standard imputation strategies. Although it does not reach the complete-data Cramér-Rao Lower Bound, the method remains well below the Missing Completely at Random (MCAR) CRLB for missingness up to 30%. Entropy analysis further confirms that PGMI-Bayesian produces the lowest-uncertainty reconstructions, demonstrating that physics-guided reconstruction can meaningfully enhance estimator efficiency under missing data. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: The increased occurrence of extreme weather events, cyber-physical disturbances, and electrification requires distribution systems to sustain critical services and recover quickly under adverse conditions. Meanwhile, the penetration of DERs, digitally controlled assets, and decentralized energy markets is transforming the traditional distribution networks into active and flexible systems. Virtual power plants (VPPs) and peer-to-peer (P2P) energy trading are two types of complementary flexibility, but their coordinated role in resilience-oriented distribution systems operation has not been sufficiently synthesized. This review investigates the incorporation of distribution systems resilience, VPP aggregation, DER and battery energy storage system (BESS) coordination, and centralized/decentralized energy trading based on around 160 peer-reviewed studies. This review offers an in-depth synthesis of the resilience metrics, VPP architectures and control strategies, P2P and transactive-energy mechanisms, and optimization approaches for the distribution systems with DERs. Besides the synthesis of the literature, a scenario-based numerical assessment of the coordinated operation of DERs and BESS under single and multi-fault conditions is performed utilizing the IEEE 33-bus radial distribution system (RDS). The four optimization methods GA, GWO, HPOA, and COA are evaluated using 30 matched experimental runs, and the difference of performance is compared by Wilcoxon signed-rank and Friedman tests. The results show that the coordinated VPP operation enhances the load restoration and decreases the energy not served (ENS), while it provides voltage support and accelerates the recovery during the outage conditions considered. The integrated resilience-aware operation further shows the complementary role of DER/BESS coordination and P2P energy trading in enhancing the technical and economic performance. The review highlights important gaps in coupled uncertainty and cascading-failure modeling, network-aware transactive-energy coordination, cyber-secure VPP operation, scalable multi-VPP control, resilience-oriented market valuation, interoperability and experimental validation. Future research should target integrated and scalable cyber-physical-economic frameworks with AI-assisted adaptive control, digital twins, distributed and federated VPP coordination, resilient P2P markets, larger-system validation, and hardware-in-the-loop and field demonstrations. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Design of large-scale floating offshore wind turbines: A review of advances and challenges
Affiliations: School of Energy and Power Engineering, University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, Shanghai, 200093, China; Huaneng Clean Energy Research Institute (CERI), Beijing, 102209, China

Abstract: Reliable design of floating offshore wind turbines requires balancing energy production, structural reliability and cost under coupled interactions among aerodynamics, hydrodynamics, structural dynamics and turbine control. This review examines horizontal-axis floating turbines, focusing on how blade, floater, mooring and control design affect system response. Physical tests, numerical models and data-assisted methods are evaluated in terms of predictive accuracy, computational cost and validation evidence. Platform motion alters the relative rotor inflow, while control strategies that suppress platform motion can increase fatigue loads under certain operating conditions. Reported fatigue changes therefore remain specific to the turbine configuration, environmental conditions and operating state. Environmental uncertainty, experimental scaling and limited field data constrain validation; predictive accuracy depends on the representation of the governing physical mechanisms and the reliability of environmental and structural inputs. A validation procedure is proposed comprising five groups of cases covering basic model checks, aerodynamics, hydrodynamics, coupled response and field comparisons. Machine learning and digital twins can support load estimation and maintenance planning, with performance evaluated under conditions excluded from calibration and training. Research priorities thus include coordinated structural and control optimization, uncertainty propagation in lifetime fatigue prediction, and independent model validation under fault and shutdown conditions. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Digital twins in toxicology: Toward predictive, personalized and real-time risk assessment
Affiliations: Centre for Basic and Applied Research, Faculty of Informatics and Management, University of Hradec Kralove, Hradec Kralove, 50003, Czech Republic; Department of Chemistry, Faculty of Sciences, University of Hradec Kralove, Hradec Kralove, 50003, Czech Republic; Center of Advanced Innovation Technologies, VSB-Technical University of Ostrava, Poruba, Ostrava, 708 00, Czech Republic

Abstract: Toxicology has accumulated many predictive tools - physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models, quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP) frameworks organ-on-chip systems, quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) models, adverse outcome pathway (AOP) networks and machine-learning approaches. Yet predictive practice remains fragmented. Each tool captures a slice of biology; few capture the whole; none captures the patient. We argue that the concept of a digital twin - a continuously updated, mechanistically grounded, data-driven digital representation of an individual biological system - offers the missing organisational layer. We first trace the origin of digital twins from aerospace engineering through biomedicine into toxicology, emphasising how the defining properties (dynamic data assimilation at the pace a decision requires, multi-scale integration, hybrid mechanistic-statistical architecture, personalisation, predictive simulation) map onto existing toxicological methods. We then position PBPK and QSP as mature proto-twin components and name the architectural gaps - continuous data flow, uncertainty quantification, feedback-driven recalibration and regulatory-grade validation - that separate today's best models from a working twin. A four-layer architecture is proposed: data, mechanistic, AI and simulation. Six published systems are tested against the five conditions; none satisfies all five. We examine applications in drug development, personalised risk assessment, mass-poisoning response, chemical-biological-radiological-nuclear (CBRN) preparedness and antidote discovery for unknown toxins. Finally, we confront the translational gap: data heterogeneity, validation standards, interpretability, regulatory acceptance and ethical custody of patient-level models. Toxicology, we conclude, has most of the ingredients needed for digital-twin implementation; what remains is the integration work, two unresolved scientific problems and the institutional willingness to address them. Title: Dynamic physics-based digital twin for supervisory, condition monitoring and fault diagnosis of industrial turboshaft engines
Affiliations: Faculty of Mechanical Engieering, University of Guilan, Rasht, Iran; Intelligent Systems and Advanced Control Lab, University of Guilan, Rasht, Iran
Authors with affiliations: Mostafavi A., Faculty of Mechanical Engieering, University of Guilan, Rasht, Iran; Chaibakhsh A., Intelligent Systems and Advanced Control Lab, University of Guilan, Rasht, Iran
Abstract: This study presents a digital-twin (DT) framework for real-time condition monitoring and fault diagnosis of industrial turboshaft engines. The proposed architecture employs physics-based semi-empirical models as the core of the twin, which are calibrated using operational data collected under both nominal and off-design conditions. Given that gas turbines are prone to diverse faults with varying onset times, magnitudes, and signatures, a time-windowed residual embedding (TWRE) method is introduced to enhance the temporal representation of diagnostic features. In addition, a data-driven dynamic adaptive thresholding scheme is applied to improve robustness against environmental variations and uncertainties. By providing a comprehensive fault table, feature spaces are systematically linked to distinct fault scenarios using pattern recognition classifiers. Finally, a decision fusion mechanism is implemented to integrate diagnostic outputs based on fault types and their severities. To assess the performance of the proposed system, four sample faults are considered for simulation studies. The results indicate that the system reliably tracks fault progression and accurately detects both evident and latent anomalies, providing clear fault timelines for early alarm generation. The effectiveness of integrating semi-empirical modelling and advanced signal processing in a digital twin framework is confirmed for real-time fault monitoring and diagnosis of industrial gas turbines. © 2025 The Author(s). Title: Co-evolution of models and solutions: a multi-objective genetic algorithm for self-correcting digital twins
Affiliations: Faculty of Pharmacy, Shahid Sadoughi University of Medical Science, Yazd, Iran; Department of Mathematics, Isf.C, Islamic Azad University, Isfahan, Iran
Authors with affiliations: Jalali-Varnamkhasti M., Faculty of Pharmacy, Shahid Sadoughi University of Medical Science, Yazd, Iran; Varnamkhasti M.J., Department of Mathematics, Isf.C, Islamic Azad University, Isfahan, Iran
Abstract: Digital-twin (DT) systems have emerged as critical enablers of intelligent cyber–physical interaction, yet their effectiveness is limited by static modelling and non-adaptive optimisation mechanisms. This article presents a co-evolutionary framework that simultaneously evolves the DT model and its optimisation strategy, achieving self-correcting performance in dynamic environments. The framework integrates a Multi-Task Genetic Algorithm (MTGA) that unifies three concurrent evolutionary processes model calibration, decision optimisation, and uncertainty-guided exploration within a closed feedback loop. A formal theoretical foundation is developed to describe the coupled fitness landscapes and feedback–response operators that govern reciprocal adaptation between model and optimiser. The architecture incorporates an uncertainty-aware selection mechanism, where predictive variance from the surrogate model dynamically influences evolutionary pressure, thereby improving both model fidelity and solution robustness. Experimental validation on a Grid ALU Processor configuration problem demonstrates that the proposed MTGA achieves up to 60% reduction in model prediction error, 22% improvement in Pareto-front hypervolume, and enhanced stability under nonstationary conditions compared with NSGA-II, SPEA2, and CNSGA-II. These findings confirm that co-evolutionary coupling yields superior convergence and sustained reliability, positioning this framework as a foundation for next-generation self-learning, adaptive DTs in complex engineering domains. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Confidence-aware synchronized digital twin and deep deterministic policy gradient for battery–ultracapacitor electric vehicle energy management
Affiliations: Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, American International University-Bangladesh, Dhaka, Bangladesh
Authors with affiliations: Anonto H.Z., Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, American International University-Bangladesh, Dhaka, Bangladesh; Shufian A., Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, American International University-Bangladesh, Dhaka, Bangladesh; Pathik B.B., Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, American International University-Bangladesh, Dhaka, Bangladesh; Hasan M., Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, American International University-Bangladesh, Dhaka, Bangladesh; Hazari M.R., Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, American International University-Bangladesh, Dhaka, Bangladesh; Mannan M.A., Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, American International University-Bangladesh, Dhaka, Bangladesh
Abstract: This study develops a confidence-aware synchronized digital-twin deep deterministic policy gradient (CA-SDT-DDPG) energy-management system for a battery–ultracapacitor electric vehicle. In contrast to a generic simulation-labelled twin, the proposed architecture separates the physical, data/communication, virtual-model and twin-service layers; synchronizes state of charge (SOC), power demand, battery temperature and resistance estimates; and uses a short-horizon demand forecast, uncertainty-aware battery-stress penalty and safety projection before commands reach the bidirectional direct current-to-direct current (DC/DC) converters. Performance was assessed with a matched, repeated-seed benchmark rather than single-run comparisons. Five dataset-informed driving-profile families were each evaluated with six independent seeds (30 runs per method) using identical delivered wheel-energy demand and explicit ultracapacitor terminal-energy normalization. The comparator set comprised rule-based control, the equivalent consumption minimization strategy (ECMS), Q-learning, model predictive control (MPC), standalone deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG), twin delayed DDPG (TD3), soft actor–critic (SAC) and proximal policy optimization (PPO). CA-SDT-DDPG achieved 94.95±0.40% mean conversion efficiency and a 0.0248±0.0140% monotonic equivalent battery-stress/degradation index with zero constraint violations. Relative to standalone DDPG, the digital-twin and confidence-aware extensions reduced the degradation index by 18.6% while changing mean efficiency by +0.11 percentage point; the 95% paired-bootstrap interval for the efficiency change crossed zero, whereas the interval for the degradation change remained entirely below zero. Against MPC, mean efficiency was statistically indistinguishable and the mean degradation proxy was about 4.0% lower, although this difference was not statistically clear. A 9,000-sample dataset-informed synthetic telemetry set, bounded by a 2025 one-second real-world battery-electric-vehicle (BEV) dataset, is additionally used for diagnostic correlation, three-dimensional (3D) stress-surface, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and classifier analyses; the light gradient-boosting machine (LightGBM) obtained a macro-F1 of 0.977 for the derived battery-stress classes. These machine-learning diagnostics are presented as interpretability checks rather than independent proof of controller superiority. The study remains simulation based; hardware-in-the-loop and vehicle validation are identified as the next validation stage. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Multiscale Digital-Twin Modeling of Energy-Storage Materials by Integrating First-Principles Calculations and Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials

Authors with affiliations: Li Y., Department of Physics and Information Engineering, Cangzhou Normal University, Cangzhou, 061001, China; Tang D., Department of Physics and Information Engineering, Cangzhou Normal University, Cangzhou, 061001, China
Abstract: Conventional modeling of energy-storage materials is constrained by the computational cost of first-principles calculations, limited electrochemical-state awareness in machine-learning interatomic potentials, and weak coupling between materials-scale models and online battery decision-making. This study proposes a first-principles-constrained electrochemically conditioned machine-learning interatomic potential (FP-EMLP) integrated with a multiscale digital-twin framework (FP-EMLP-DT). A multistate configuration space spanning ion concentration, temperature, defects, strain, and phase boundaries is combined with active learning based on committee uncertainty, structural novelty, and physics-based risk. The equivariant graph model incorporates electrochemical-state gating, charge-conserving projection, and differentiable long-range electrostatics, and is trained using energies, forces, stresses, equilibrium voltages, and migration barriers. Predicted diffusion coefficients, free energies, elastic tensors, and chemical expansion coefficients are transferred to an electrochemical-mechanical-thermal-damage model. The resulting model is further integrated with a physics-based reduced-order network, uncertainty-gated residual learning, online data assimilation, and degradation-aware control. FP-EMLP achieves mean absolute errors of 6.5meV atom-1, 33meV Å-1, 0.051V, and 0.038eV for energy, force, voltage, and migration barrier, respectively, with a 4.8 aggregate relative error across multiscale fields. Active learning reduces required first-principles labels by 33.3 while covering 91.2 of high-risk configurations. FP-EMLP-DT achieves mean absolute errors of 0.93 for state of charge and 1.21 for state of health. Degradation-aware control reduces maximum material stress and damage increment by 16.5 and 36.8, respectively, demonstrating an effective multiscale pathway from electronic structure to online battery management. © 2026 Yan Li et al., licensed to EAI. Title: AI-, DIGITAL-TWIN-, AND QUANTUM-ENABLED ROLLING-HORIZON OPTIMIZATION FOR YARD ALLOCATION AND GATE APPOINTMENT COMPLIANCE IN MODULAR CONTAINER TERMINALS
Source title: International Maritime Transport and Logistics Conference
Affiliations: Department of Political and International Sciences, University of Genoa, Piazza Emanuele Brignole 3A, Central Tower, Genoa, 16126, Italy
Authors with affiliations: Revetria R., Department of Political and International Sciences, University of Genoa, Piazza Emanuele Brignole 3A, Central Tower, Genoa, 16126, Italy; Rozhok A., Department of Political and International Sciences, University of Genoa, Piazza Emanuele Brignole 3A, Central Tower, Genoa, 16126, Italy
Abstract: Container terminals operate under increasingly tight capacity, energy, and service-level constraints, while facing growing uncertainty in arrival patterns, handling operations, and hinterland interactions. This paper proposes a hybrid decision-support framework that integrates advanced Artificial Intelligence techniques, Digital Twin modeling, and quantum-inspired optimization to address yard planning and operational optimization in container terminals. The core problem is formulated as a block-to-area assignment under soft and hard capacity constraints, priority rules, and rolling-horizon forecasts. The problem is mapped to a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) formulation and solved using both classical and quantum-inspired approaches, including the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA). Two alternative modeling strategies are investigated: a one-hot encoding with deterministic feasibility repair, and a feasibility-by-design binary encoding that reduces the number of decision variables and enforces assignment constraints structurally. A Digital Twin of the container yard acts as a truth model and constraint oracle, translating abstract optimization decisions into operational Key Performance Indicators such as reshuffling effort, crane interference, and truck waiting times. Computational experiments on a modular yard scenario highlight the trade-offs between encoding choice, feasibility, solution quality, and computational cost under time-bounded quantum-inspired optimization. The results demonstrate that quantum-inspired methods can effectively support combinatorial decision-making in port operations when combined with appropriate encodings and simulation-based validation. Rather than replacing existing planning tools, the proposed framework positions quantum optimization as a complementary accelerator within a scalable, explainable, and industry-ready Digital Twin-based decision-support architecture. Title: Exploring the metaverse: integrating emerging technologies for Industry 5.0 advancement
Affiliations: Khatam University, Tehran, Iran; Western Sydney University, Sydney, Australia
Authors with affiliations: Faraji A., Khatam University, Tehran, Iran, Western Sydney University, Sydney, Australia; Homayoon Arya S., Khatam University, Tehran, Iran; Ghasemi E., Khatam University, Tehran, Iran; Abagheri Mahabadi H., Khatam University, Tehran, Iran; Perera S., Western Sydney University, Sydney, Australia
Abstract: Purpose – This paper aims to explore the application of the Metaverse in the construction industry through an in-depth literature review. It highlights the core enabling technologies and investigates how they contribute to creating immersive, intelligent and sustainable construction practices in line with Industry 5.0 ideals. Design/methodology/approach – This study utilizes a systematic literature review methodology, examining 194 peer-reviewed articles published from 2015 to 2024. The papers were selected from top academic databases using specific inclusion and exclusion criteria. The review centers on Metaverse applications, the foundational technologies involved and their influence on various aspects of the construction industry. Findings – The results highlight the growing scholarly interest in the application of Metaverse technologies in the building sector, which has grown significantly since 2021. Key technologies identified include augmented reality, virtual reality, mixed reality, extended reality (XR), building information modeling, Digital Twin, the Internet of Things, artificial intelligence and blockchain technology (BCT). These technologies facilitate real-time collaboration, immersive visual environments, secure data exchange and smart decision-making processes. Seven major areas of the construction industry – project management, architectural design, urban planning, construction education, civil engineering, energy management and supply chain coordination – are seeing a surge in innovation because of the Metaverse. Full integration is nevertheless hindered by persistent issues with data privacy, interoperability and regulatory uncertainty, despite its potential. Practical implications – This study provides practical insights for industry stakeholders aiming to leverage Metaverse technologies for digital transformation in construction. It emphasizes the need for integrated frameworks, skilled workforce development and consideration of environmental and economic impacts. Originality/value – This paper offers a novel synthesis of current literature at the intersection of Metaverse technologies and construction, highlighting research gaps and suggesting directions for future exploration. It contributes to the theoretical and practical understanding of how Metaverse adoption can drive smart, sustainable and human-centric innovation in the construction industry. © 2025 Emerald Publishing Limited

Abstract: Chemical research spans multiple scales from molecules to processes and industrial systems, and is inherently characterized by high dimensionality, strong coupling, and pronounced nonlinearity. Traditional research paradigms relying on empirical heuristics, isolated simulations, and iterative experimentation are increasingly inadequate to meet the emerging demands for green transformation, intelligent manufacturing, and sustainable development. In this work, we systematically review a state-of-the-art “four-dimensional integrated” intelligent research paradigm driven by large language models (LLMs), and elucidate its theoretical foundation, technical architecture, and implementation pathways for reconstructing the chemical research framework. Centered on LLMs as the cognitive core, the proposed paradigm integrates four key dimensions: knowledge engine, molecular reasoning, process simulation, and intelligent decision-making. At the knowledge level, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and knowledge graph technologies are synergistically combined to construct a dynamic and computable knowledge infrastructure that semantically unifies literature, patents, and experimental data. This enables the transition from conventional information retrieval to evidence-based knowledge discovery and reasoning-oriented scientific research. At the molecular level, generative foundation models, multi-objective optimization models, and multimodal molecular representation learning are integrated with physical constraints and chemical ontologies, forming a closed intelligent loop from molecular conception and structure generation to reaction planning, energy verification, and synthesizability assessment. This framework significantly accelerates the discovery of functional molecules and advanced materials while mitigating chemical hallucination risks. At the process level, physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), neural operators, and digital twin technologies are introduced to bridge mechanistic models with data-driven surrogates, enabling cross-scale, high-fidelity, and computationally efficient modeling of complex multiphase transport, reaction, and energy conversion processes. In parallel, LLM-driven multi-agent automation frameworks enable end-to-end workflows for CFD/ FEM model generation, simulation execution, and intelligent post-analysis, substantially lowering the technical barrier for high-level process simulations. At the decision-making level, ontology engineering serves as the semantic foundation that formalizes chemical entities, equipment, unit operations, and control logic into a unified machine-interpretable structure. On this basis, reinforcement learning and uncertainty-aware optimization construct an interpretable, traceable, and transferable knowledge-driven decision loop, enabling semantic-level integration of process control, alarm diagnosis, batch optimization, and system-wide sustainable operation. The four dimensions work synergistically to form an intelligent cognitive chain that links molecules, processes, and systems, driving the transformation of chemical research from experience-driven to inference-driven paradigms. Furthermore, we propose the emerging concept of an ontology-driven multi-agent collaborative system (OD-MAS), which envisions a transition from isolated task-level intelligence toward system-level collaboration and knowledge-level autonomy. OD-MAS enables multiple specialized intelligent agents to operate within a unified semantic space for coordinated discovery, simulation, optimization, and safety evaluation. This framework provides a fundamental semantic infrastructure for the interoperability of data, models, and decisions, and establishes methodological and strategic foundations for the deep integration of green chemistry, intelligent manufacturing, and autonomous scientific discovery. © 2026 Science Press. Title: Digital Twins for Nuclear Reactor Monitoring and Operational Intelligence: A Systematic Scoping Review
Affiliations: Department of Computer Systems and Technologies, Technical University of Sofia, Sofia, 1000, Bulgaria
Authors with affiliations: Gancheva V., Department of Computer Systems and Technologies, Technical University of Sofia, Sofia, 1000, Bulgaria
Abstract: Digital twins (DTs) are increasingly proposed for nuclear-reactor monitoring, diagnosis, prediction, control, and decision support, but the maturity of reported systems is difficult to compare because DT realization, physical anchoring, synchronization, adaptation, validation, real-time execution, and trustworthiness are often conflated. This systematic scoping review maps substantive DT research for nuclear fission reactors and nuclear power plants using a strict substantive-DT definition and a multidimensional evidence-coding framework covering DT realization, physical anchoring, adaptation, validation, real-time capability, and trustworthiness. Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and IEEE Xplore yielded 845 database records and 590 unique records after deduplication. A multi-pass title/abstract workflow classified 182 records as Include, 397 as excluded from the primary-study stream, and 11 as Uncertain, yielding 193 reports sought for retrieval. Despite iterative multi-source retrieval attempts, 96 reports could not be retrieved. One additional Uncertain conference report was linked to an already retained journal report and was not treated as an independent report; 96 retrieved reports underwent primary full-text eligibility assessment. Seventy-one retrieved and eligible peer-reviewed primary reports met the inclusion criteria. Of these, 44/71 (62%) were Tier A implemented or integrated DT systems. Physical anchoring ranged from P0 simulation-only realization (39/71, 55%) to P3 operating-reactor or plant evidence (9/71, 13%); within P3, four reports used retrospective/offline operating data and five demonstrated live or near-live reactor/plant linkage. Validation evidence comprised 40/71 reports (56%) with development-linked validation (V1), 26/71 (37%) with separated empirical or benchmark validation (V2), and 5/71 (7%) with prospective, challenge-based, or independently confirmed validation (V3). Adaptation was limited: 51/71 reports (72%) demonstrated no adaptation (A0), 3/71 (4%) episodic or intermittent recalibration (A1), 5/71 (7%) online state synchronization/estimation (A2-S), 12/71 (17%) online parameter/model adaptation (A2-P), and none met the A3 criterion. Computational real-time capability was supported in 42/71 reports (59%), whereas integrated real- or near-real-time execution was demonstrated in 27/71 (38%); live physical-data ingestion, explicit recurring physical-to-digital synchronization, and automatic DT-to-physical actuation were demonstrated in 11/71 (15%), 5/71 (7%), and 1/71 (1%), respectively. Hybrid modelling was the dominant paradigm (34/71, 48%). Trustworthiness was asymmetric: calibration and robustness/OOD assessment were much more common than uncertainty quantification, explainability, cybersecurity, traceability, human oversight, or demonstrated regulatory readiness. A targeted data audit identified only four reports linked to clearly open and reusable benchmark or downloadable resources. Family-aware, quality, physical-evidence, temporal, and data-access sensitivity analyses did not materially change the central conclusions. Nuclear-DT maturity is best understood as multidimensional; future progress requires staged physical validation, bounded adaptive synchronization, trustworthy decision support, reproducible data/model provenance, and independent deployment-oriented validation. © 2026 by the author.

Title: Multi-Criteria Decision-Making and Digital Twins for Sustainable Environmental Planning and Management: Methods, Applications, and Limitations: A Review
Affiliations: School of Agriculture and Food Sciences, The University of Queensland, Brisbane, 4072, QLD, Australia
Authors with affiliations: Dayananda B., School of Agriculture and Food Sciences, The University of Queensland, Brisbane, 4072, QLD, Australia
Abstract: Environmental planning and management must reconcile multiple sustainability objectives, uncertain impacts, and diverse stakeholder priorities, often under data-rich but fragmented information environments. Multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) offers structured approaches for comparing alternatives, while digital twins and related smart tools (e.g., GIS, BIM, IoT monitoring, and decision support platforms) can represent system behaviour and support scenario testing. This article is a comprehensive narrative review (not a registered systematic review or meta-analysis). It synthesises a documented evidence base of 68 sources identified through Scopus/Web of Science-style Boolean strings, citation chasing, and a reproducible OpenAlex retrieval executed on 2 September 2026. Coding of that evidence base shows AHP/ANP as the most frequent MCDM family emphasis, GIS as the most frequent digital layer, and GIS/spatial MCDM (Pattern A) as the most frequent explicit coupling path; fully operational bidirectional twins and closed adaptive ranking loops remain uncommon. The typology contribution is an organising lens that jointly classifies (i) decision structure, (ii) digital representation class (conventional smart tool, partial twin, or fully operational twin), and (iii) coupling Patterns A–D; this differs from method-only MCDM surveys and architecture-only twin reviews by making coupling the unit of synthesis. Recurring limitations include uneven uncertainty treatment and validation, interoperability and cost barriers, governance and equity gaps, and rare monitoring-to-ranking loops. Priorities are transparent data lineage, uncertainty-aware and equity-conscious coupling, interoperable decision layers, and post-implementation learning. © 2026 by the author.

Title: Artificial-Intelligence-Enabled Wind-Grid Intelligence Systems: A Systematic Review of AI Evolution, Functional Intelligence Layers, and Deployment Readiness

Abstract: The accelerated adoption of renewable energy (RE) systems has heightened the complexity of electricity grid operations, primarily due to the uncertainty, variability, and distributed nature of wind power generation. Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a transformative tool for addressing these challenges by facilitating advanced forecasting, adaptive control, optimization, and intelligent decision-making. Nevertheless, the maturity of AI-enabled Wind-Grid Intelligence Systems (WGIS), encompassing functional capabilities, methodological development, and practical deployment readiness, remains inadequately characterized. This systematic review assesses the current landscape of AI-enabled WGIS by synthesizing findings from 56 empirical studies. The literature was categorized using a structured framework that examined each study’s evidence source, AI methodologies, WGIS layer, target application, and validation maturity. The analysis indicates that WGIS research encompasses both wind-specific applications and transferable intelligent-grid technologies. Specifically, 48.2% of studies focus on wind-related challenges, while 51.8% address broader intelligent-grid solutions. Methodological trends reveal a shift toward advanced AI architectures, with deep learning as the predominant approach (50.0%), followed by reinforcement learning (33.9%) and traditional machine learning (8.9%). Although techniques such as graph intelligence and physics-informed AI are currently underrepresented, they offer considerable potential to enhance the reliability and contextual awareness of WGIS architectures. Analysis using a five-layer WGIS intelligence framework demonstrates that layer 2, predictive intelligence, is the primary research focus, accounting for 51.8% of studies, followed by layer 4, adaptive control intelligence, at 21.4%. In contrast, layer 5, strategic intelligence, is underexplored, with only 7.1% of studies addressing this area. This distribution indicates that current research prioritizes prediction and operational support rather than autonomous strategic decision-making. Furthermore, the validation maturity assessment reveals a substantial gap between AI development and practical implementation. Of the studies reviewed, 60.7% were classified at V1 using offline/stored-dataset validation, 37.5% at V2 using software simulation or co-simulation, and a single study (1.8%) reached V3 dedicated real-time hardware-coupled laboratory validation. No study satisfied the predefined criteria for pilot-scale demonstration or full operational deployment. Methodological-quality appraisal classified 39 studies (69.6%) as Higher-confidence and 17 (30.4%) as Moderate-confidence, with no Lower-confidence studies; restriction to the Higher-confidence subset did not alter the principal rank order conclusions. Accordingly, 98.2% of the evidence remained within the V1–V2 stages, while no study reached pilot-scale (V4) or operational (V5) deployment, underscoring the need for more robust validation pathways and industry-scale demonstrations. This review proposes a future WGIS development roadmap focused on integrated AI architectures, trustworthy AI, digital twin technologies, physics-informed learning, and real-world validation frameworks. The findings indicate that progress in WGIS will require a shift from prediction-oriented AI models to adaptive, explainable, and operational intelligent energy infrastructures that can support resilient renewable energy integration. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Generative adversarial networks with Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty quantification for structural health monitoring: Fibre Bragg grating data augmentation comparison in Hawk T1A aircraft
Affiliations: Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of Bath, Bath, BA2 7AY, United Kingdom
Authors with affiliations: Peiro A., Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of Bath, Bath, BA2 7AY, United Kingdom; Impraimakis M., Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of Bath, Bath, BA2 7AY, United Kingdom
Abstract: The signal generation capabilities of a novel data augmentation framework are examined in aerospace structures. First, the framework learns class-conditional temporal and spectral characteristics of the measured structural responses. It uses conditional generative adversarial network training and Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty quantification as a Bayesian approximation. This step enables stochastic signal synthesis and uncertainty quantification. Second, the generated responses are rigorously compared against experimental measurements across time, frequency, uncertainty, variability, and feature domains to assess physical realism, statistical consistency, and distributional fidelity. Finally, the synthetic data are evaluated to determine whether they should be incorporated into a supervised damage classification workflow. The framework is validated on the full-scale benchmark dataset from a BAE Systems Hawk T1A aircraft tested at the University of Sheffield’s Structural Dynamics Laboratory for Verification and Validation. The test involves acceleration, fibre Bragg grating strain, and nonlinear dynamic response measurements. The results demonstrate that the model accurately captures dominant structural dynamics, it guides on signal use for classification improvement based on uncertainty characteristics, and it provides meaningful uncertainty estimates linked to signal complexity and excitation characteristics. Importantly, the framework offers a realistic generative modelling plan as a robust digital twin component for data-driven structural health monitoring, supporting resilient decision-making for condition assessment in safety-critical aerospace systems. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: A systematic review and thematic analysis of physics-informed machine learning in construction and infrastructure systems
Affiliations: Department of Urban and Regional Planning, Faculty of Architecture, Center of Excellence in Urban Strategies and Healthy Cities, Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok, Thailand; Center of Excellence in Green Tech in Architecture, Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok, Thailand; Department of Materials Science, Faculty of Science, Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok, Thailand

Abstract: This study conducts a systematic review and thematic analysis to explore how physics-informed machine learning (PIML) can enhance reliability in infrastructure assessment and construction management. Previous studies are classified based on state estimation, digital twin updating, performance prediction, deterioration prediction, multi-hazard response analysis, and maintenance and inspection decision support. Embedding governing physical laws in the learning process ensures that models adhere to mechanical principles. The analysis shows that PIML can enhance prediction stability, decrease data needs, and allow for the identification of concealed structural and construction parameters through inverse methods. Importantly, integrating mechanics into data-driven models transforms machine learning from a curve-fitting tool into a verification-compatible analysis method. Constraining predictions with physical laws reduces unrealistic outputs; enables extrapolation to unobserved hazard scenarios such as earthquakes, winds, and floods; and facilitates estimation of deterioration states needed for risk-informed maintenance planning. The reviewed literature shows that these capabilities enable operational digital twins that continuously update infrastructure conditions using real-time monitoring data. However, there are persistent challenges, including computational expenses, inadequate uncertainty quantification, limited multi-physics integration, and the lack of benchmark datasets and regulatory approval. This review concludes that PIML offers a pathway to next-generation artificial intelligence in construction and infrastructure systems by bridging monitoring data and engineering mechanics. As a reliability engine within digital twin frameworks, PIML supports predictive maintenance, performance-based design, and resilience-oriented management of existing and future infrastructure systems. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Training LLMs with Reinforcement Learning over Digital Twin Representations for Reasoning-Intensive Surgical VideoQA
Affiliations: Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, United States
Authors with affiliations: Shen Y., Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, United States; Zhang H., Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, United States; Unberath M., Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, United States
Abstract: Surgical video question answering requires multi-step reasoning across semantic, spatial, and temporal dimensions. Existing methods architecturally compress videos into discrete token representations and couple visual perception with reasoning. This approach fragments continuous spatial-temporal relationships and has been shown to restrict multi-step reasoning capabilities. We introduce a reinforcement learning (RL) framework that trains large language models (LLMs) to decouple perception from reasoning by operating over digital twin representations constructed from surgical foundation models. Additionally, we introduce hierarchical representations across frame, temporal window, and procedure levels with probabilistic uncertainty estimates. Finally, we propose a novel reward that combines format validation with accuracy assessment through clinical plausibility evaluation and uncertainty-aware calibration for training. To demonstrate the capabilities of this approach, we introduce REAL-Colon-Reason, a colonoscopic benchmark with 2000 question-answer pairs across three complexity levels. We achieve state-of-the-art performance on REAL-Colon-Reason and two existing surgical VideoQA benchmarks REAL-Colon-VQA and EndoVis18-VQA. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: From smart sensing to adaptive remediation: artificial intelligence and Internet of Things for persistent organic pollutants
Affiliations: Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hung Hom, Hong Kong; Advanced Radiation Technology Institute (ARTI), Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute, Jeongeup, 56212, South Korea; Department of Radiation Science, University of Science and Technology, Daejeon, 34113, South Korea; Institute of Water Management and Treatment Technologies, Sustainability and Environment Sector, King Abdulaziz City for Science and Technology (KACST), Riyadh, 11442, Saudi Arabia; Environmental Engineering Department, Egypt-Japan University of Science and Technology, Alexandria, 21934, Egypt

Abstract: Persistent organic pollutants (POPs) remain a major environmental challenge because of their persistence, long-range transport, bioaccumulation, and resistance to degradation. Conventional monitoring and remediation systems provide reliable analytical performance but are largely fragmented, laboratory dependent, and unable to deliver the continuous, predictive, and adaptive management required for complex, dynamic contamination scenarios. Recent literature reports substantial advances in biosensors, Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled sensing, machine learning (ML), and artificial intelligence (AI) for pollutant detection, forecasting, source identification, and remediation optimization. However, these developments often operate separately, with limited coordination between environmental sensing, data analytics, treatment processes, and decision-making. The literature further highlights persistent barriers to field deployment, including limited and geographically heterogeneous datasets, inconsistent sensor performance and calibration, restricted model transferability, insufficient independent validation, uncertainty in AI predictions, and the lack of mature regulatory frameworks for AI-assisted environmental assessment. From our perspective, the next advance in POP management should move beyond isolated AI applications toward integrated, closed-loop AI–IoT architectures that continuously connect sensing, prediction, remediation, and feedback control. Such systems could transform POP management from reactive assessment to proactive and adaptive environmental governance. Future progress will depend on standardized, Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR) environmental datasets, explainable and uncertainty-aware AI, robust field validation, and interoperable sensing infrastructures. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: From state estimation to active intelligence: safety-aware battery management for electric vehicles
Affiliations: College of Mechanical Engineering, Shandong Huayu University of Technology, Shandong, Dezhou, China; Office of Scientific Research, Shandong Huayu University of Technology, Shandong, Dezhou, China
Authors with affiliations: Li F., College of Mechanical Engineering, Shandong Huayu University of Technology, Shandong, Dezhou, China; Li Y., College of Mechanical Engineering, Shandong Huayu University of Technology, Shandong, Dezhou, China; Wu W., Office of Scientific Research, Shandong Huayu University of Technology, Shandong, Dezhou, China; Qiao H., College of Mechanical Engineering, Shandong Huayu University of Technology, Shandong, Dezhou, China; Jiang L., College of Mechanical Engineering, Shandong Huayu University of Technology, Shandong, Dezhou, China
Abstract: Battery management systems (BMSs) are increasingly required to convert incomplete electrical and thermal measurements into safe control actions rather than merely report battery states. This Mini Review focuses on two deployment questions that connect electrochemistry with control: how electrochemical states can be made observable with affordable diagnostics, and how charging, thermal, balancing, and health objectives can be arbitrated when their constraints conflict. We compare physics-based, equivalent-circuit, and data-driven representations using reported quantitative benchmarks, and show why cross-dataset accuracy alone is insufficient evidence of deployability. Particular attention is given to electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), distribution of relaxation times (DRT), galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT), and active pulse diagnostics as routes for linking measurable responses to interfacial kinetics, resistance growth, and transport limitations. A layered vehicle–edge–cloud architecture is proposed in which a deterministic safety supervisor enforces voltage, temperature, lithium-plating, power, imbalance, and uncertainty limits before performance optimization. The same framework is then examined for solid-state, lithium–sulfur, and sodium-ion batteries, where pressure, observability, and chemistry-specific calibration introduce new constraints. We conclude with a testable short-, mid-, and long-term roadmap centered on uncertainty calibration, pack-level validation, electrochemical observability, version-controlled learning, and safety-case evidence. Title: Circular manufacturing in sustainable production systems for building materials: A systematic scoping review of emerging pathways

Abstract: Circular manufacturing is gaining attention as the construction sector seeks to reduce resource extraction, construction and demolition waste, and environmental burdens from building material production. The current evidence, however, remains fragmented across material pathways, digital tools, assessment methods, and implementation barriers. A PRISMA based systematic scoping review was conducted using Scopus and Google Scholar for English language publications from 2015 to 2026. The review synthesized evidence on waste streams, circular manufacturing strategies, building material applications, environmental assessment, technical performance, digital tools, challenges, and future research needs. The findings indicate that circular manufacturing pathways may enable sustainable production of building materials, as long as feedstock quality, processing conditions, substitution rates, and the contexts in which materials are applied are rigorously managed. Alkali activated and geopolymer systems, recycled aggregate concrete, waste glass and ceramic based materials, bio-based composites, and polymer based products show potential to reduce reliance on virgin resources while maintaining functional material performance in selected applications. Digital and analytical tools, including LCA, BIM, GIS, digital twins, machine learning, sensor monitoring, and material characterization, can support environmental assessment, traceability, performance prediction, and decision making. Nevertheless, adoption remains constrained by material variability, incomplete LCA comparability, limited external validation of predictive models, durability uncertainty, leaching and safety concerns, fragmented standards, and weak integration between research evidence and industrial practice. Future studies should strengthen comparable LCA protocols, performance based standards, leaching and durability verification, externally validated predictive models, interoperable circular material data systems, and cross-sector collaboration. These priorities are essential for moving circular manufacturing from isolated material feasibility toward reliable and scalable construction practice. Title: SHINE: An Entropy-Guided Digital Twin Framework for 3D Myocardial Scar Reconstruction from Sparse CMR

Abstract: Accurate reconstruction of the arrhythmogenic myocardial substrate—specifically the conducting isthmuses essential for ventricular tachycardia (VT) ablation—depends on capturing fine-scale scar topology from sparse, anisotropic Late Gadolinium Enhancement (LGE) MRI. Given the pronounced anisotropy (e.g., 1.2 × 1.2 × 8.0 mm) and limited slice sampling, volumetric reconstruction constitutes a highly ill-posed inverse problem, often leading to aliasing artifacts and discontinuous “staircase” geometries under discrete interpolation schemes. To address this challenge, we propose substrate reconstruction as a continuous function learning task defined on a patient-specific anatomical manifold. We introduce SHINE (Scar Heterogeneity via Implicit Neural Encoding), a framework that constructs a mathematically consistent “Digital Twin” of the diseased myocardium. The pipeline integrates automated biventricular segmentation with a Statistical Shape Model (SSM) to establish a continuous anatomical prior. To reconstruct detailed scar morphology, we employ a Bayesian SIREN architecture with sinusoidal activation functions, enabling the representation of high-frequency geometric structures and mitigating the spectral bias persistent in conventional Neural Fields. Importantly, we introduce an Entropy-Weighted Dirichlet Energy loss, which uses epistemic uncertainty to adaptively enforce smoothness in data-sparse regions while preserving high-fidelity details in data-rich regions. Evaluated on a clinical VT cohort of 40 patients, SHINE significantly outperformed discrete interpolation and weakly supervised benchmarks, achieving a Dice Similarity Coefficient of 0.93 and a volumetric error of 3.1%. Notably, our method effectively addresses the Nyquist sampling gap, enabling recovery of sub-voxel conducting channels within a unified, topology-preserving 3D framework to support precision electrophysiology planning. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: A data-driven dynamic Bayesian network for health monitoring and maintenance decision support of marine diesel engines

Abstract: Performance monitoring and maintenance decision-making are critical components of machinery management for ensuring the safety, reliability, and operational efficiency of maritime systems. Recent advances in sensor technologies, data transmission capabilities, machine learning, and knowledge management have accelerated the transition from traditional fixed-interval maintenance towards condition-based and predictive maintenance strategies in the maritime industry. However, the health assessment of large two-stroke marine diesel engines remains challenging due to the presence of multiple interdependent operational parameters and their temporal uncertainties under varying sea and operational conditions. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel data-driven Dynamic Bayesian Network (DBN) framework for the health monitoring and maintenance decision support of large two-stroke marine diesel engines. The proposed framework integrates 15 operational parameters within a unified probabilistic model to capture temporal degradation and quantify health uncertainty through dynamic probabilistic reasoning. The framework was validated using operational data from a six-cylinder MAN B&W 6S50MC-C main engine. A five-day case study showed that cylinders 4 and 6 remained in the AMBER health state, while cylinder 5 was predicted to deteriorate from GREEN to AMBER after two days of operation, demonstrating the model's capability to predict health degradation trends. Sensitivity analysis identified Total Base Number (TBN) and iron content as the most influential indicators affecting engine health. Furthermore, water mist catcher performance, fuel viscosity, and exhaust temperature deviation exhibited the largest temporal variations, with average deviations of 4.31%, 3.91%, and 3.37%, respectively. The results demonstrate that the proposed DBN framework effectively captures temporal dependencies and operational uncertainty, enabling dynamic health assessment and risk-informed maintenance decision-making. By integrating multiple interdependent degradation factors within a unified probabilistic framework, the proposed approach provides an effective tool for condition-based maintenance and establishes a practical foundation for future maritime digital twin and intelligent maintenance applications. Abstract: Food Packaging 4.0 represents a paradigm shift in packaging systems, driven by the integration of Industry 4.0 technologies that transform packaging from a passive containment solution into an intelligent, connected, and data-enabled component of the food supply chain. This chapter examines the opportunities, limitations, and future perspectives of Food Packaging 4.0, with a focus on key enabling technologies, including artificial intelligence, big data analytics, blockchain, the Internet of Things and smart sensors, robotics, nanotechnology, digital twins, additive manufacturing, and augmented and immersive interfaces. These technologies offer significant potential to enhance food safety, real-time quality monitoring, traceability, operational efficiency, and sustainability, while reducing food waste and strengthening consumer trust. However, their large-scale adoption remains constrained by technical challenges related to, for example, data quality, interoperability, and scalability, as well as economic barriers, regulatory uncertainty, safety concerns, and variable consumer acceptance. By synthesizing recent advances and identifying persistent gaps, this chapter highlights critical considerations for the responsible and effective implementation of Food Packaging 4.0, paving the way for more human-centric, transparent, and resilient packaging strategies in the emerging context of Food Packaging 5.0.s © 2027 selection and editorial matter, Abdo Hassoun; individual chapters, the contributors.

Abstract: Model updating plays an important role in obtaining a more accurate finite element model (FEM) based on measured vibration data. Based on the updated FEM, it is more convenient to carry out further analysis, e.g., structural health monitoring, digital twin, and so on. Bayesian model updating methods are attracting more attention since they can provide rigorous models and evaluate the uncertainty of the updated results. However, in the real application, it still has some problems such as computational efficiency and accuracy. In this paper, a two-stage Bayesian function combined with MCMC algorithm is proposed and used to perform model updating of a real complicated long-span cable-stayed bridge. The two-stage Bayesian function can automatically consider the heteroscedasticity of each utilized modal degree and it allows for incomplete modal information for model updating. Before conducting model updating, two different sensitivity analysis functions are used for local and global sensitivity analysis of bridge model. A set of interaction process between different computation tools has been established to improve computational speed by using an improved stopping criterion. The updated results are demonstrated for both model classes, and ultimately a Bayesian model class evidence was used to judge their superiority. The proposed method was verified by a numerical example and then applied in the updating of the bridge. The experimental results show that the model updating method successfully corrects initial FEMs with reverse mode order errors using incomplete modal information. Simultaneously, the results exhibit a relatively low level of uncertainty. Furthermore, the Bayesian model class selection algorithm proves that new sensitivity analysis functions are superior. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd on behalf of Institution of Structural Engineers.
