Abstract: Nonviral nanocarrier delivery remains a major translational bottleneck for Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)-based genome editing because functional outcome emerges from coupled losses across biodistribution, cell uptake, intracellular trafficking, endosomal escape, access to the relevant cellular compartment, editing and tolerability. This Perspective develops three complementary conceptual tools. The Delivery-Specificity-Toxicity (DST) framework treats formulation design as a constrained multi-objective problem. The Composite Nanobio Delivery Efficiency (CNBDE) framework represents functional delivery as a chain of conditional probabilities rather than a product of statistically independent barriers, with shared formulation and biological variables allowed to alter multiple stages simultaneously. We explicitly distinguish the chain-rule formulation from the simpler independence approximation and clarify that the novelty of CNBDE lies in CRISPR-specific mechanistic decomposition and its linkage to measurable state variables, not in multiplication itself. Heterogeneous literature values are reclassified by evidence maturity instead of being treated as universal cross-platform constants. An explicitly hypothetical in silico stress test is added to demonstrate uncertainty propagation and structural sensitivity; importantly, it shows that the bare multiplicative form cannot by itself prove that any single stage, including endosomal escape, is universally dominant. A worked hepatic Lipid-Nanoparticle (LNP) example, contrasted with lung-targeted LNP studies, illustrates why organ-specific parameterization is required. Finally, the Nanobio Digital Twin System (NB-DTS) is defined as a digital-twin-ready multiscale architecture requiring a biological counterpart, iterative data assimilation, uncertainty-aware state updating, prediction and feedback. CNBDE and NB-DTS remain hypothesis-generating frameworks and require prospective experimental and external validation before predictive or clinical use. © 2026 World Scientific Publishing Company

Abstract: Wireless sensor networks (WSNs) increasingly support sensing-to-decision loops in which the value of a transmission depends on task utility, freshness, uncertainty, privacy, and safety rather than on bit fidelity alone. This article presents a review-led evidence synthesis and, as a secondary contribution, an author-proposed conceptual framework; it does not report a validated control algorithm. The review analyzes a 178-record evidence corpus, complemented by seven separately logged mathematical-outlook references, across WSN and IoT foundations, semantic communication, TinyML and split inference, federated learning, generative AI, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), digital twins, wireless foundation models, and language-model-assisted operations. The supplementary materials release a machine-readable extraction sheet with one row per record, a field codebook, a reference and screening ledger, qualification and completeness audits, and an integrity manifest. A work qualifies as LLM-augmented semantic edge intelligence only when an identifiable large language model (LLM) consumes task-relevant WSN/IoT state or operator intent and can affect sensing, communication, diagnosis, resource allocation, or control through a typed and auditable path. Under this boundary, only one retained work supplies direct E2 simulation evidence of an LLM-mediated communication or control path. Most LLM/RAG evidence is bridging or adjacent and remains at E0–E2. The synthesis therefore distinguishes the roles and maturity of the component technologies instead of treating them as an interchangeable stack. It identifies bounded examples of LLM/RAG utility in communication-policy generation, cross-task networking adaptation, global evidence synthesis, tool orchestration, and natural-language formulation for an external solver. It does not support a general claim of superiority over rules, exact optimization, structured retrieval, or task-specific machine learning and reinforcement learning. To translate the documented gaps into testable requirements, the article proposes an IoT-native reference architecture, a seven-axis taxonomy, a threat model, a formal synthesis and selection/cost model, typed cross-layer interface contracts, and an eight-phase benchmark protocol. These normative artifacts are proposed by the author. They are not established methods extracted from the corpus, consensus standards, a deployable solver or controller, or experimentally validated results. An explicitly hypothetical wildfire-monitoring case makes the formalism inspectable: it defines semantic distortion, normalizes and elicits the penalty weights, evaluates a finite candidate set under hard constraints, applies the non-dominance and LLM-admission rules, reports switch-point sensitivity, and exercises one LLM-to-optimizer interface contract. Its values are tutorial inputs, not measurements. A provenance audit separates cited evidence, author-defined review and coding constructs, conventional notation, and proposed framework artifacts. Each contribution is linked to measurable outcomes and a minimum support condition, but these quantities define future tests rather than imply new performance gains. An LLM is retained only when it closes a declared open-vocabulary or heterogeneous-knowledge capability gap, satisfies hard energy, deadline, privacy, safety, and verifier constraints, and provides positive incremental value over the strongest feasible simpler baseline. Resource-constrained nodes continue to handle sensing, routing, medium access control, and lightweight inference. Grounded LLM/RAG components operate at gateway, edge, cloud, or digital-twin tiers, and their outputs are limited to evidence-linked, tool-checked, reversible proposals. The review remains the evidentiary core; the conceptual framework converts its gaps into falsifiable design and evaluation requirements for future semantic IoT systems. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Title: Toward Self-organizing Production Logistics: A Multi-agent Approach
Source title: IFIP Advances in Information and Communication Technology
Affiliations: KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, 10044, Sweden
Authors with affiliations: Klein J.-F., KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, 10044, Sweden; Jeong Y., KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, 10044, Sweden; Flores-García E., KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, 10044, Sweden; Wiktorsson M., KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, 10044, Sweden
Abstract: Production logistics is increasingly exposed to variability, dynamic interdependencies, and operational disturbances that challenge conventional centralized planning and control approaches. Following a Design Science Research Methodology, this paper establishes a conceptual foundation for the design, implementation, and evaluation of Self-Organizing Production Logistics (SOPL) systems. First, key technological and systemic drivers motivating SOPL are identified, including autonomous logistics resources, advances in distributed AI-based decision-making, and the transition toward circular production systems, which further amplify operational uncertainty and complexity. Based on these drivers, system-level objectives and design requirements for SOPL are derived. Building on these requirements, the paper proposes an initial multi-agent architecture that integrates embodied and non-embodied agents, event-driven coordination, semantic knowledge structures, and digital twins. In addition, a three-phase demonstration roadmap is presented, progressing from an initial laboratory demonstrator toward increasingly distributed and adaptive SOPL systems. The Phase I demonstrator provides an experimental environment for investigating disturbance handling, human involvement, and supervisory coordination within an order-driven kitting and supply scenario. © IFIP International Federation for Information Processing 2027.

Abstract: Gasification provides a flexible route for converting coal, biomass, plastics, and waste-derived feedstocks into syngas, hydrogen, fuels, chemicals, power, and carbon materials. Its modeling and operation remain difficult because feedstock composition, reaction regimes, multiphase transport, reactor configuration, sensor availability, and downstream integration vary simultaneously. Machine learning (ML) has consequently expanded from static performance prediction to CFD surrogate modeling, soft sensing, fault diagnosis, predictive control, digital twins, and sustainability assessment. However, the literature remains dominated by application-specific accuracy reports, and R2, RMSE, and MAE values are often compared without accounting for sample size, data provenance, validation strategy, domain shift, uncertainty, or deployment conditions. This review combines a broad Web of Science corpus of 951 records with a 417-record direct-topic sensitivity subset and a separately screened technical evidence layer. It reorganizes the evidence through a system-level framework linking gasification science, descriptor engineering, task–model matching, trustworthy validation, cyber–physical integration, and sustainability-oriented decision making. Representative studies demonstrate large reductions in surrogate-computation time and credible industrial optimization, but few establish closed-loop deployment. In an adjacent solar-thermochemical membrane-reactor study, a learning-assisted feedforward–feedback controller reduced the control integral error by 82.4%, increased hydrogen recovery and yield by 43% and 33%, respectively, and reduced the input preheat ratio by 30%; these results are informative for controller architecture but are not direct gasification evidence. The review proposes gasification-specific descriptor classes, a task–data–model selection matrix, evidence levels for validation and deployment, and a decision chain coupling uncertainty-aware prediction with scenario evaluation, robust Pareto optimization, risk filtering, governed execution, and feedback learning. The central conclusion is that progress depends less on marginal in-distribution accuracy than on transferable, physically consistent, uncertainty-aware, and governed ML systems that convert predictions into verifiable operating and sustainability decisions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Abstract: The digital twin (DT) of battlefield environment is a cornerstone for real time, high fidelity decision support in modern joint operations. Traditional numerical simulation methods face inherent trade offs between computational speed, accuracy for nonlinear multi scale phenomena, and robust uncertainty quantification. This paper investigates physics informed machine learning as a paradigm to overcome these limitations, focusing on two representative techniques: adaptive physics informed neural networks (PINNs) for underwater acoustic field reconstruction, and graph neural network (GNN) based weather forecasting (GraphCast) for global atmospheric simulation. For underwater acoustics, we analyze an adaptive PINN framework that dynamically balances data fidelity and physics constrained losses, enabling accurate reconstruction of multimodal pressure fields from sparse hydrophone measurements; the method reduces inference time by two orders of magnitude compared to traditional parabolic equation solvers while maintaining relative errors below 5% in complex shallow water environments. For global weather, GraphCast generates 10 day deterministic forecasts at 0.25° resolution in under one minute, outperforming the ECMWF high resolution system in more than 90% of atmospheric variables when verified against operational analyses. A side by side comparison highlights complementary strengths, applicability boundaries, and common challenges including forecast smoothness, bias accumulation, and lack of intrinsic uncertainty quantification. Drawing on recent advances in conformal prediction and adversarial uncertainty quantification, we discuss pathways to produce statistically valid prediction intervals. Finally, we propose a layered simulation architecture for military digital twin environments that integrates global GNN based forecasting with local PINN based high resolution refinement, and we address verification, validation, and accreditation (VV&A) considerations based on DoD and U.S. Navy guidelines. The results demonstrate that physics guided artificial intelligence provides a viable, scalable path toward intelligent, real time battlefield environment digital twins. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Abstract: The increasing complexity of anaerobic digestion processes, characterized by nonlinear biochemical interactions, delayed dynamics, and sensitivity to feedstock variability, necessitates the development of advanced control and prediction systems. This study proposes an adaptive digital twin framework that integrates a physics-based anaerobic digestion model (ADM1) with a data-driven long short-term memory (LSTM) network and a delay-aware model predictive control (MPC) strategy. The proposed framework incorporates an adaptive residual synchronization mechanism that continuously updates the hybrid model parameters based on deviations between simulated and measured methane production, supported by an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) for state estimation. Unlike conventional approaches that treat prediction and control as separate tasks, the proposed framework unifies these components within a single cyberphysical architecture, enabling real-time optimization of methane production. Experimental evaluation based on synthetic ADM1-consistent datasets and validated operational profiles demonstrates improved predictive reliability with an F1-score reaching 0.92 and a methane yield increase of up to 23.4% compared to baseline methods. The results confirm that the integration of temporal learning and predictive control significantly enhances process stability and efficiency under uncertain and time-delayed conditions. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: Digital twin technology enables real-time monitoring and predictive analysis of complex structural systems. However, traditional finite element analysis (FEA) remains computationally expensive for real-time applications, while existing deterministic machine learning models often lack robust uncertainty quantification. This paper presents a Twin-Branch Probabilistic Stress Estimator (TB-PSE) specifically designed for digital twin-enabled large-scale structural static responses analysis, with application to liquid rocket engine frame static testing. The TB-PSE architecture employs a dual-branch neural network structure in which each branch utilizes multi-layer residual connections to independently predict the mean and standard deviation of stress distributions across all structural nodes. By formulating stress prediction as a probabilistic process rather than deterministic estimation, the proposed method captures inherent uncertainties in structural response and provides confidence intervals for critical stress assessments. Experimental validation conducted on a 24-step static test of rocket engine frame structures demonstrates that TB-PSE improves stress-field estimation accuracy while providing uncertainty information for risk-informed assessment of safety–critical aerospace structures. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Jiang D.; Lyu M.; Liu Z.; Wen M.
Title: Knowledge-Driven Parameter Optimization for Combat Experimentation Simulation Models: Evolution, Mechanisms, and Application Prospects
Source title: Communications in Computer and Information Science
Affiliations: Institute of War Studies, Academy of Military Sciences, Beijing, 100091, China; People’s Liberation Army Unit 63677, Xinjiang, Urumqi, 830000, China
Authors with affiliations: Jiang D., Institute of War Studies, Academy of Military Sciences, Beijing, 100091, China, People’s Liberation Army Unit 63677, Xinjiang, Urumqi, 830000, China; Lyu M., Institute of War Studies, Academy of Military Sciences, Beijing, 100091, China; Liu Z., Institute of War Studies, Academy of Military Sciences, Beijing, 100091, China; Wen M., Institute of War Studies, Academy of Military Sciences, Beijing, 100091, China
Abstract: With the transition of combat experimentation from scheme demonstration to intelligent decision support, the computational efficiency and credibility of simulation model parameter optimization have become key bottlenecks in system-of-systems wargaming. Traditional black-box optimization methods face severe challenges, including high computational cost, high-dimensional mixed-variable spaces, and deep battlefield uncertainty. To address these challenges, knowledge-driven parameter optimization integrates military domain knowledge, physical mechanisms, tactical rules, and historical simulation data into the optimization process, thereby reducing ineffective search spaces and improving the feasibility of candidate solutions. This paper systematically reviews knowledge-driven parameter optimization methods for combat experimentation simulation models. First, it clarifies the conceptual boundaries between parameter calibration and parameter optimization, and summarizes a four-stage technological evolution from offline heuristic search to surrogate-assisted optimization, online closed-loop assimilation, and cognitive optimization assisted by large models. Second, it analyzes the core mechanisms of heuristic and evolutionary optimization, high-dimensional Bayesian optimization, multi-fidelity surrogate modeling, physical-prior injection, Kalman-filter-based data assimilation, reinforcement learning, and large-language-model-assisted semantic reasoning. Third, it compares the advantages, limitations, applicable scenarios, and validation requirements of different mechanisms, and summarizes their applications in simulation experiment design, combat entity behavior modeling, system-of-systems effectiveness evaluation, and digital twin battlefield construction. Finally, it discusses future research directions, including multimodal foundation models, simulation resource sharing, heterogeneous multi-task collaborative optimization, and human-machine hybrid cognitive simulation. The review aims to provide a structured reference for method selection and trustworthy application of parameter optimization in combat experimentation simulation. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: Mapping Emerging Trends in Artificial Intelligence for Quality Control and Management: A Large-Scale Computational Literature Review Using Semantic Natural Language Processing

Authors with affiliations: Afassi O., Laboratory of Research and Development in Engineering Sciences, Faculty of Sciences and Techniques Al-Hoceima, Abdelmalek Essaadi University, Tetouan, Morocco; Benaya N., Laboratory of Research and Development in Engineering Sciences, Faculty of Sciences and Techniques Al-Hoceima, Abdelmalek Essaadi University, Tetouan, Morocco; Dib F., Laboratory of Research and Development in Engineering Sciences, Faculty of Sciences and Techniques Al-Hoceima, Abdelmalek Essaadi University, Tetouan, Morocco
Abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence into industrial quality control (QC) and management encompassing automated defect detection, real-time process monitoring, and zero-defect manufacturing has generated a rapidly expanding yet fragmented research landscape. This study addresses the need for comprehensive mapping of quality and reliability engineering practice through a computational systematic review of 9618 publications spanning the 2020–2025 period. A hybrid natural language processing (NLP) pipeline combining FlashText, Sentence-BERT, KeyBERT, and spaCy performs semantic extraction of AI architectures, learning paradigms, defect typologies, and deployment contexts. The review pursues three objectives: mapping the architectural evolution of deep learning in industrial inspection, characterizing operational challenges of AI-driven manufacturing, and identifying methodological frontiers for improving production reliability and supporting intelligent quality assurance (QA) systems. Results reveal that AI-based quality control advances through coevolution of neural architectures, learning paradigms, and deployment requirements. CNNs remain central to discriminative visual inspection, while Transformers extend capabilities for multimodal reasoning. The field exhibits strong bias toward surface defects while overlooking safety-critical internal defects. Emerging trends show transition from algorithm-centric research toward deployment-oriented paradigms including Uncertainty Quantification, Edge AI, Explainable AI, and Digital Twins. This work provides practitioners with an evidence-based foundation for developing reliable, scalable AI quality systems aligned with Industry 4.0 principles. © 2026 John Wiley & Sons Ltd.

Abstract: Accurate modelling of the performance of a vapor-compression cycle across broad operating ranges is essential for the design, optimization and supervisory control of refrigeration systems. But traditional data-driven surrogate models can perform poorly out of training distribution and do not guarantee thermodynamic feasibility. Here we introduce a physics-guided Fourier-transformer surrogate model to model a single-stage vapor-compression cycle with R1234yf and nano-lubricant additives, such as alumina, graphene, and carbon nanotubes. The model leverages Fourier feature lifting for smoother non-linear interactions, Transformer blocks to learn interactions across the four thermodynamic states, and physics-guided soft penalties designed to encourage physically plausible predictions by penalizing violations of output bounds and a prescribed monotonicity prior, without explicitly enforcing the governing thermodynamic conservation equations. To facilitate a systematic evaluation, a Koopman-inspired physics-guided state-space model is also proposed and compared with ANN, PIML, PGML, and PG-FNT models. The novelty of this study lies in its combination of spectral, relational, and physics-guided learning within a single compact architecture and its comparison with a specially designed state-space model under explicit distribution shift testing. To the authors’ knowledge, this combination has not been previously investigated for vapor compression refrigeration systems using nanolubricants with low GWP refrigerants. In the original five-fold cross-validation benchmark, PG-FNT[full] achieved a mean validation RMSE of 0.005202 and MAE of 0.003895, corresponding to reductions of approximately 55.5% and 55.7%, respectively, compared with the conventional ANN baseline under the same evaluation protocol. PG-KSSM also demonstrated competitive predictive performance, achieving up to 28.7% lower RMSE than ANN in the corresponding benchmark. Furthermore, under a high-condenser-temperature operating-envelope shift within the same experimental campaign, PG-FNT achieved a mean R2 of 0.9541 ± 0.0082 across five initialization seeds following few-shot adaptation with 10 labelled observations. Performance was evaluated on a separate 20-sample held-out test set, with no overlap between adaptation and test observations. These findings demonstrate the strong predictive capabilities of the proposed architectures and highlight the effectiveness of limited-data adaptation for maintaining accurate thermodynamic performance prediction under changing operating conditions. This work presents a transferable benchmarking and cross-validation, out-of-dispersion assessment, perturbation analysis, and significance testing protocol applicable to other thermofluidic systems with limited small and noisy datasets for the scientific community. The proposed framework provides a physics-guided, data-driven approach for predicting vapor-compression-cycle performance, demonstrating improved accuracy relative to the evaluated machine-learning baselines. Its comparative performance against conventional thermodynamic cycle solvers remains to be established. Looking ahead, this framework provides a foundation for fault-tolerant digital twins and real-time supervisory control, while the competitive performance of PG-KSSM points to reduced-order, control-oriented thermodynamic models for future closed-loop applications. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: A Broadcasting-Based Approach to Create Distributed Situational Awareness in Construction Projects
Source title: IOP Conference Series: Earth and Environmental Science

Abstract: Construction projects operate as temporary socio-technical systems in which interdependent actors must coordinate under uncertainty, making situational awareness (SA) essential for effective decision-making. Although digital technologies such as BIM, IoT, drones, and digital twins improve data visibility, they often centralise information within hierarchical structures, producing uneven awareness across organisational roles. Existing research largely assumes that improved access to information leads to improved awareness, yet limited attention has been given to how communication practices enable distributed actors to develop aligned understanding. This study examines broadcasting as a communication practice through which interpreted project information is simultaneously disseminated to participants to support distributed situational awareness (DSA). Drawing on a qualitative case study of a digitally enabled construction project, the findings show that awareness depends not only on data availability but also on how interpretations are synchronised through communication structures. Broadcast-oriented practices supported shared comprehension and anticipation by reducing delays associated with sequential reporting while complementing existing digital systems. The study contributes to DSA research by demonstrating how communication architecture shapes the emergence of aligned awareness in temporary project environments and highlights broadcasting as a coordination mechanism for improving collective interpretation in digitally enabled construction projects. © 2026, Published under licence by IOP Publishing Ltd. Abstract: The global ocean carbon sink is a critical component of the Earth’s climate but current ocean models are limited in their predictive capabilities because of the high computational cost that a biogeochemical (BGC) model, required to simulate air-sea CO2 fluxes, entails. Our research investigates the reconstruction of ocean CO2 flux focusing on local physical oceanographic drivers, such as sea surface temperature, salinity, and sea-ice coverage, which are outputs of the simulations conducted with a global ocean BGC model. We frame the flux estimation problem as a temporal sequence problem and evaluate the efficacy of both Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCN) architectures augmented with attention mechanisms. The models ingest eight different physical parameters over a six-month sliding window at each grid point without explicit spatial information, and are designed to identify and weigh the historical physical states that most strongly influence current ocean-atmosphere carbon fluxes. Our framework employs LSTMs to capture sequential dependencies through recurrent hidden states. Moreover, we evaluate TCNs as a distinct alternative that uses dilated convolutions to identify multi-temporal patterns. Besides, we build a probabilistic framework utilizing Gaussian Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) loss to account for aleatoric uncertainty in the dynamical drivers of ocean CO2 flux. To ensure credible reconstructions, we apply Conformal Prediction as a post-hoc calibration layer. This methodology yields calibrated uncertainty intervals with guaranteed 95% coverage. Our results show that for most oceanographic regimes deep temporal models can function as reliable digital twins for point-wise carbon flux estimates. The proposed framework provides a data-driven foundation for reconstruction of air-sea carbon fluxes through an AI emulator built upon dynamic physical parameters. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: A Safety-Aware Agentic LLM–Digital Twin Framework for Fuzzy Multi-Objective Control of Industrial Fed-Batch Bioreactors

Abstract: This study develops a safety-aware supervisory framework for industrial fed-batch bioreactors by integrating an adaptive digital twin, fuzzy multi-objective optimization, Agentic LLM reasoning, and an independent Safety Governor within a closed-loop architecture. The digital twin continuously reconstructs process states and updates sensitive parameters, while α-cut fuzzy intervals preserve biological and operational uncertainty throughout prediction and optimization. The Agentic LLM coordinates prediction, optimization, process knowledge, and candidate evaluation, and supports context-dependent reevaluation and replanning as operating conditions evolve. The framework was evaluated using data from 12 industrial 72 h fed-batch runs, together with 600 uncertainty-aware simulated trajectories. Across three fully independent validation batches, the digital twin achieved an average NRMSE of 4.7%, MAPE of 4.4%, and R2 of 0.985. Closed-loop operation achieved a volumetric productivity of 0.347 g/L·h while maintaining a positive minimum dissolved-oxygen margin of 5 percentage points and zero hard-constraint violations. Across nominal and stressed scenarios, the Safety Governor preserved feasible operation with no residual hard-constraint violations, while the Agentic LLM successfully activated reevaluation and replanning following changes in process conditions. The ablation results further showed that the complete architecture provided the strongest overall balance among productivity, biological risk, robustness, and disturbance recovery. These findings demonstrate the value of combining adaptive process representation, uncertainty-aware optimization, agentic supervisory reasoning, and independent safety validation for reliable intelligent bioprocess operation. © 2026 by the authors.

Abstract: Forest Land Use Intensity (F-LUI) is a multidimensional and dynamic property of forest ecosystems that cannot be directly observed by Remote Sensing (RS). Existing approaches commonly quantify individual management activities, forest attributes or ecological responses and therefore capture only specific dimensions of forest-use intensity. This concept-driven narrative review proposes a trait-based conceptual framework in which forest traits constitute the common observational interface linking anthropogenic forest use, ecosystem responses and RS observations. Based on this principle forest traits and their spatial, temporal and functional expressions are interpreted within six complementary F-LUI indicator families: Trait, Genesis, Structure, Taxonomy, Function and Socio-economics. Rather than defining a universal F-LUI index, the framework provides a multidimensional, sensor-independent architecture for integrating RS with in situ observations, forest inventories, management information and environmental data. Emerging approaches including Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Foundation Models, multi-sensor data fusion, semantic technologies, Knowledge Graphs and Digital Twins may support its operationalisation. Key challenges remain in standardisation, uncertainty quantification, attribution of management effects and transferability across forest types, management regimes and spatial and temporal scales. The proposed framework provides an open and extensible basis for harmonised, reproducible and operational trait-based monitoring of F-LUI. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: From Geometry to Behavior: A Smoothness-Certified Digital-Twin Framework for Information Management, Sustainability, and Resilience in Built Heritage Conservation
Affiliations: International Business School, Qingdao Huanghai University, Qingdao, 266427, China; School of Smart City Engineering, Qingdao Huanghai University, Qingdao, 266427, China

Abstract: Existing heritage digital twins document geometry and monitor condition with high fidelity, but rarely model the behavioral process through which owners, authorities, and peer-exchange networks jointly determine the long-run conservation profile of a historic district, and therefore cannot answer the subsidy-design questions heritage authorities face. This paper supplies that missing behavioral layer. We formalize heritage conservation credit systems (indivisible credits, capped holdings, balanced aggregate stock) as a matching model and establish four analytical guarantees for twin operation: predictions exist, are unique, are globally stable, and vary continuously differentiably with policy parameters. Global stability acts as a resilience certificate, guaranteeing recovery from any shock within roughly twenty annual cycles, and smoothness bounds prediction uncertainty in closed form. These certificates are properties of the behavioral engine, established analytically; they are not claims about field-validated operation. A three-layer architecture embeds the engine behind a state-synchronization loop that re-estimates behavioral parameters from registry observables at a cadence set by the data source rather than by the model; in a controlled in silico sensing experiment the synchronized twin reduces post-disruption tracking error by 71% relative to a static twin, and a window-length sweep shows the loop dominates the static twin by 62–71% at every cadence tested. Calibrated to a traditional village in the Mount Tai Piedmont and verified against an agent-based Monte Carlo counterpart, the twin yields three model-dependent policy results: a subsidy trap (higher subsidy rates activate conservation exchange yet reduce steady-state top-tier counts), the dominance of within-tier cooperation over cross-tier mentorship, and an inverted-U sustainability frontier locating Mount Tai villages in the under-funded regime. All outputs consolidate into a single HBIM-compatible information-management deliverable. We report the framework as a specified and in-silico-verified behavioral twin whose sensing interfaces await field deployment, and we state explicitly which components remain conceptual. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Digital Twin Construction and Simulation Technologies for Urban Organism; [城市生命体数字孪生构建与模拟推演技术框架]
Affiliations: Department of Electronic Engineering, Tsinghua University, Beijing, 100084, China; School of Architecture, Tsinghua University, Beijing, 100084, China
Authors with affiliations: Zhou Z., Department of Electronic Engineering, Tsinghua University, Beijing, 100084, China; Lin Y., School of Architecture, Tsinghua University, Beijing, 100084, China; Jin D., Department of Electronic Engineering, Tsinghua University, Beijing, 100084, China; Tian L., School of Architecture, Tsinghua University, Beijing, 100084, China; Li Y., Department of Electronic Engineering, Tsinghua University, Beijing, 100084, China
Abstract: [Significance] As a complex organism characterized by self-organization, metabolism, and adaptive evolution, a city exhibits highly systematic and dynamic behaviors in both its operation and long-term development. With rapid urbanization and increasing system complexity, contemporary cities are confronted with persistent and intertwined challenges, such as environmental degradation, traffic congestion, resource imbalance, and public safety risks. Traditional urban governance paradigms, which often rely on static planning and reactive interventions, are increasingly inadequate for addressing these non-linear and multi-scale urban problems. This situation calls for a fundamental shift toward a full life-cycle governance paradigm that treats the city as an integrated and evolving organism. Digital twin technology, serving as a bridge between the physical city and its virtual counterpart, offers a promising technical pathway for realizing such a paradigm. By enabling continuous interaction between real-world observations and computational models, digital twins provide new possibilities for finegrained perception, system-level understanding, and proactive governance. Against this background, this paper focuses on digital twin technologies from the perspective of the urban organism, aiming to establish a methodological foundation that supports perception, understanding, inference, and decision-making throughout the entire life cycle of future urban organisms. [Analysis] This paper systematically analyzes the core functionalities and development pathways of digital twins for urban organisms, with a particular focus on urban modeling, operational simulation, and intelligent decision-making. First, acknowledging the inherent incompleteness and uncertainty of urban data, we explore data completion strategies based on Bayesian inference and graph diffusion models. These approaches enable the reconstruction of missing or sparse observations and support the construction of digital twin models that span multiple interconnected subsystems of the urban organism. Second, to capture the coupled dynamics of physical infrastructure and social behaviors, we integrate dynamic system models with agent-based simulation methods, and propose a co-simulation mechanism that enables coordinated modeling of physical and social urban elements. This mechanism is designed to be continuously updated through real-time monitoring data, ensuring consistency between simulated states and real-world urban conditions. Furthermore, to support the early warning and governance of urban diseases, we introduce a spatiotemporal foundational modeling approach for urban indicator prediction and counterfactual inference. This approach allows different governance strategies to be simulated, evaluated, and iteratively optimized within the digital twin environment before real-world implementation. [Prospect] From the perspective of the urban organism, this study establishes a systematic technical framework and research approach for urban digital twins that goes beyond static physical mapping. By emphasizing data completion, multi-system co-simulation, and predictive inference, the proposed framework aims to enhance the capability of digital twins to support perception, understanding, inference, and decision-making across the full life cycle of urban governance. This work provides methodological insights for developing next-generation urban digital twins that are better aligned with the complexity, dynamics, and evolutionary nature of real cities. © 2026, Science Press. Title: Cyber-Resilient Digital Twin Architectures for Smart Grids: A Review of Attack Modeling, Detection, Mitigation, and Secure Control Strategies
Affiliations: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, The https://ror.org/04wn28048University of Tulsa, Tulsa, 74104, OK, United States
Authors with affiliations: Ogiesoba-Eguakun O.C., Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, The https://ror.org/04wn28048University of Tulsa, Tulsa, 74104, OK, United States; Rath S., Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, The https://ror.org/04wn28048University of Tulsa, Tulsa, 74104, OK, United States
Abstract: The digitalization of smart grids has expanded the cyberattack surface of critical energy infrastructure, creating a need for security mechanisms that integrate communication behavior, physical-system dynamics, and resilient control. Digital twins provide a promising foundation for this integration, but existing research remains fragmented across system architectures, threat models, defense methods, and validation environments. The aim of this review is to identify, classify, and critically compare how cyber-resilient DT architectures support the smart-grid cybersecurity lifecycle across DT architecture, cyber–physical attack modeling, detection and mitigation, secure control and recovery, and experimental validation. A structured multi-database search of Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and the ACM Digital Library identified 1627 records. After duplicate removal, publication-type exclusions, and eligibility assessment, 149 publications were retained for thematic synthesis and quality appraisal. The evidence indicates that a qualifying cyber-resilient digital twin is distinguished not merely by the presence of a virtual model, but by bidirectional physical–virtual synchronization combined with explicit cyber-resilience functions. Cyberattack studies span measurement, communication, control, device and infrastructure, and coordinated attack surfaces, although study-specific assumptions regarding attacker access and compromised interfaces frequently limit direct comparison. Physics-based detectors offer strong interpretability and real-time suitability but remain sensitive to model and topology errors, whereas data-driven methods capture complex attack patterns but depend on representative data and may generalize poorly. Federated learning preserves data locality but introduces privacy, poisoning, and communication concerns, while moving target defense and deception provide complementary proactive capabilities. No detection or mitigation strategy is uniformly superior across attack coverage, interpretability, false-alarm behavior, latency, scalability, and computational burden. DT-enabled secure control and self-healing further require safety-constrained mitigation under detection uncertainty, communication delay, model mismatch, and partially compromised information. Validation is dominated by simulation, with comparatively little hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) or utility-scale field evidence. Key research gaps include inconsistent digital twin terminology, limited benchmark datasets, synchronization and model-fidelity challenges, inadequate interoperability, and insufficient validation of autonomous mitigation. This review contributes an integrated taxonomy and decision-oriented framework for evaluating and selecting cyber-resilient digital twin strategies for smart grids. © 2026 by the authors.

Abstract: Anaerobic fermentation converts crop residues, livestock manure, and other agricultural wastes into energy-rich products, particularly methane and hydrogen, simultaneously enabling waste treatment and resource recovery. However, stable operation and industrial scale-up remain difficult because feedstock properties, microbial metabolism, fluid behavior, and mass transfer vary continuously throughout fermentation. Their interactions generate nonlinear, time-varying, and multiscale dynamics that are difficult to observe, predict, and regulate using conventional methods. This review synthesizes progress in modeling and intelligent control for the anaerobic fermentation of agricultural wastes, with particular attention to biochemical hydrogen production. The reviewed advances are organized around a hierarchical data-mechanism-control framework that connects process characterization, hybrid modeling, online estimation, optimization, and system-level decision support. First, the review examines heterogeneous data generated during feedstock characterization, pretreatment, reactor operation, microbial conversion, and product formation. Laboratory and pilot-scale datasets are often sparse, noisy, imbalanced, and dependent on specific feedstocks or reactor configurations. Second, the review compares major modeling strategies and clarifies their respective roles. Random forests and support vector machines are effective for modeling feedstock characteristics and pretreatment responses, whereas artificial neural networks and long short-term memory networks are capable of capturing nonlinear relationships and temporal dependencies. Gaussian process regression supports uncertainty analysis under limited data, while transfer learning can reuse information across related feedstocks or operating scenarios. Despite these capabilities, purely data-driven models may generate unreliable predictions outside their training domains and may violate conservation laws, thermodynamic constraints, or microbial kinetics. Mechanistic models, including anaerobic digestion model No. 1 (ADM1), provide interpretable process descriptions but require extensive calibration and may inadequately represent complex slurry transport and microbial succession. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) provide a gray-box modeling approach by embedding conservation relationships and microbial kinetic equations into the learning objective. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), particularly SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), complements this approach by identifying influential variables, interactions, inhibitory conditions, and potential process thresholds. These tools can translate model outputs into operationally meaningful evidence for process diagnosis and control, although their reliability under practical operating conditions remains to be validated in reactors treating agricultural wastes. Third, the review links hybrid modeling to closed-loop process control. Internet of things (IoT) sensor networks and edge computing can support local filtering, drift correction, feature extraction, communication management, and rapid fault detection. Soft sensors can estimate difficult-to-measure state variables, including volatile fatty acids, chemical oxygen demand, alkalinity, and microbial activity, from readily available online measurements. Multi-objective optimization and model predictive control (MPC) can then balance gas productivity, process stability, and energy consumption while satisfying equipment and safety constraints. At the system level, digital twins integrate biochemical kinetics, computational fluid dynamics, sensor data, equipment models, and scenario simulation. Nevertheless, applications in agricultural waste fermentation remain largely conceptual or limited to individual components because biological and hydrodynamic processes are difficult to couple efficiently. Future research should prioritize standardized multimodal databases, shared biochemical and hydrodynamic model libraries, adaptive hybrid models, robust sensing, uncertainty-aware control, and integrated device-edge-cloud architectures. Progress in these areas can advance interpretable prediction, resilient process operation, and reliable bioenergy recovery, thereby supporting the digital and intelligent transformation of agricultural waste management systems. © 2026 Chinese Society of Agricultural Engineering. Abstract: Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) is transitioning from a predictive flow-simulation technique into a central enabling technology for the design, intensification, scale-up, and digitalization of catalytic reactors. This review critically synthesizes advances reported across fixed-bed, packed-bed, fluidized-bed, trickle-bed, slurry bubble-column, monolithic, membrane, and microreactor systems, spanning chemical, petrochemical, environmental, and energy applications. Rather than treating reactor configurations and numerical methods independently, the review establishes a multiscale framework linking hydrodynamics, heterogeneous reaction kinetics, porous-media transport, heat and mass transfer, radiation, catalyst-scale phenomena, and reactor-scale performance. Particular emphasis is placed on the evolving integration of Large Eddy Simulation, Direct Numerical Simulation, Population Balance Models, artificial intelligence, Physics-Informed Neural Networks, digital twins, and high-performance computing. Their capabilities are critically compared in resolving conversion, selectivity, pressure drop, thermal gradients, species transport, catalyst utilization, and multiphase interactions, with explicit consideration of the trade-offs among predictive fidelity, computational cost, scalability, and industrial relevance. The influence of turbulence closure, mesh resolution, reaction-mechanism complexity, reactor geometry, boundary conditions, parameter uncertainty, and experimental validation on model credibility is systematically assessed. Key unresolved barriers include multiscale coupling, catalyst deactivation, numerical stiffness, uncertainty propagation, computational expense, and reliable scale-up from laboratory reactors to industrial systems. Emerging opportunities in AI-assisted CFD, GPU-accelerated simulation, uncertainty-aware modelling, autonomous optimization, and continuously updated digital twins are critically evaluated. The review ultimately proposes a pathway toward physics-informed, data-augmented, and decision-oriented CFD frameworks capable of accelerating the development of safer, more efficient, flexible, and sustainable catalytic reactor systems. © 2026 the author(s), published by De Gruyter, Berlin/Boston 2026.

Title: Smart drying systems: machine learning, digital twins, soft sensors, and predictive control (2021–2025)

Abstract: Smart drying has emerged as a research field that combines drying science, sensing, process systems engineering, and artificial intelligence. This review critically synthesizes a deliberately bounded 2021–2025 evidence corpus to assess the recent technological maturity of machine learning, digital twins, soft sensors, and predictive control in food, agricultural, biomass, and pharmaceutical drying. Using a screened Scopus-based evidence base, the article evaluates predictive modeling, sensing and inferential state estimation, optimization and control, representative implementation cases, and application-specific deployment. The synthesis indicates that moisture and drying-kinetics prediction are among the most mature components, whereas cross-product generalization, uncertainty-aware validation, industrial deployment, closed-loop control, and dynamically synchronized digital-twin operation remain less consistently demonstrated. The review distinguishes digital monitoring, digital shadows, and validated digital-twin operation; identifies implementation levels from laboratory prediction to pilot and operational control; and analyzes practical barriers including scale-dependent nonuniformity, sensor fouling, calibration drift, domain shift, latency, actuator constraints, maintenance, interoperability, and economic burden. Overall, progress depends on validated, transferable, maintainable, and control-relevant architectures rather than algorithmic accuracy alone. This journal is © The Royal Society of Chemistry, 2026.

Abstract: High-performance computing (HPC) workflows for partial differential equations (PDEs) often require repeated simulations over many initial conditions, boundary conditions, or physical parameters. Although a single high-fidelity solve may be tractable on modern computing systems, large ensembles, optimization loops, uncertainty quantification studies, and digital-twin applications can make the aggregate computational cost substantial. This study presents a neural operator augmented with dynamic mode decomposition (DMD). The architecture combines a DeepONet-style branch–trunk mapping with additional branches that encode DMD modes and modal dynamics. The resulting model is intended as a trajectory-informed surrogate: DMD features are computed from states available before the prediction point and the subsequent state is reserved as the target. The method is evaluated for the Laplace, heat, and Burgers equations on 64×64 grids. On the heat benchmark, controlled five-seed comparisons include DeepONet, a parameter-matched DeepONet, FNO, and a KNO-style baseline; a capacity-controlled input ablation additionally evaluates the contribution of the DMD inputs without changing the trainable parameter count. Computational measurements separate classical solution time, DMD preprocessing, training, and network inference. The trained network has low evaluation latency, while case-specific DMD preprocessing dominates the present end-to-end path. Thus, the results support DMD-NO as a structured operator-learning approach for trajectory-conditioned prediction and identify modal preprocessing as the principal target for future parallel optimization, without claiming an end-to-end speedup over the classical solver. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: GAN-enhanced digital twins for biomarker-guided cancer immunotherapy and adoptive cell therapy: a mini review
Affiliations: Shandong University of Technology, Shandong, Zibo, China
Authors with affiliations: Yang J., Shandong University of Technology, Shandong, Zibo, China
Abstract: Cancer immunotherapy and adoptive cell therapy have transformed modern oncology, yet durable benefits remain limited by tumor heterogeneity, immune escape mechanisms, biomarker variability, and the dynamic remodeling of the tumor immune microenvironment. Current biomarker strategies, including PD-L1 (programmed death-ligand 1) expression, microsatellite instability (MSI), tumor mutational burden (TMB), immune gene signatures, liquid biopsy measurements, and target antigen profiles, provide clinically useful information but are often static and insufficient to capture longitudinal tumor–immune–therapy interactions. Digital twin technology offers a computational paradigm for integrating multi-omics, immune profiling, clinical variables, imaging, and treatment-response data into patient-linked virtual models. Generative artificial intelligence, including generative adversarial networks (GANs), may enrich sparse biomarker-defined state spaces and support the simulation of underrepresented treatment response or toxicity trajectories. This mini review critically compares mechanistic quantitative systems pharmacology, spatial and agent-based modeling, data-driven prediction, and emerging digital twin approaches and proposes a platform-agnostic architecture that can be implemented in MATLAB/Simulink or other computational environments. The adoptive cell therapy scope focuses on chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T), chimeric antigen receptor natural killer cell (CAR-NK), and T-cell receptor-engineered T-cell (TCR-T) therapies, with related principles applicable to tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy. We describe conditional and longitudinal GAN strategies, dynamic tumor–immune state modeling, biomarker integration, validation metrics, governance, and prospective implementation pathways. The proposed framework is conceptual and has not yet been clinically validated; synthetic data are treated as methodological support rather than clinical evidence. Its intended near-term uses are hypothesis generation, virtual-cohort enrichment, trial design, and uncertainty-aware decision support. Copyright © 2026 Yang.

Title: Toward reliable physics-informed neural networks under degradation uncertainty: An implicit-volume framework for dynamic modeling of gas turbine engines
Affiliations: The Key Laboratory of Power Machinery and Engineering of Education Ministry, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, 200240, China; Shanghai Jiao Tong University Sichuan Research Institute, Chengdu, 610213, China
Authors with affiliations: Jia X., The Key Laboratory of Power Machinery and Engineering of Education Ministry, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, 200240, China; Zhou D., The Key Laboratory of Power Machinery and Engineering of Education Ministry, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, 200240, China, Shanghai Jiao Tong University Sichuan Research Institute, Chengdu, 610213, China
Abstract: Accurate dynamic modeling of gas turbine engines under real-operating conditions is important for digital-twin assessment and system monitoring. Traditional component-level models rely on repeated nonlinear iterations for dynamic simulation, while standard physics-informed neural networks may suffer robustness degradation when ideal physical priors are inconsistent with degradation-affected data. To overcome this limitation, this paper proposes the Implicit Volume Physics-Informed Neural Network (IVP-PINN) to improve dynamic modeling reliability for gas turbine engines under degradation uncertainty. First, a statistical error-tolerance mechanism employing a divergence metric relaxes the zero-residual constraint imposed on the flow-matching relation of the non-degraded reference model, thereby accommodating degradation-induced model mismatch without relaxing the physical mass-conservation law. Second, an implicit-volumetric architecture considering unsteady wave coupling utilizes neural network nonlinear mapping to bypass traditional iterative solvers. This simultaneously substantially reduces the computational cost and preserves authentic volumetric hysteresis effects. Validations under diverse transient disturbances and actual operational data show that IVP-PINN closely captures complex trajectories. Within the validated outside-training degradation range of [−10%, −6%), 87.75% of healthy-state predictive performance was retained at −10%. Compared with PI-LSTM, PINN, and MLP, IVP-PINN reduces peak MaxAE by 58.5%, 71.2%, and 68.0%. The proposed IVP-PINN shows potential for digital-twin dynamic assessment of gas-turbine systems. Title: Dynamic Bayesian network for aircraft wing health monitoring digital twin

Authors with affiliations: Li C., Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, 37235, TN, United States; MahaDeVan S., Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, 37235, TN, United States; Ling Y., GE Global Research Center, Niskayuna, 12309, NY, United States; Choze S., GE Global Research Center, Niskayuna, 12309, NY, United States; Wang L., GE Global Research Center, Niskayuna, 12309, NY, United States
Abstract: Current airframe health monitoring generally relies on deterministic physics models and ground inspections. This paper uses the concept of a dynamic Bayesian network to build a versatile probabilistic model for diagnosis and prognosis in order to realize the digital twin vision, and it illustrates the proposed method by an aircraft wing fatigue crack growth example. The dynamic Bayesian network integrates physics models and various aleatory (random) and epistemic (lack of knowledge) uncertainty sources in crack growth prediction. In diagnosis, the dynamic Bayesian network is used to track the evolution of the time-dependent variables and calibrate the time-independent variables; in prognosis, the dynamic Bayesian network is used for probabilistic prediction of crack growth in the future. This paper also proposes a modification to the dynamic Bayesian network structure, which does not affect the diagnosis results but reduces the time cost significantly by avoiding Bayesian updating with load data. By using a particle filter as the Bayesian inference algorithm for the dynamic Bayesian network, the proposed approach handles both discrete and continuous variables of various distribution types, as well as nonlinear relationships between nodes. Challenges in implementing the particle filter in the dynamic Bayesian network, where 1) both dynamic and static nodes exist and 2) a state variable may have parent nodes across two adjacent networks, are also resolved. © 2016 by the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Inc.

Title: Near real-time probabilistic damage diagnosis using surrogate modeling and high performance computing
Affiliations: NASA Langley Research Center, Durability, Damage Tolerance, and Reliability Branch, Hampton, 23666, VA, United States; Old Dominion University, Computer Science Department, Norfolk, 23665, VA, United States

Abstract: This work investigates novel approaches to probabilistic damage diagnosis that utilize surrogate modeling and high performance computing (HPC) to achieve substantial computational speedup. Motivated by Digital Twin, a structural health management (SHM) paradigm that integrates vehicle-specific characteristics with continual in-situ damage diagnosis and prognosis, the methods studied herein yield near real-time damage assessments that could enable monitoring of a vehicle’s health while it is operating (i.e., online SHM). High-fidelity modeling and uncertainty quantification (UQ), both critical to Digital Twin, are incorporated using finite element method simulations and Bayesian inference, respectively. The crux of the proposed Bayesian diagnosis methods, however, is the reformulation of the numerical sampling algorithms (e.g., Markov chain Monte Carlo) used to generate the resulting probabilistic damage estimates. To this end, three distinct methods are demonstrated for rapid sampling that utilize surrogate modeling and exploit various degrees of parallelism for leveraging HPC. The accuracy and computational efficiency of the methods are compared on the problem of strain-based crack identification in thin plates. While each approach has inherent problem-specific strengths and weaknesses, all approaches are shown to provide accurate probabilistic damage diagnoses and several orders of magnitude computational speedup relative to a baseline Bayesian diagnosis implementation. © 2017, American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics Inc, AIAA. Title: Agrizero: An O2O adversarial framework and triangulation for agricultural forecasting
Source title: IOP Conference Series: Materials Science and Engineering

Authors with affiliations: Chen Y.J., Department of Logistics Management, National Kaohsiung University of Science and Technology, Kaohsiung, Taiwan
Abstract: This study proposes an online to offline (O2O) learning framework, ArgiZero, based on three components: a generative adversarial network, an online auction market, and offline simulated agents (digital twins: buyers, farmers, natures, and markets). The generative time series and digital twins are massively generated in a manner of Monte Carlo but with extremely efficient algorithms. The goal of the generator is to produce time series that are statistically indistinguishable with the records from auction market. The goal of the discriminator is to develop a triangulation method based on semi-modeless assimilation to separate generated from actual time series. Most farmers believe agriculture is impossible to be planned because uncertainty, crowding, crisis, and risk cannot be foreseen and accommodated. This AgriZero framework alleviates the challenges through the techniques of Bayesian deep learning and data assimilation as well as the mega power of GPU computation. Thanks to Bayesian hierarchical estimation, which is akin to deep learning but more sophisticate and longer history. We are able to estimate human behaviour in the agents of buyers and farmers, natural disaster in the agents of natures, and price fluctuations in the agents of markets. The framework has been validated by a large amount of records in vegetable auctions of Taiwan and USA. The hierarchical Bayesian estimation and Monte Carlo Markov Chain particle filters used in hidden Markov model are appreciated during the massive construction of the most probable digital twins. The feature space mapping in wavelet time series, Bayesian deep learning in recurrent neural network, kernel induced Hamiltonian dynamics ABC, and hybrid SDE-kernel based forecasting for time series analysis embodies the particle generator in the GAN structure. We also apply time series clustering, RNN, bagging and boosting, and semi-modeless assimilation to assist the performance of the triangulated discriminator. © Published under licence by IOP Publishing Ltd.

Title: Process compensated resonance testing (PCRT) inversion for material characterization and digital twin calibration
Affiliations: Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL/RXCA), Wright-Patterson AFB, OH, United States; Vibrant Corporation, Albuquerque, NM, United States; Computational Tools, Gurnee, IL, United States; University of California, Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA, United States

Abstract: The Digital Twin paradigm is based on the idea that a component's serviceable life and performance can be better predicted and monitored by creating a faithful virtual counterpart of a real component, which in turn leads to improvements in end-product safety and cost. Such a model requires accurate inputs for the initial material state of the part as well as in-service loads and damage states throughout its service life. The resonance frequencies of a part correlate to a part's material state and damage state. Similarly, changes in resonance frequencies correlate to changes in the part's material state resulting from in-service loads and damage. Process Compensated Resonance Testing (PCRT) leverages these physical relationships to perform nondestructive evaluation (NDE) and material characterization using the measured resonance frequencies of a component. Prior work has established techniques for modeling the effects of material property variation, crystal orientation, and damage states on resonance, as well as quantifying uncertainty propagation from model inputs to outputs. This study examines the use of PCRT model inversion to obtain material properties and calibrate digital twins of real components. Digital twin instances were first created for a population of single crystal Nickel-base superalloy samples using dimension and mass measurements. Then, after collecting resonance spectra from the physical counterparts, model inversion techniques were employed to estimate elastic properties and crystal orientation for each part. The digital twins were then calibrated with the model inversion output. These digital twins were subsequently validated by comparing the inversion results to resonance and x-ray diffraction measurements on a statistically significant population of physical specimens. The results highlight the value of part-specific material properties for digital twin performance, as well as the ability of PCRT to evaluate and improve digital twin fidelity. © 2019 Author(s).

Title: Dealing with Uncertainty in Software Architecture on the Internet-of-Things with Digital Twins
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science (including subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics)
Affiliations: IRISA – UMR CNRS 6074, University Bretagne Sud, Vannes, France
Authors with affiliations: Oquendo F., IRISA – UMR CNRS 6074, University Bretagne Sud, Vannes, France
Abstract: When architecting Software-intensive Systems-of-Systems (SoS) on the Internet-of-Things (IoT), architects face two sorts of uncertainties. First, they have only limited knowledge about the operational environment where the SoS will actually be deployed. Second, the constituent systems which will compose the SoS might not be known a priori (at design-time) or their availability (at run-time) is affected by dynamic factors, due to the openness of the IoT. The consequent research question is thereby how to deal with uncertainty in the design of an SoS architecture on the IoT. To tackle this challenging issue, this paper addresses the notion of uncertainty due to partial information in SoS and proposes an enhanced SoS Architecture Description language (SosADL) for expressing SoS architectures on the IoT under uncertainty. The core SosADL is extended with concurrent constraints and the concept of digital twins coupling the physical and virtual worlds. This novel approach is supported by an integrated toolset, the SosADL Studio. Validation results demonstrate its effectiveness in an SoS architecture for platooning of self-driving vehicles. © 2019, Springer Nature Switzerland AG.

Affiliations: College of Systems Engineering, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, 410073, China
Authors with affiliations: Wang P., College of Systems Engineering, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, 410073, China; Yang M., College of Systems Engineering, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, 410073, China; Peng Y., College of Systems Engineering, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, 410073, China; Zhu J., College of Systems Engineering, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, 410073, China; Ju R., College of Systems Engineering, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, 410073, China; Yin Q., College of Systems Engineering, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, 410073, China
Abstract: Since the submarine has become the major threat to maritime security, there is an urgent need to find a more efficient method of anti-submarine warfare (ASW). The digital twin theory is one of the most outstanding information technologies, and has been quite popular in recent years. The most influential change produced by digital twin is the ability to enable real-time dynamic interactions between the simulation world and the real world. Digital twin can be regarded as a paradigm by means of which selected online measurements are dynamically assimilated into the simulation world, with the running simulation model guiding the real world adaptively in reverse. By combining digital twin theory and random finite sets (RFSs) closely, a new framework of sensor control in ASW is proposed. Two key algorithms are proposed for supporting the digital twin-based framework. First, the RFS-based data-assimilation algorithm is proposed for online assimilating the sequence of real-time measurements with detection uncertainty, data association uncertainty, noise, and clutters. Second, the computation of the reward function by using the results of the proposed data-assimilation algorithm is introduced to find the optimal control action. The results of three groups of experiments successfully verify the feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed approach. © 2019 by the authors.

Title: Cardiovascular models for personalised medicine: Where now and where next?

Abstract: The aim of this position paper is to provide a brief overview of the current status of cardiovascular modelling and of the processes required and some of the challenges to be addressed to see wider exploitation in both personal health management and clinical practice. In most branches of engineering the concept of the digital twin, informed by extensive and continuous monitoring and coupled with robust data assimilation and simulation techniques, is gaining traction: the Gartner Group listed it as one of the top ten digital trends in 2018. The cardiovascular modelling community is starting to develop a much more systematic approach to the combination of physics, mathematics, control theory, artificial intelligence, machine learning, computer science and advanced engineering methodology, as well as working more closely with the clinical community to better understand and exploit physiological measurements, and indeed to develop jointly better measurement protocols informed by model-based understanding. Developments in physiological modelling, model personalisation, model outcome uncertainty, and the role of models in clinical decision support are addressed and ‘where-next’ steps and challenges discussed. © 2019 IPEM

Abstract: As one of the important development directions of "Made in China 2025", remanufacturing plays a huge role in resource recycle, reducing energy consumption and promoting transformation and upgrading of manufacturing. As a new technology, digital twin can fully connect and integrate the physical world and information world in real time, and can effectively promote the integration of informationization and industrialization in the shop-floor. Aiming at the uncertainties in the process of remanufacturing and the situation that information space of virtual remanufacturing and actual remanufacturing process can't be interactively integrated in real time, the digital twin was applied into the remanufacturing operation process, and the architecture for digital twin-based remanufacturing shop-floor was constructed. This architecture and it's operation paradigm were elaborated respectively, the application analyses for key technologies involved was made, and the remanufacturing operation paradigm for automobile based on digital twin in future was also explored. The application prospects for digital twin-based remanufacturing in related fields were discussed. © 2019, Editorial Department of CIMS. All right reserved.

Abstract: Aiming at the three typical problems in solid rocket motor design such as the separation of solid rocket motor design and simulation, the separation of numerical simulation and physical tests and the difficulty of data unmeasurable, uncertainty and incompletely in ground tests, and to innovate the traditional experience based and semi-experience based mode of solid motor design, a concept system of digital twin of solid rocket motor was established. The digital twin of solid rocket motor was defined from the view of process, model and data. On this basis, a 5-layer architecture model of the digital twin in the design stage of solid rocket motor was established and illustrated. The connotation of each layer was explained, as well as the relationship between layers. According to the conception of process twinning, model twinning and data twinning, the operation mechanism of digital twin was discussed. The formal description of process twinning, model twinning and data twinning was presented. The characteristic of digital twin was analyzed, the possible application method of digital twin in solid rocket design was discussed, and the preliminary realization scheme was given, which provided theoretical reference for future application. © 2019, Editorial Department of CIMS. Abstract: Under the small batch and customized production mode, the complex and dynamic production environment caused by uncertainty of resources and processes requires higher control accuracy for operation and control of large multi-unit systems. It is a key challenge for process control of large multi-unit production logistics system that how to accurately model and real-time reflect the execution status of production unit and implement the adaptive, iterative and accurate management and control of system to support the efficient collaborative operation of each segment through multi-unit online synchronized decision-making. By taking the real-time synchronized operation of typical industrial park system composed of three typical units of production, transportation and storage as the research object, and under the Digital Twin (DT) framework, the cross-unit synchronized decision-making information architecture was proposed to implement the online synchronized control of large system through the dynamic and precise mapping and real-time feedback control of "physical environment-virtual model". Meanwhile, the Analytical Target Cascading (ATC) method was adopted to synchronize and control the system systematically in the mode of global optimization and distributed control. By taking the multi-unit synchronized production process of a large chemical production enterprise as an example, the synchronized decision-making model and ATC quantitative synchronized method were simulated, compared and analyzed based on the actual production data. The results showed that the proposed method could effectively realize the multi-unit synchronized operation and reduce the total production cost and the in-stock time of orders. © 2019, Editorial Department of CIMS. Abstract: To solve the problem of electro-optical system for its performance monitoring, a digital twin model based on Dynamic Bayesian Network (DBN) was proposed. In this model, a system-level performance indicator from the perspective of energy domain using Modulation Transfer Function (MTF) was developed, which avoided tedious modelling of performance interactions between the multiple subsystems of electro-optical system. DBN was constructed from the evolution of MTF to denote the dynamic performance degradation process and the propagation of epistemic uncertainty. To make the digital twin model capable of tracking and predicting the system performance states, Particle Filter (PF) was proposed as the inference algorithm for DBN. A real dataset collected in the laboratory environment was used to validate the feasibility of the digital twin model and verify the effectiveness of PF inference algorithm. The results showed that the proposed method was effective for joint estimation of states and parameters, and the prediction of electro-optical system on-line health-status was achieved. © 2019, Editorial Department of CIMS. Title: Resource-efficient sensor data management for autonomous systems using deep reinforcement learning
Affiliations: Department of Software, Sungkyunkwan University, Suwon, 16419, South Korea; Department of Mathematics, Sungkyunkwan University, Suwon, 16419, South Korea
Authors with affiliations: Jeong S., Department of Software, Sungkyunkwan University, Suwon, 16419, South Korea; Yoo G., Department of Mathematics, Sungkyunkwan University, Suwon, 16419, South Korea; Yoo M., Department of Mathematics, Sungkyunkwan University, Suwon, 16419, South Korea; Yeom I., Department of Software, Sungkyunkwan University, Suwon, 16419, South Korea; Woo H., Department of Software, Sungkyunkwan University, Suwon, 16419, South Korea
Abstract: Hyperconnectivity via modern Internet of Things (IoT) technologies has recently driven us to envision “digital twin”, in which physical attributes are all embedded, and their latest updates are synchronized on digital spaces in a timely fashion. From the point of view of cyberphysical system (CPS) architectures, the goals of digital twin include providing common programming abstraction on the same level of databases, thereby facilitating seamless integration of real-world physical objects and digital assets at several different system layers. However, the inherent limitations of sampling and observing physical attributes often pose issues related to data uncertainty in practice. In this paper, we propose a learning-based data management scheme where the implementation is layered between sensors attached to physical attributes and domain-specific applications, thereby mitigating the data uncertainty between them. To do so, we present a sensor data management framework, namely D2WIN, which adopts reinforcement learning (RL) techniques to manage the data quality for CPS applications and autonomous systems. To deal with the scale issue incurred by many physical attributes and sensor streams when adopting RL, we propose an action embedding strategy that exploits their distance-based similarity in the physical space coordination. We introduce two embedding methods, i.e., a user-defined function and a generative model, for different conditions. Through experiments, we demonstrate that the D2WIN framework with the action embedding outperforms several known heuristics in terms of achievable data quality under certain resource restrictions. We also test the framework with an autonomous driving simulator, clearly showing its benefit. For example, with only 30% of updates selectively applied by the learned policy, the driving agent maintains its performance about 96.2%, as compared to the ideal condition with full updates. © 2019 by the authors.
